unique.title: Deleted-page chain is never linked into the header free list when a safepoint flushes the chain's tail page, permanently leaking every page freed by a large transaction
unique.mech: DeletePage builds the transaction's deleted-page list by prepending, so LastDeletedPageID is the *first* page ever deleted in the transaction. The only code that publishes that list is TransactionService.PersistDirtyPages (TransactionService.cs:175-185), and it does so opportunistically: it links `page.NextPageID = _header.FreeEmptyPageList; _header.FreeEmptyPageList = _transPages.FirstDeletedPageID;` only while iterating a page whose PageID equals LastDeletedPageID, at commit time. That page is only iterated if it is still dirty and still present in the snapshot's _localPages at commit. A safepoint destroys that precondition: TransactionService.Safepoint (TransactionService.cs:115) calls PersistDirtyPages(false), which writes the Empty page to the log and calls TakeBuffer(), then calls Snapshot.Clear() (SnapShot.cs:127) which empties _localPages. The page is never re-read or re-dirtied (it is Empty, off every free list, and _header.FreeEmptyPageList still points at pages from earlier transactions, so TryAllocateFreePage will not touch it). At commit, GetWritablePages therefore never yields it, the link is skipped, and _header.FreeEmptyPageList stays unchanged even though the header *is* rewritten (HeaderChanged is true because DeletedPages > 0). The Empty pages are confirmed on disk and reachable by pageID but unreachable from the free list, so no future allocation can reuse them. Consequence is silent permanent loss of reusable file space, not data corruption.
unique.fail: Insert 200k documents, then `col.DeleteMany(x => true)` (or engine Delete over 200k ids) in one auto-transaction. TransactionSize passes MaxTransactionSize (1000, Constants.cs:82 via MemoryProfileDefaults Balanced) within the first few hundred documents, so Safepoint fires and flushes the first-deleted page — which is LastDeletedPageID. At commit, PersistDirtyPages(true) finds no page matching LastDeletedPageID, so _header.FreeEmptyPageList is left at its old value and the ~tens of thousands of freed data/index pages are orphaned. Re-inserting the same 200k documents then extends the file instead of reusing them (NewPage falls through TryAllocateFreePage to ++_header.LastPageID), so the .db file grows without bound across insert/delete cycles and `SELECT * FROM $database` reports freeEmptyPageID unchanged. A delete small enough to stay under 1000 pages behaves correctly, which is why tests do not catch it.
unique.fix: Do not depend on the tail page still being resident at commit. Either keep the tail page pinned/dirty for the lifetime of the transaction, or perform the header splice unconditionally at commit time (under lock(_header)): read/patch the recorded log position of LastDeletedPageID from _transPages.DirtyPages and set _header.FreeEmptyPageList = _transPages.FirstDeletedPageID whenever DeletedPages > 0.
unique.rationale: The deleted-page chain is linked into the header free list only if the chain's tail page is still dirty in _localPages at commit, which a Safepoint destroys - so any delete larger than MaxTransactionSize permanently orphans its freed pages. Silent unbounded file growth across insert/delete cycles, recoverable only by Rebuild.

unique.title: IndexService.DropIndex frees index nodes but never reclaims the pages, permanently leaking them from the file
unique.mech: Every other node-removal path calls `_snapshot.AddOrRemoveFreeIndexList(page, ref index.FreeIndexPageList)` after `DeleteIndexNode` (see DeleteSingleNode, line 297), which is what moves a page between free-list buckets and, when ItemsCount reaches 0, calls Snapshot.DeletePage -> MarkAsEmtpy + links the page into `_transPages.FirstDeletedPageID` so that TransactionService.PersistDirtyPages joins it onto `_header.FreeEmptyPageList` at commit. DropIndex bypasses this entirely: it deletes every node of the dropped index (and its head/tail) directly through the page, so the pages end the transaction with ItemsCount == 0, PageType still Index, a stale PageListSlot/Prev-Next chain, and no entry in the deleted-page list. LiteEngine.DropIndex then calls CollectionPage.DeleteCollectionIndex(name), discarding Head/Tail/FreeIndexPageList, so nothing references those pages any more. They are never returned to the header free list and are not discoverable by Snapshot.DropCollection either (it enumerates index pages only through FindAll over the still-registered indexes, SnapShot.cs:675-691), so even dropping the collection afterwards does not reclaim them.
unique.fail: Insert 1,000,000 documents into a collection and `EnsureIndex("name", "$.name")` (say ~25,000 index pages, ~200 MB), then `DropIndex("name")`. The 25,000 pages stay allocated: LastPageID never decreases, FreeEmptyPageList does not grow, so subsequent inserts extend the file instead of reusing them, and the space is unrecoverable without a full Rebuild. Repeating EnsureIndex/DropIndex in a loop grows the data file without bound even though logical content is unchanged.
unique.fix: In the node-deletion loop and for the head/tail nodes, call `_snapshot.AddOrRemoveFreeIndexList(node.Page, ref index.FreeIndexPageList)` after each DeleteIndexNode (as DeleteSingleNode does) so emptied pages are marked empty and enqueued in the transaction's deleted-page list.
unique.rationale: DropIndex deletes nodes straight through the page and never calls AddOrRemoveFreeIndexList/DeletePage, so every page the index owned stays allocated, empty and unreachable - not even a later DropCollection reclaims it. Canonical of the pair; repeated drop/recreate cycles grow the file without bound.

unique.title: Snapshot local page cache is keyed only by pageID and cast unchecked, so a page first fetched as BasePage throws InvalidCastException when later fetched as DataPage/IndexPage
unique.mech: _localPages stores BasePage instances keyed by pageID with no record of the concrete type they were materialised as. The concrete type is chosen by BasePage.ReadPage<T> at first load (SnapShot.cs:260). A later GetPage<T> for the same pageID with a *narrower* T performs a plain reference cast on the cached instance, which throws InvalidCastException because a `BasePage` object is not a `DataPage`/`IndexPage`/`VectorIndexPage`. Two callers load pages as bare BasePage into a snapshot that is also used for typed access: (a) SysPageList.GetList (LiteDB/Engine/SystemCollections/SysPageList.cs:85 and :106) walks every collection's FreeDataPageList and FreeIndexPageList with snapshot.GetPage<BasePage>(...) on a Read snapshot created for that *user* collection (SysPageList.cs:54), and that snapshot is registered in TransactionService._snapshots under the collection name and reused by any later operation in the same transaction (TransactionService.cs:84-99); (b) Snapshot.TryAllocateFreePage (LiteDB/Engine/Services/Snapshot.FreePages.cs:17) loads the header free-list head as BasePage and, in its auto-heal branch (FreePages.cs:28-33, taken when the head is not Empty), leaves that BasePage in _localPages instead of removing it, so a live page of this same collection stays cached under the wrong type for the rest of the transaction. The failure is an unhandled InvalidCastException escaping mid-transaction, not a clean LiteException.
unique.fail:
var col = db.GetCollection("docs"); col.Insert(many docs); db.BeginTrans(); db.Execute("SELECT * FROM $page_list").ToList(); // SysPageList creates the Read snapshot for "docs" and caches all of its data pages as BasePage instances
col.FindAll().ToList(); // QueryExecutor.CreateSnapshot(LockMode.Read, "docs", false) reuses that same snapshot; IndexService.GetNode -> GetPage<IndexPage>(pageID) or DataService.Read -> GetPage<DataPage>(address.PageID) hits the cached BasePage and throws System.InvalidCastException: "Unable to cast object of type 'LiteDB.Engine.BasePage' to type 'LiteDB.Engine.DataPage'"
The same crash occurs for a write snapshot on a database whose header free-list head points at a live page of that collection (the corrupt/legacy case FreePages.cs:30 explicitly tolerates): the stale BasePage entry then makes the next GetPage<DataPage>/<IndexPage> on that pageID throw, defeating the auto-heal it was added for. (Confidence is medium only for reachability of the $page_list sequence; the cast mechanism itself is certain.)
unique.fix: Make the local cache type-aware: in GetPage<T>, if the cached instance is not assignable to T, either re-wrap the existing PageBuffer as T and replace the dictionary entry, or throw LiteException.InvalidPageType; and have TryAllocateFreePage remove the probe page from _localPages in the non-Empty branch (and after handing its buffer to CreatePage<T>).
unique.rationale: The cast mechanism is certain (_localPages is keyed only by pageID and cast unchecked), but the author rates reachability of the $page_list-then-query sequence only medium. A maintainer should confirm the snapshot really is reused across SysPageList and a later typed GetPage before reworking the cache.

unique.title: Document/Array comparison silently drops the Collation argument, so nested strings are always compared ordinally
unique.mech: `CompareTo(BsonValue, Collation)` forwards Document and Array to `this.AsDocument.CompareTo(other)` / `this.AsArray.CompareTo(other)` — the single-argument overload. BsonDocument and BsonArray override only `CompareTo(BsonValue)` (BsonDocument.cs:65, BsonArray.cs:122) and never the collation overload, and internally recurse via `this[key].CompareTo(other[key])`, which re-enters the single-argument overload and therefore Collation.Binary (line 551). The configured collation is thus discarded for every value nested inside a document or array key, even though the caller (IndexService, SortService, Collation.Compare) passed it explicitly.
unique.fail: Database with collation `en-US/IgnoreCase`. `EnsureIndex("meta", "$.meta", unique: true)`. Insert `{_id:1, meta:{n:"abc"}}` then `{_id:2, meta:{n:"ABC"}}`. IndexService.AddNode calls `rightNode.Key.CompareTo(key, _collation)`; the Document case drops `_collation`, so "abc" vs "ABC" is compared ordinally -> non-zero -> the unique constraint is NOT violated and both documents are indexed. A later `SELECT $ FROM c WHERE meta = {n:'ABC'}` uses `collation.Equals` at the top level but the nested compare is again ordinal, so which of the two duplicate rows (if any) is found becomes order-dependent. The same drop makes `ORDER BY meta` ignore the database culture while `ORDER BY meta.n` honours it.
unique.fix: Add `public override int CompareTo(BsonValue other, Collation collation)` to BsonDocument and BsonArray that threads the collation into every nested `CompareTo(value, collation)` call (as Engine/Sort/SortKey.cs:43 already does), and have the base switch call those overloads.
unique.rationale: The Document/Array arms of CompareTo(value, collation) drop the collation and recurse through the binary-collation overload, so nested strings are always ordinal - a unique index on a document field silently accepts collation-duplicate keys. Same root cause as [64]/[66]/[103], narrower path.

unique.title: MIN/MAX compare with hard-coded ordinal collation, disagreeing with the database collation and ORDER BY
unique.mech: MIN/MAX call `value.CompareTo(min)`, the single-argument overload, which is hard-coded to `this.CompareTo(other, Collation.Binary)` (LiteDB/Document/BsonValue.cs) — invariant culture with CompareOptions.Ordinal. The engine's real collation is `_pragmas.Collation`, default `Collation.Default` = current LCID with CompareOptions.IgnoreCase (LiteDB/Utils/Collation.cs:44, LiteDB/Engine/EnginePragmas.cs:39), and it is passed into the expression (`groupBy.Select.ExecuteScalar(cache, null, null, _pragmas.Collation)`, LiteDB/Engine/Query/Pipeline/GroupByPipe.cs:198). MIN/MAX simply have no Collation parameter, so they silently ignore it, while indexes, ORDER BY and equality filters all honour it. The method-resolution code supports a leading `Collation` parameter (BsonExpressionParser.cs:941), so this is an omission, not a platform limit.
unique.fail: Default collation (e.g. en-US/IgnoreCase), collection with `{name:'apple'}` and `{name:'Banana'}`. `SELECT $.name FROM col ORDER BY $.name LIMIT 1` returns 'apple' (culture-aware, case-insensitive), but `SELECT MIN($.name) FROM col` compares ordinally ('B'=0x42 < 'a'=0x61) and returns 'Banana'. Both are reported as correct results; MIN/MAX therefore contradict the database's own ordering, and a GROUP BY report built on MIN/MAX disagrees with the same data sorted by the index.
unique.fix: Add a leading `Collation collation` parameter to MIN/MAX (as DOUBLE/DECIMAL/DATETIME already do) and call `value.CompareTo(min, collation)`.
unique.rationale: MIN/MAX have no Collation parameter and use the binary-collation CompareTo, so they contradict ORDER BY and the indexes on the same data. Wrong aggregate value, but confined to MIN/MAX.

unique.title: Equals/GetHashCode contract violation: values that compare equal hash differently, breaking Distinct() over index keys
unique.mech: `Equals` is defined as `CompareTo(other) == 0`, which deliberately treats different numeric BsonTypes as equal (line 561-564) and compares documents/arrays/binaries structurally. `GetHashCode` mixes in `this.Type` and `this.RawValue.GetHashCode()`, so (a) Int32(1), Int64(1), Double(1.0) and Decimal(1m) are all Equals-equal but hash differently because Type differs, and (b) two structurally equal BsonDocuments/BsonArrays/byte[] hash by the reference identity of their underlying Dictionary/List/array. `EqualityComparer<BsonValue>.Default` resolves to the IEquatable path, so LINQ hash-based operators silently fail to deduplicate. BsonExpression.GetIndexKeys (LiteDB/Document/Expression/BsonExpression.cs:222) relies on exactly that: `return this.Execute(doc, collation).Distinct();`, and is the sole key source for Insert.cs:80, Update.cs:133 and Index.cs:66.
unique.fail: `EnsureIndex("list", "$.list[*]")` (non-unique) and insert the document `{ "list": [ {"a":1}, {"a":1} ] }` (two distinct BsonDocument instances with identical content, e.g. from JsonSerializer.Deserialize). GetIndexKeys yields both; `Distinct()` hashes them into different buckets (different Dictionary references) so neither is dropped, and Insert adds TWO index nodes with keys that compare equal, both pointing at the same DataBlock. `SELECT $ FROM c WHERE list = {a:1}` then goes through IndexEquals, which yields the found node and walks forward while `Key.CompareTo(_value, collation) == 0` (IndexEquals.cs:42), returning the SAME document twice. With `unique: true` the second AddNode instead throws IndexDuplicateKey for a document that contains only one logical value. The equivalent numeric case is `{ "list": [1, 1.0] }` (Int32 1 and Double 1.0 from JSON).
unique.fix: Make GetHashCode agree with Equals: hash numeric types through a single canonical representation (and omit Type for the numeric family), and hash documents/arrays/binaries structurally over their contents — or stop defining Equals as CompareTo==0 and keep value equality type-strict.
unique.rationale: Equals is CompareTo==0 while GetHashCode mixes in Type and RawValue's reference hash, so GetIndexKeys' Distinct() fails to dedupe: duplicate index nodes with equal keys (duplicate rows returned) or a spurious IndexDuplicateKey on a unique index. Needs a multikey index over structurally equal or cross-type-numeric elements.

unique.title: ReadDocument/ReadArray accept an out-of-range BSON length prefix and silently return an empty document instead of reporting corruption
unique.mech: `length` is read verbatim from disk and `end = _position + length - 5` is computed with unchecked int arithmetic. A valid BSON document always has length >= 5, but nothing validates that: for length in 0..4 `end` lands at or below the current position, and for length near int.MaxValue `_position + length` overflows to a negative value. In both cases the `while (_position < end)` element loop is skipped entirely, `MoveForward(1)` consumes one byte, and the method returns a *successful* `Result<BsonDocument>` wrapping an empty document. No exception is produced, so the `GetValue()` calls in DatafileLookup.cs:33, BsonSerializer.cs:41, Engine/Index.cs:59 and HeaderPage.cs:147 all see a clean result. The same arithmetic exists in ReadArray at line 443.
unique.fail: A data block whose first four bytes are zero (a partially written page, a torn write, or an externally corrupted file) is read by DataService.Read -> DatafileLookup.Load -> reader.ReadDocument(_fields).GetValue(): length = 0 -> end = _position - 5 -> loop body never runs -> returns `{}`. col.FindAll() then yields an empty BsonDocument for that row (and `doc["_id"]` is BsonNull) as if it were a legitimate document, instead of surfacing LiteException.InvalidDatafileState. The same input with length = 0x7FFFFFFF overflows `end` negative and produces the identical silent empty document.
unique.fix: Validate the prefix before use: require `length >= 5` and `length - 5 <= remaining readable bytes`, and compute `end` in long arithmetic (or use checked), throwing LiteException.InvalidDatafileState otherwise.
unique.rationale: An out-of-range BSON length prefix makes `end` land at or below the position and the method returns a successful empty document, so a torn page surfaces as a legitimate-looking `{}` row instead of InvalidDatafileState. Silent but requires corrupt input.

unique.title: AesStream derives its blank-page sentinel from an uninitialized ArrayPool buffer, silently disabling zeroed-page detection
unique.mech: `_decryptedZeroes` must hold AES-ECB-Decrypt(16 zero bytes) so that `Read()` (line 183) can recognise a page whose ciphertext is physically all-zero and hand back a blank page, which `PageBuffer.IsBlank()` (LiteDB/Engine/Structures/PageBuffer.cs:96) then lets WalIndexService skip (WalIndexService.cs:204 and :326). The 16 ciphertext bytes fed to the decryptor come from `msBuffer = _bufferPool.Rent(16)` (line 65) and are never zeroed. `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent` explicitly does not guarantee zero-filled contents; it hands back whatever the previous renter left there (LiteDB always returns with clearArray:true, but the pool is process-wide and shared with the host app and the BCL, and `Rent(12)` in BufferReader/BufferWriter uses the same 16-byte bucket). Upstream LiteDB used `new byte[16]`, which is always zeroed; the pooled rent is a fork change (commit 49f1b48 region, present since the fork import).
unique.fail: Host process (e.g. an ASP.NET/Npgsql/System.Text.Json workload) has previously returned a dirty 16-byte array to ArrayPool<byte>.Shared. A LiteDatabase with a password is opened: `_decryptedZeroes` becomes Decrypt(garbage) instead of Decrypt(0^16). The log file contains a physically zeroed page (exactly the state this mitigation exists for - a grown/torn write). DiskService.ReadFull(FileOrigin.Log) -> AesStream.Read decrypts the zero page into pseudorandom bytes, `IsBlank` returns false, so the page is NOT blanked; WalIndexService.RestoreIndex (line 204) sees IsBlank()==false and reads pageID/isConfirmed/transactionID out of pseudorandom bytes. A random transactionID is registered as confirmed and CheckpointInternal (line 326) copies that garbage page into the data file at pageID*PAGE_SIZE - corrupting a live data page or exploding the file size - or the open aborts with an unrelated 'invalid page type' LiteException. The same file opens cleanly in another process where the pool happens to return a zeroed array, so the failure is non-reproducible.
unique.fix: Use `new byte[16]` (as upstream does) for the ciphertext source, or `Array.Clear(msBuffer, 0, 16)` before wrapping it in the MemoryStream.
unique.rationale: _decryptedZeroes is derived from an ArrayPool rent that is never zeroed, so the blank-page sentinel can be wrong and RestoreIndex/CheckpointInternal then parse an all-zero page as real. Cross-process-nondeterministic, which makes it nasty, but it needs a dirty shared-pool buffer plus a physically zeroed page. Canonical of three reports.

unique.title: Key derivation uses Rfc2898DeriveBytes defaults: 1000 PBKDF2 iterations with HMAC-SHA1
unique.mech: `new Rfc2898DeriveBytes(password, salt)` selects the ctor defaults - 1000 iterations and HMAC-SHA1 (this overload is obsoleted as SYSLIB0041 on the net8.0/net10.0 targets precisely because of that default). Current guidance is ~600k-1.3M iterations for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1, so offline guessing against a LiteDB file is roughly three orders of magnitude cheaper than it should be. The verification block makes each guess trivially checkable: bytes 32..64 decrypt to 0x01 repeated (line 143), a perfect offline oracle requiring one AES block decryption per candidate key.
unique.fail: An attacker copies an encrypted .db file. For each candidate password they run 1000 HMAC-SHA1 iterations over the 16-byte salt read from file offset 1..17 and decrypt one block at offset 32, checking for 0x01 bytes. On commodity GPU hardware this is billions of candidates per hour, so a typical 8-character human password is recovered in hours; at 600k iterations the same search would take years.
unique.fix: Use the (password, salt, iterations, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256) overload with a modern iteration count, and persist the iteration count/algorithm in the salt page for forward compatibility.
unique.rationale: Rfc2898DeriveBytes ctor defaults (1000 iterations, HMAC-SHA1) plus an in-file verifier make offline password recovery roughly three orders of magnitude cheaper than current guidance. A tunable hardening parameter rather than a bypass, hence medium against [57].

unique.title: LiteFileStream.Flush/Write dereference the null write buffer on read-mode streams
unique.mech: `_buffer` is only allocated for FileAccess.Write streams (LiteFileStream.cs:42). Neither `Flush()` nor `Write()` checks `_mode`, so on a stream returned by OpenRead they run straight into `_buffer.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin)` (line 36) and throw NullReferenceException. Stream's contract says Flush on a read-only stream is a no-op, and Write on a stream with CanWrite==false should be NotSupportedException (which Read does check for, LiteFileStream.Read.cs:14).
unique.fail: `using (var s = db.FileStorage.OpenRead(id)) using (var gz = new GZipStream(s, CompressionMode.Decompress)) { ...; gz.Flush(); }` - or any wrapper/pipeline that flushes the source stream, or a direct `s.Flush()` - throws NullReferenceException from deep inside LiteDB instead of being a no-op. Likewise `storage.OpenRead(id).Write(buf, 0, 10)` throws NullReferenceException rather than NotSupportedException.
unique.fix: Make Flush() a no-op when `_mode != FileAccess.Write` and have Write() throw NotSupportedException in read mode.
unique.rationale: _buffer is allocated only for write-mode streams and neither Flush nor Write checks _mode, so a defensive Flush on an OpenRead stream NREs where Stream's contract requires a no-op, and Write NREs instead of NotSupportedException. Canonical of the pair.

unique.title: Restoring the CHECKPOINT pragma before engine close can disable the shutdown checkpoint and discard the in-memory WAL
unique.mech: `Dispose` restores the original CHECKPOINT value and only then disposes the engine. `LiteEngine.Close()` performs the shutdown checkpoint only `if (_header?.Pragmas.Checkpoint > 0)` (LiteDB/Engine/LiteEngine.cs:191-195). When the header's original CHECKPOINT was 0, the restore sets it back to 0 *before* Close, so (a) the shutdown checkpoint is skipped entirely and (b) the header page written by the restore transaction itself is stranded in the log. Because this constructor path has no LogStream, `EngineSettings.CreateLogFactory()` falls through to `new StreamFactory(new MemoryStream(), ...)` (LiteDB/Engine/EngineSettings.cs:162) — the log is volatile, so everything not yet checkpointed is lost when the process drops the object. The forced CHECKPOINT=1 does not guarantee eager flushes either, because `CommitAndReleaseTransaction` uses `WalIndexService.TryCheckpoint()`, which returns 0 without checkpointing whenever `_transaction.IsReadLockHeld || CurrentReadCount > 0` (LiteDB/Engine/Services/LockService.cs:118-121).
unique.fail: A database file whose header already carries CHECKPOINT=0 (set by an earlier session via `db.CheckpointSize = 0`) is reopened as `new LiteDatabase(File.Open(path, FileMode.Open, FileAccess.ReadWrite))`. The constructor forces CHECKPOINT=1 and remembers 0. A worker thread is iterating a long `Find(...)` result (holding a transaction read lock) while another thread inserts and commits documents; each commit's `TryCheckpoint()` returns 0 because of the open reader, so those pages stay in the MemoryStream log. On `db.Dispose()` the pragma is restored to 0, `Close()` sees `Checkpoint == 0` and skips the shutdown checkpoint, and the committed inserts are silently gone from the data file. In the benign single-threaded case the user's CHECKPOINT=0 setting is itself silently lost and the file comes back as CHECKPOINT=1.
unique.fix: Do not restore the pragma before close. Either leave the forced value in place for the session and restore it only after a guaranteed `_walIndex.Checkpoint()` (blocking, not Try), or keep the override out of the persisted header entirely so Close's `Checkpoint > 0` test still reflects the forced value.
unique.rationale: Restoring CHECKPOINT=0 before Close() makes Close skip the shutdown checkpoint, and with the volatile MemoryStream log that silently discards committed pages TryCheckpoint could not flush. Same five lines as [133]; kept separate because the fix (ordering/ownership of the override) differs from the try/finally fix.

unique.title: LiteQueryable.Into() permanently leaves Query.Into set, so reusing the queryable re-inserts the whole result set
unique.mech: `Into` writes `_query.Into` / `_query.IntoAutoId` into the shared mutable `Query` instance and never clears them, unlike `Count()`/`LongCount()`/`Exists()`, which carefully save and restore `_query.Select` in a `finally`. `QueryExecutor.ExecuteQuery()` dispatches purely on `_query.Into != null` (LiteDB/Engine/Query/QueryExecutor.cs:57-64), so every later execution of the same `LiteQueryable` (or of any other queryable sharing the `Query` object handed out by `Select`/`GroupBy`, which return a new wrapper over the *same* `_query`) re-runs the INTO insert. The reader returned by `ExecuteQueryInto` is `new BsonDataReader(result)` holding a BsonInt32, so `ToDocuments()`'s `reader.Current as BsonDocument` yields `null` (LiteQueryable.cs:299) and `ToEnumerable()` then calls `_mapper.Deserialize(typeof(T), null)`, which dereferences the null argument at BsonMapper.Deserialize.cs:109.
unique.fail:
```
var q = col.Query().Where(x => x.Year == 2024);
var copied = q.Into("archive_2024");   // 5 000 docs copied
var rows   = q.ToList();               // intended: read the same 5 000 docs
```
`ToList()` silently inserts the 5 000 documents into `archive_2024` a **second time** (duplicating the archive, or failing with a duplicate-key LiteException once auto-ids collide), then throws NullReferenceException out of BsonMapper.Deserialize instead of returning rows.
unique.fix: Save and clear `_query.Into`/`_query.IntoAutoId` in a `try/finally` the way `Count()` handles `_query.Select`, and make `ToDocuments()` throw a descriptive error instead of yielding `null` when `reader.Current` is not a document.
unique.rationale: Into() permanently sets Query.Into on the shared mutable Query, so reusing the queryable silently re-inserts the whole result set and then NREs in BsonMapper.Deserialize. Duplicate writes plus a confusing crash; needs queryable reuse.

unique.title: LiteRepository disposes a caller-supplied ILiteDatabase it does not own, and never null-checks it
unique.mech: `Dispose(bool)` calls `_db.Dispose()` unconditionally, with no flag distinguishing the three self-created databases (string/ConnectionString/Stream constructors) from `LiteRepository(ILiteDatabase database)`, where the database is injected and owned by the caller. There is no ownership flag anywhere in the class. `LiteDatabase.Dispose` closes the engine, after which every subsequent engine entry point fails `_state.Validate()`. The same constructor also skips the `ArgumentNullException` guard that every other constructor in the file (and in `LiteDatabase`) performs, so a null database surfaces as a NullReferenceException from an unrelated call site.
unique.fix: Add a `readonly bool _disposeDatabase` set to true only in the constructors that create the LiteDatabase, and gate `_db.Dispose()` on it (mirroring `LiteDatabase._disposeOnClose`); add `?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(database))` in the injecting constructor.
unique.rationale: Dispose unconditionally disposes an injected ILiteDatabase with no ownership flag, so one scoped repository closes a DI singleton database for the whole application. Plus the missing null guard on that ctor.

unique.title: Min<K>/Max<K> throw NullReferenceException when the extreme key is a BSON null and K is a non-nullable value type
unique.mech: `TryGetAggregateValue` (lines 203-221) runs `Query().OrderBy(keySelector).Select(keySelector).ToDocuments().FirstOrDefault()`. For a document that has no value for the key, the query pipe wraps `ExecuteScalar`'s BsonNull into `{ <field>: null }` (LiteDB/Engine/Query/Pipeline/QueryPipe.cs:100), and BSON null sorts lowest, so it is the *first* row for `Min`. `TryGetAggregateValue` therefore returns `true` with `value = BsonValue.Null`. `BsonMapper.Deserialize` returns a CLR `null` for a null BsonValue (LiteDB/Client/Mapper/BsonMapper.Deserialize.cs:109), so `result == null` but `hasValue == true`, the `default(K)` short-circuit on line 161 is skipped, and `return (K)result` compiles to `unbox.any !K` — unboxing a null reference into a value type throws NullReferenceException. Commit a302aed ("Distinguish empty aggregates from stored null") replaced the previous `return result == null ? default(K) : (K)result;`, which was safe, so this is a regression.
unique.fix: If `result == null` and `typeof(K)` is a non-nullable value type, either return `default(K)` (restoring the old contract) or throw an explicit `LiteException`/`InvalidCastException` naming the field and type — never let a null unbox.
unique.rationale: Min<K> over a collection where the extreme key is BSON null returns hasValue=true with a null result, and `(K)result` unboxes null into a value type - NRE from a read-only query, a regression from the previous default(K) return. Narrow to schema-evolved/partial documents.

unique.title: EnsureIndex silently reports success for a name already taken by a vector index, so no B-tree index is created
unique.mech: CollectionPage._indexes holds both B-tree indexes (IndexType 0) and vector indexes (IndexType 1) - see CollectionPage.InsertVectorIndex (Pages/CollectionPage.cs:218-240), which stores a CollectionIndex with indexType 1 in the same dictionary. EnsureIndex's existence check (GetCollectionIndex(name)) does not filter on IndexType, so a vector index with the same name and the same expression source makes EnsureIndex return false as though a B-tree index already existed. EnsureVectorIndex does perform the reverse check (Index.cs:124-127: `if (existing != null && existing.IndexType != 1) throw LiteException.IndexAlreadyExist(name)`), so the asymmetry is clearly unintended. QueryOptimization.cs:242 filters candidate indexes with `.Where(x => x.IndexType == 0)`, so the vector entry is never usable as a B-tree index.
unique.fail: col.EnsureIndex("embedding", "$.embedding", new VectorIndexOptions(4, VectorDistanceMetric.Cosine)) creates a vector index named 'embedding'. A later col.EnsureIndex("embedding", "$.embedding") returns false with no error, and no B-tree index exists: queries filtering on $.embedding fall back to a full collection scan with no diagnostic. Worse, the caller's subsequent col.DropIndex("embedding") - believing it is dropping the B-tree index it thinks it created - takes the IndexType == 1 branch (Index.cs:191-202) and destroys the vector index instead.
unique.fix: Add `if (current.IndexType != 0) throw LiteException.IndexAlreadyExist(name);` before the expression comparison, mirroring the guard in EnsureVectorIndex.
unique.rationale: The existence check does not filter IndexType, so a name taken by a vector index makes EnsureIndex report success while no B-tree index exists (queries silently full-scan), and the caller's DropIndex then destroys the vector index. EnsureVectorIndex performs the reverse check, so the asymmetry is clearly unintended.

unique.title: HeaderPage.LoadPage() replaces the Pragmas instance, orphaning the reference LockService and SortDisk captured at engine open, so later PRAGMA changes are silently ignored
unique.mech: `LiteEngine` captures the pragma object once at open time: `_locker = new LockService(_header.Pragmas)` (LiteDB/Engine/LiteEngine.cs:139) and `_sortDisk = new SortDisk(..., _header.Pragmas)` (line 151); both store it in a readonly field and read `_pragmas.Timeout` / `_pragmas.UtcDate` / `_pragmas.Collation` on every use. `HeaderPage.Restore(savepoint)` calls `LoadPage()`, which does `this.Pragmas = new EnginePragmas(_buffer, this)` — a brand-new object. From that point on `_header.Pragmas` and `LockService._pragmas` are two different instances. `LiteEngine.Pragma(name, value)` mutates the header's current instance (`h.Pragmas.Set(name, value, true)`, LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Pragma.cs:33), so the update never reaches the lock service or the sort disk.
unique.fail: A commit that changes the header (create/drop/rename collection) hits an IO error while writing the log — `TransactionService` line 393 runs `_header.Restore(safepoint)` and rethrows. The application catches the error and continues. The user then issues `PRAGMA TIMEOUT = 5`. `_header.Pragmas` (the post-restore instance) records 5 s and persists it to the header, and `SELECT * FROM $database` reports timeout = 5, but `LockService` keeps reading the orphaned pre-restore instance and still waits the old 60 s on every `EnterTransaction`/`EnterWrite`/`EnterExclusive`. The same applies to `PRAGMA UTC_DATE` versus `SortDisk`/`SortService`. The reverse path exists too: `Snapshot.NewPage` restores the header when `_reader.NewPage()` throws (SnapShot.cs:407).
unique.fix: Make the pragma object identity stable for the life of the HeaderPage: keep a single `EnginePragmas` and give it a `Reload(BufferSlice)` that re-reads each pragma in place (mirroring the `EnginePragmas(BufferSlice, HeaderPage)` ctor body), and call that from `LoadPage()` when `this.Pragmas` already exists instead of allocating a replacement.
unique.rationale: HeaderPage.LoadPage replaces the Pragmas instance that LockService and SortDisk captured at open, so after any header Restore later PRAGMA TIMEOUT/UTC_DATE changes are persisted and reported but never honoured. Silent divergence between reported and effective configuration.

unique.title: Upsert always runs a full-graph BFS to locate the node, making bulk insert O(N^2) and allocating a queue proportional to 32*N per operation
unique.mech: There is no dataBlock -> node mapping, so Delete (line 57) resolves the node by BFS over the whole reachable graph from metadata.Root. Upsert (line 42) unconditionally calls Delete before Insert (line 53), including for brand-new documents that have no node — in that case the BFS necessarily visits every node in the index before returning false. Each visit is a Snapshot.GetPage plus a Snapshot.Safepoint (line 525), so a safepoint (dirty-page flush + local page cache clear) can be triggered once per visited node. The queue is filled without a membership pre-check (unlike ClearTree at line 568), so up to MaxLevels*MaxNeighborsPerLevel = 32 entries per node are buffered: the queue can hold ~32N addresses. SelectNewRoot (line 448) has the identical pattern.
unique.fail: Insert 50,000 documents into a collection carrying one vector index (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Insert.cs:92 calls Upsert per document). Document k's insert BFSes the k-1 existing nodes, so the run performs ~1.25e9 node reads and a comparable number of Safepoint calls, turning a seconds-long bulk load into hours; at N = 1,000,000 nodes the transient BFS queue alone holds ~32M PageAddress entries (hundreds of MB) for every single insert or delete.
unique.fix: Skip the Delete probe on the insert path (the engine already knows whether the document is new), and give the index a dataBlock -> node lookup (e.g. a slot in the existing _id index node chain, as b-tree indexes use) instead of a graph-wide BFS. Also pre-check `visited` before Enqueue in TryFindNode and SelectNewRoot.
unique.rationale: Upsert unconditionally BFSes the whole reachable graph before inserting, with a Safepoint per visited node and no membership pre-check on the queue, making bulk load O(N^2) with ~32N queued addresses. Turns a seconds-long load into hours; real cost, no incorrectness.

unique.title: External vector payloads are written as non-extend DataBlocks in the collection's data pages, so Rebuild/Recovery parses raw float bytes as BSON documents
unique.mech: StoreVector reuses the collection's data pages for out-of-page vectors and passes extend = (bytesWritten > 0), so the FIRST block of every external vector is marked extend = false — the exact marker DataBlock uses for "start of a document" (LiteDB/Engine/Structures/DataBlock.cs:14, P_EXTEND). FileReaderV8.GetDocuments (LiteDB/Engine/FileReader/FileReaderV8.cs:113) enumerates every slot of every data page whose ColID matches the collection (LoadDataPages, line 277), skips only blocks with extend == true (line 168), concatenates the block chain and feeds it to BufferReader.ReadDocument. Vector payload bytes are therefore read as a document: the first four floats' bytes are interpreted as the BSON length prefix, the parse fails (or the _id ENSUREs fire) and HandleError records a bogus corruption entry.
unique.fail: Create an index with dimensions > 1996 (e.g. new VectorIndexOptions(4096), the only dimension range that works at all given finding #1), insert 100 documents, then call db.Rebuild(). RebuildService opens FileReaderV8 with options.Errors and IncludeErrorReport defaulting to true (LiteDB/Engine/Structures/RebuildOptions.cs:33). GetDocuments hits the 100 first-vector blocks, each fails BSON parsing, and RebuildService.Rebuild inserts them into a `_rebuild_errors` collection — the rebuilt database reports ~100 phantom corruption errors on a perfectly healthy file. The same enumeration runs in the Recovery path (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Recovery.cs:24).
unique.fix: Pass extend: true for every block StoreVector writes (the chain is reached only through VectorIndexNode.ExternalVector, never scanned as a document root), or store vector payloads in their own page type/collection so document scanners never see them.
unique.rationale: External vector payloads are stored as extend=false first blocks in the collection's data pages, which is exactly DataBlock's start-of-document marker, so FileReaderV8 parses float bytes as BSON and Rebuild/Recovery reports phantom corruption for a healthy file.

unique.title: String-overload WhereNear/TopKNear build `$.{field}` by concatenation, so a non-word field name silently parses into a different expression and matches every document
unique.mech: The field name is interpolated straight into an expression source with no validation that it is a legal bare path segment. Tokenizer.IsWordChar (LiteDB/Utils/Tokenizer.cs:247) accepts only letters, digits, '_' and '$', so a name containing '-' terminates the path early: `$.Embedding-Value` is parsed by ParseFullExpression as the arithmetic expression SUBTRACT($.Embedding, $.Value) with Source `$.Embedding-$.Value` ('-' is a registered operator at BsonExpressionParser.cs:35, and a bare word in root scope resolves to $.<word> via TryParsePath at line 990). No exception is raised. SUBTRACT of a vector and a missing field returns BsonValue.Null (BsonExpressionOperators.cs:66), VECTOR_SIM(Null, target) returns Null (Vector.cs:10-11), and `Null <= maxDistance` is true - so the filter degenerates to 'accept everything'. The same concatenation is used by the TopKNear string overload at line 73. The correct form for such a name is the bracketed path `$.["Embedding-Value"]`, which only the BsonExpression overload can express (see LiteDB.Tests/Query/Issue2881_QuotedVectorField_Tests.cs).
unique.fail: Documents stored with a hyphenated JSON field: {"_id":1,"Embedding-Value":[1,0]}, {"_id":2,"Embedding-Value":[0,1]}, plus a vector index created as EnsureIndex("emb", "$.[\"Embedding-Value\"]", new VectorIndexOptions(2)). col.Query().WhereNear("Embedding-Value", new[]{1f,0f}, 0.25).ToArray() compiles the predicate `$.Embedding-$.Value VECTOR_SIM @0 <= @1`, matches no index, evaluates to Null <= 0.25 = true for every row, and returns the whole collection as 'near' matches. TopKNear("Embedding-Value", target, k) likewise returns k arbitrary documents.
unique.fix: Validate the name (e.g. reject when !vectorField.IsWord()) and throw ArgumentException pointing at the BsonExpression overload, or quote it into the bracketed member form: BsonExpression.Create(vectorField.IsWord() ? $"$.{vectorField}" : "$.[" + JsonSerializer.Serialize(vectorField) + "]").
unique.rationale: The string overload interpolates the field name into `$.{field}` with no validation, so a hyphenated name parses as SUBTRACT, VECTOR_SIM(Null,...) is Null and `Null <= max` matches everything. Silently returns the whole collection, but only for non-word field names.

unique.title: Query.ToSQL emits the WHERE clause after ORDER BY / LIMIT / OFFSET / FOR UPDATE, producing SQL that LiteDB itself cannot parse
unique.mech: The vector commit (66ec615 'Implement vectors') moved the WHERE emission out of its correct slot - it used to sit between INCLUDE and GROUP BY, and `git log -L 76,150:LiteDB/Engine/Query/Query.cs` shows the block deleted there (leaving the blank gap at lines 83-85) and re-added at the very end of the method, after GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET and FOR UPDATE. SqlParser.ParseSelect (LiteDB/Client/SqlParser/Commands/Select.cs lines 86-189) reads clauses in the fixed order INCLUDE, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET, FOR UPDATE and finishes with ReadToken().Expect(EOF, SemiColon) at line 189, so a trailing WHERE is an UnexpectedToken error. ToSQL is public API on the public Query type and its output is also what users see in the sql column of $open_cursors (LiteDB/Engine/SystemCollections/SysOpenCursors.cs:25) and in the QUERY debug log (QueryExecutor.cs:49) - both now show a malformed statement for every query that has any filter, vector or not.
unique.fail: var q = new Query(); q.Where.Add("$.Age > 30"); q.OrderBy.Add(new QueryOrder(BsonExpression.Create("$.Name"), Query.Ascending)); q.Limit = 10; then db.Execute(q.ToSQL("customers")) - the generated text is 'SELECT $ FROM customers ORDER BY $.Name ASC LIMIT 10 WHERE $.Age > 30' and throws LiteException UNEXPECTED_TOKEN instead of running. Equally, SELECT * FROM $open_cursors while a filtered query is open reports that same unparseable statement.
unique.fix: Move the `if (this.HasVectorFilter) ... else if (this.Where.Count > 0) ...` block back to where the blank lines at 83-85 are, i.e. after the INCLUDE block and before GROUP BY.
unique.rationale: ToSQL emits WHERE after ORDER BY/LIMIT/OFFSET/FOR UPDATE, which SqlParser cannot parse, so a public API method and the $open_cursors sql column produce malformed statements for every filtered query. Diagnostics and round-trip only.

unique.title: TopKNear mutates the shared Query before the OrderBy that can throw, leaving a half-configured vector query behind a misleading 'Multiple OrderBy calls' error
unique.mech: VectorTopKNear writes VectorField / VectorTarget / VectorMaxDistance into the shared _query and only then calls LiteQueryable.OrderBy, which throws ArgumentException("Multiple OrderBy calls are not supported. Use ThenBy for additional sort keys.") when _query.OrderBy.Count > 0 (LiteDB/Client/Database/LiteQueryable.cs:110). Two problems follow. (1) The error text names an API the caller never called twice: nothing in the TopKNear documentation says the query must not already be sorted, so the real cause (TopKNear installs its own single sort key) is masked. (2) The exception escapes after the three vector fields are already set, so Query.HasVectorFilter (VectorField != null && VectorTarget != null, Engine/Query/Query.cs:36) is now true while no vector predicate, ORDER BY or LIMIT was installed. A subsequent WithScore() passes the HasVectorFilter guard at LiteQueryable.Vector.cs:151, builds a VectorScoreProjection, and the engine happily scores and returns every document in the collection as a vector search hit.
unique.fail: var q = col.Query().OrderBy(x => x.Name); try { q.TopKNear(x => x.Embedding, target, 5); } catch (ArgumentException) { /* message blames OrderBy */ } var hits = q.WithScore().ToArray(); - instead of throwing 'WithScore requires WhereNear or TopKNear', this returns every document in the collection with a cosine score, ordered by Name, presented as vector search results.
unique.fix: Validate first and mutate last: check `_query.OrderBy.Count == 0` at the top of VectorTopKNear and throw a vector-specific InvalidOperationException (e.g. 'TopKNear installs its own ordering; remove the existing OrderBy'), and only assign VectorField/VectorTarget/VectorMaxDistance after OrderBy/Limit have succeeded.
unique.rationale: TopKNear writes the vector fields before the OrderBy that can throw, so after a caught ArgumentException HasVectorFilter is true with no predicate installed and a later WithScore() scores and returns the entire collection as vector hits. Also a misleading error message.

unique.title: $open_cursors / $snapshots / $transactions enumerate other threads' live List/Dictionary, throwing "Collection was modified"
unique.mech: GetTransactionsSnapshot() copies the *transaction references*, but the per-transaction collections it then walks are plain, non-thread-safe containers owned by other threads. `TransactionService.OpenCursors` is a `List<CursorInfo>` (TransactionService.cs:49) that QueryExecutor mutates from the owning thread on every query (Add at QueryExecutor.cs:75, Remove via OnDispose at :79). `TransactionService.Snapshots` is a live view over `Dictionary<string, Snapshot> _snapshots` (TransactionService.cs:23,39) that CreateSnapshot inserts into (TransactionService.cs:93,100) whenever the owning thread touches a new collection. Enumerating either while another thread mutates it bumps the container's version and throws InvalidOperationException from the enumerator. Same defect at SysSnapshots.cs:15 and SysTransactions.cs:14-27.
unique.fail: Thread A: `db.Execute("SELECT * FROM $open_cursors")` and iterates the reader. Thread B concurrently runs queries in a loop (each one Adds then Removes a CursorInfo on B's transaction). A's inner `foreach` over B's OpenCursors observes the version change and throws `InvalidOperationException: Collection was modified; enumeration operation may not execute` out of the user's query. Identically, `SELECT * FROM $snapshots` throws when thread B's transaction opens a snapshot on a second collection (e.g. an INCLUDE or a multi-collection transaction) mid-enumeration.
unique.fix: Snapshot the inner collections too: expose `CursorInfo[] GetOpenCursorsSnapshot()` and `Snapshot[] GetSnapshotsSnapshot()` on TransactionService using a lock or an immutable/array copy, and have the $-collections iterate those copies.
unique.rationale: $open_cursors/$snapshots enumerate other threads' plain List/Dictionary, so a concurrent query or new snapshot throws 'Collection was modified' out of the user's diagnostics query. Same family as [95], different containers.

unique.title: $indexes and $page_list dereference a null CollectionPage when a collection is dropped mid-enumeration
unique.mech: CreateSnapshot is called with addIfNotExists = false, and Snapshot's constructor leaves _collectionPage null when CollectionService.Get finds no header entry (SnapShot.cs:85-86 -> CollectionService.cs:38-55 returns without assigning when GetCollectionPageID == uint.MaxValue). SysIndexes then unconditionally dereferences `snapshot.CollectionPage`. Because HeaderPage.GetCollections() is a lazy iterator (HeaderPage.cs:219) the name is yielded at one instant and the snapshot is created at a later instant; a concurrent drop commits `h.DeleteCollection(name)` in between. LiteEngine.DropCollection only rejects a transaction on the *calling* thread (`_locker.IsInTransaction`, Collection.cs:27 — that flag is per-thread ReaderWriterLockSlim state) and takes only a per-collection write lock, so it runs concurrently with a reader on another thread. SysPageList.cs:58 and :66 have the identical unguarded dereference (`snap.CollectionPage.FreeDataPageList[slot]`, `snap.CollectionPage.GetCollectionIndexes()`), reached from a dictionary snapshot of the same header.
unique.fail: Thread A: `db.Execute("SELECT * FROM $indexes")` on a database with collections [a, b, c]; the enumerator has already yielded a's indexes and is about to create the snapshot for b. Thread B: `db.DropCollection("b")` commits, removing "b" from the header. Thread A's CreateSnapshot("b") returns a snapshot with CollectionPage == null and the next line throws NullReferenceException out of the user's query. Identically, `SELECT * FROM $page_list` throws NRE at SysPageList.cs:58.
unique.fix: Null-check the snapshot's CollectionPage and `continue` (the collection is gone), and take the collection list as an atomic array under lock(_header) first.
unique.rationale: CreateSnapshot(addIfNotExists:false) leaves CollectionPage null when the collection was dropped between the lazy yield and the snapshot, and $indexes/$page_list dereference it unguarded - NRE out of a read-only system query.

unique.title: CSV export writes JSON-escaped strings, so any value containing a quote, delimiter or newline corrupts the file
unique.mech: WriteValue's default branch (covering String, Boolean, Int32, Double and Vector) emits `value.ToString()`, which is `JsonSerializer.Serialize(this)` (BsonValue.cs:540-543). For a string that produces a JSON literal escaped per JSON rules — `"` becomes `\"` (JsonWriter.cs:182-186) — not per RFC 4180, which requires `""`. A Vector serializes to `[1.0,2.0]`, embedding the default comma delimiter. Nothing quotes or doubles the configured delimiter. The matching reader (ReadString, line 203-230) implements RFC 4180 doubling and has no `\` handling, so it mis-splits exactly these values.
unique.fail: A document with `{name: "he said \"hi\""}` exports as the field `"he said \"hi\""`. Re-importing: ReadString sees the opening quote, consumes `he said \`, then hits `"` followed by `h` (not another quote), so it ends the field there and parses `hi\"` as an additional CSV field — the value is truncated to `he said \` and the row's remaining columns shift. A `{tags: [1,2,3]}` vector/array field likewise splits into three columns, shifting every later value in the row.
unique.fix: Escape for CSV, not JSON: for string-like values emit `"` + value.Replace("\"", "\"\"") + `"`, and quote any value containing the delimiter, a quote, CR or LF.
unique.rationale: CSV export emits JSON-escaped strings (\" rather than "") and unquoted array/vector literals containing the delimiter, while the reader implements RFC 4180 - so quotes, delimiters or newlines in values truncate the value and shift every later column on re-import.

unique.title: $database reports dataFileSize/logFileSize through an unchecked (int) cast of a long
unique.mech: DiskService.GetFileLength returns `long` (DiskService.cs:253-263). The unchecked `(int)` cast truncates to the low 32 bits and reinterprets the result as signed, so any length at or above 2 GiB is reported as a wrong (often negative) number. Line 34 has the same cast for the log file, which grows without bound between checkpoints.
unique.fail: A 3 GiB data file (3,221,233,664 bytes) makes `SELECT dataFileSize FROM $database` return -1,073,733,632. Monitoring or admin tooling that reads this field to size-check or alert on growth sees a negative value and silently concludes the file shrank; the same applies to logFileSize once the log passes 2 GiB before a checkpoint.
unique.fix: Emit the long directly (BsonValue supports Int64) instead of casting to int.
unique.rationale: Unchecked (int) cast of a long file length makes $database report negative dataFileSize/logFileSize past 2GiB, so monitoring concludes the file shrank. Silently wrong but diagnostics-only.

unique.title: BsonValue(object) can produce Document/Array-typed values that are not BsonDocument/BsonArray, making AsDocument/AsArray null and every consumer throw NullReferenceException
unique.mech: The `object` constructor sets `Type = BsonType.Document` / `BsonType.Array` on a plain `BsonValue` instance (lines 138-139 for an already-typed dictionary/list, and 163-186 for the generic IDictionary/IEnumerable fallback, and 150-155 when copying from another BsonValue). But `AsDocument => this as BsonDocument` and `AsArray => this as BsonArray` (lines 221, 224) are downcasts of `this`, so they return null for such an instance. Every switch that dispatches on `Type` and then dereferences AsDocument/AsArray therefore NREs: GetBytesCount (lines 717-718), CompareTo (lines 588-589), JsonWriter.WriteValue (LiteDB/Document/Json/JsonWriter.cs:54, 59), and BufferSliceExtensions.WriteIndexKey (line 366).
unique.fail: `var doc = new BsonDocument(); doc["tags"] = new BsonValue(new List<string>{ "a", "b" });` — the `object` overload is selected, the IEnumerable fallback builds a `List<BsonValue>` and sets `Type = BsonType.Array` on a plain BsonValue. `collection.Insert(doc)` then calls `GetBytesCountElement` -> `value.GetBytesCount(true)` -> `case BsonType.Array: return this.AsArray.GetBytesCount(recalc);` where AsArray is null -> NullReferenceException, with no indication that the problem is the constructed value. `doc.ToString()` NREs the same way inside JsonWriter.WriteArray. The identical failure occurs for `new BsonValue(new Dictionary<string, BsonValue>{ ["a"] = 1 })`.
unique.fix: Have the object constructor return/produce real BsonDocument/BsonArray instances (e.g. make it a static factory, or throw InvalidCastException for dictionary/list inputs directing callers to `new BsonDocument(...)` / `new BsonArray(...)`), or make AsDocument/AsArray construct a wrapper from RawValue instead of downcasting `this`.
unique.rationale: The object ctor sets Type=Document/Array on a plain BsonValue while AsDocument/AsArray are downcasts of this, so `new BsonValue(new List<string>{...})` NREs in GetBytesCount/JsonWriter/WriteIndexKey with no hint about the constructed value.

unique.title: UInt64 implicit conversions are asymmetric: BsonValue stores a Double but the reverse cast unboxes a UInt64, throwing InvalidCastException on round trip
unique.mech: `implicit operator BsonValue(UInt64)` converts to Double and stores a boxed `double` with `Type = BsonType.Double`. `implicit operator UInt64(BsonValue)` performs `(UInt64)value.RawValue`, which is an unboxing cast — it requires the boxed runtime type to be exactly `ulong`. Since nothing ever stores a boxed `ulong` in RawValue (the `object` constructor has no UInt64 branch either and would reach the InvalidCastException at line 189), the getter can never succeed for a value produced by the setter. Additionally, routing through Double loses precision above 2^53.
unique.fail: `BsonValue v = 12345UL; ulong back = v;` -> the first statement stores boxed `double 12345.0`; the second executes `(ulong)(object)12345.0` -> System.InvalidCastException ("Specified cast is not valid"). Every read-back of a ulong written through the implicit operator fails. Separately, `BsonValue v = ulong.MaxValue;` silently persists 18446744073709551616 (the nearest double) instead of 18446744073709551615, so a round trip through the database returns a different number.
unique.fix: Implement the UInt64 getter as `Convert.ToUInt64(value.RawValue)` (or route through Decimal, which represents the full UInt64 range exactly) and store UInt64 as Decimal rather than Double to avoid precision loss.
unique.rationale: The UInt64 implicit conversions are asymmetric - stored as a boxed double, read back with an unboxing (UInt64) cast - so every round trip through the operator throws InvalidCastException, and values above 2^53 lose precision silently.

unique.title: Unbounded recursion in GetBytesCount/ToString for self-referencing BsonDocument kills the process with StackOverflowException
unique.mech: BsonDocument/BsonArray are mutable public containers with no cycle detection: `doc["x"] = doc` is accepted by the indexer (BsonDocument.cs:59). `GetBytesCount` recurses through `AsDocument.GetBytesCount(recalc)` -> `GetBytesCountElement` -> `value.GetBytesCount(true)` with no depth limit or visited set, and the `_length` cache is bypassed because `recalc` is always `true` on the element path (BsonValue.cs:736). `ToString()` -> JsonSerializer.Serialize -> JsonWriter.WriteValue/WriteObject has no depth guard either (JsonWriter.cs:44-120; `_indent` is only used for formatting). A .NET StackOverflowException cannot be caught and terminates the process.
unique.fail: `var doc = new BsonDocument { ["_id"] = 1 }; doc["self"] = doc; col.Insert(doc);` -> Insert computes the document size via `doc.GetBytesCount(true)`, which recurses doc -> element "self" -> doc -> ... until the stack is exhausted, and the whole host process (not just the request) is killed by an uncatchable StackOverflowException. The same happens on `doc.ToString()` or `JsonSerializer.Serialize(doc)`, and on `BsonSerializer.Serialize(doc)` (BsonSerializer.cs:22).
unique.fix: Enforce a maximum nesting depth (BSON documents are already bounded in practice) in GetBytesCount, WriteElement and JsonWriter, throwing a LiteException when exceeded, or track visited container references to detect cycles.
unique.rationale: No cycle detection or depth limit in GetBytesCount/JsonWriter, and the _length cache is bypassed on the element path, so a self-referencing BsonDocument terminates the host process with an uncatchable StackOverflowException. Requires the caller to build a cycle.

unique.title: Recursive-descent expression parser has no nesting-depth limit: a few thousand nested parentheses/brackets/braces terminate the process with StackOverflowException
unique.mech: `ParseFullExpression` -> `ParseSingleExpression` -> `TryParseInnerExpression` -> `ParseFullExpression` (line 854) is mutually recursive with one frame group per nesting level, and the same holds for `TryParseArray` (line 773) and `TryParseDocument` (line 637). There is no depth counter, no input-length limit and no `RuntimeHelpers.EnsureSufficientExecutionStack` call anywhere in the parser or tokenizer (verified by grep). `BsonExpression.Create(string)` — and the implicit `string`->`BsonExpression` conversion, and `LiteDatabase.Execute(sql)` — accept arbitrary caller-supplied text. StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET; the whole host process is killed.
unique.fail: `BsonExpression.Create(new string('(', 20000) + "1" + new string(')', 20000))` (a ~40 KB string) recurses ~20000 x 3 frames and aborts the process; the same happens for `new string('[', 20000)` or a filter string coming from an untrusted HTTP parameter in an application that forwards it to `col.Find(filter)`. An attacker who can influence any expression/SQL string crashes the application with a tiny payload, and the open write transaction is lost.
unique.fix: Thread a depth counter through ParseFullExpression/ParseSingleExpression (or keep it on ExpressionContext/Tokenizer) and throw LiteException.UnexpectedToken / a syntax error above a fixed limit (e.g. 64-128 levels); the same limit is needed in JsonReader, which shares this Tokenizer.
unique.rationale: Mutually recursive ParseFullExpression/TryParseInnerExpression/TryParseArray/TryParseDocument with no depth counter or EnsureSufficientExecutionStack; a ~40KB payload kills the process. Rated below [125] because expression/SQL text is usually developer-controlled.

unique.title: Tokenizer recurses once per `--` comment line, so a script with many comment lines overflows the stack
unique.mech: After consuming a `--` line comment, `ReadNext` calls itself to fetch the next token instead of looping. The call is not in tail position (the result flows through `break` and `return token ?? ...`), so no tail-call elimination occurs and each consecutive comment line adds a stack frame. Consecutive comment lines are unbounded, and StackOverflowException is not catchable.
unique.fail: `db.Execute(string.Concat(Enumerable.Repeat("-- generated line\n", 50000)) + "SELECT 1")` — a legitimate-looking generated/exported .sql script with a long comment header — recurses 50000 levels inside `Tokenizer.ReadNext` and kills the process instead of returning a result or a LiteException.
unique.fix: Replace the recursion with an outer loop: after `ReadLine()`, `continue` a `while(true)` wrapped around the switch (or goto the start of ReadNext) so comment skipping consumes no stack.
unique.rationale: ReadNext recurses (not in tail position) once per '--' comment line, so a generated script with tens of thousands of comment lines overflows the stack instead of parsing. Same class as [111].

unique.title: `ANY`/`ALL` followed by AND/OR/VECTOR_SIM builds an operator key absent from the precedence table, and the reduce loop walks past the end of the table (ArgumentOutOfRangeException)
unique.mech: `ReadOperant` (line 1287-1309) accepts `ANY`/`ALL` followed by *any* token whose `IsOperand` is true, and `Token.IsOperand` returns true for the words AND, OR and VECTOR_SIM (Tokenizer.cs:95-103, 190-191). It returns e.g. `"ANY AND"`, which `_operators` does not contain (only ANY/ALL + LIKE/BETWEEN/IN/comparison keys exist). In the reduce loop, `ops.IndexOf(op.Key)` never matches, so `order` is incremented past the 35 entries and `_operators.ElementAt(order)` throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException rather than a syntax error; the loop condition `values.Count >= 2` is still true so there is no other exit.
unique.fail: `BsonExpression.Create("$.a ANY AND $.b")` (or `db.Execute("SELECT $ FROM c WHERE arr ANY OR 1")`) throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Index was out of range` from inside LINQ's ElementAt instead of a LiteException with a token position, so callers that catch LiteException to report syntax errors see an unhandled exception and no position information.
unique.fix: In `ReadOperant`, validate the composed `ANY xxx`/`ALL xxx` key against `_operators` and throw `LiteException.UnexpectedToken("Expected valid operand", token)` when absent; additionally guard the reduce loop with `if (order >= _operators.Count) throw LiteException.UnexpectedToken(...)`.
unique.rationale: Verified against the reduce loop: ReadOperant accepts ANY/ALL + AND/OR/VECTOR_SIM, building a key absent from _operators, and `order` is incremented past the table so ElementAt throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException instead of a positioned syntax error.

unique.title: ParseFunction does not check that a MAP/FILTER/SORT overload was found, so a wrong argument count throws ArgumentNullException from Expression.Call
unique.mech: `args` always starts with root/collation/parameters, so `args.Count - 5` is the number of user arguments beyond the first; when the `=>` part is missing it becomes -1, and when too many extra arguments are given it exceeds the available overloads. `BsonExpression.GetFunction` returns null in both cases (dictionary miss via `GetOrDefault`), and the null is passed straight to `Expression.Call(method, ...)` at line 105. `TryParseMethodCall` has the corresponding null check (BsonExpressionParser.cs:932) but `ParseFunction` does not.
unique.fail: `db.Execute("SELECT MAP($.items) FROM col")` — a plausible typo for `MAP($.items => @.name)` — parses to args.Count == 4, so `GetFunction("MAP", -1)` returns null and `Expression.Call(null, args)` throws `ArgumentNullException: Value cannot be null. (Parameter 'method')`. Same for `FILTER(a => @.x, 1)` (one extra argument) and `SORT(a => @, 1, 2)`. The user gets an ArgumentNullException with no position instead of a syntax error.
unique.fix: Mirror TryParseMethodCall: `if (method == null) throw LiteException.UnexpectedToken($"Function '{functionName}' does not exist or contains invalid parameters", tokenizer.Current);`
unique.rationale: ParseFunction passes GetFunction's null straight to Expression.Call, so a wrong MAP/FILTER/SORT argument count surfaces as ArgumentNullException('method') with no position; TryParseMethodCall has the missing null check.

unique.title: IIF immutability is computed with C# `&&`/`||` precedence, marking volatile expressions as immutable and letting them be used as index expressions
unique.mech: `test.IsImmutable && ifTrue.IsImmutable || ifFalse.IsImmutable` parses as `(test && ifTrue) || ifFalse`, so an immutable *false-branch* alone makes the whole IIF immutable regardless of the other two branches (the intent, matching every other node in this file, is `test && ifTrue && ifFalse`). `IsImmutable` feeds `BsonExpression.IsIndexable`, which is the only guard `EnsureIndex` has against indexing volatile expressions (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Index.cs:20).
unique.fail: `col.EnsureIndex("idx", "IIF($.kind = 'A', NOW(), 0)")` is accepted because IsImmutable is computed as `(true && false) || true == true`, so IsIndexable is true. Index keys are frozen at insert time (the NOW() value of the insert), while a later `WHERE IIF($.kind='A', NOW(), 0) = ...` seek computes a different key, so the index lookup misses documents and the query returns fewer rows than a full scan would — a silently wrong result set from a query the engine claims is indexable.
unique.fix: `IsImmutable = test.IsImmutable && ifTrue.IsImmutable && ifFalse.IsImmutable,`
unique.rationale: IIF immutability is computed as (test && ifTrue) || ifFalse instead of all three, so a volatile expression passes IsIndexable and EnsureIndex accepts an index whose keys are frozen at insert time - seeks then miss matching documents. Silently wrong, narrow construction.

unique.title: Tokenizer silently deletes unrecognised string escape sequences instead of erroring or keeping them literally
unique.mech: `ReadString` handles `\\`, `\/`, `\b`, `\f`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\uXXXX` and the active quote char; the switch has no `default`, so for any other escaped character nothing is appended and the loop's trailing `ReadChar()` skips past it. The escape marker *and* the escaped character both vanish from the resulting string constant, with no exception and no diagnostic.
unique.fail: `db.Execute(@"SELECT $ FROM files WHERE path = 'C:\dir\file'")`: `\d` is dropped and `\f` is turned into a form feed, so the string constant becomes "C:ir\u000Cile" instead of "C:\dir\file"; the predicate silently matches nothing and the query returns zero rows as if the data were absent. The same silently corrupts `\'` inside a double-quoted literal (`"it\'s"` -> "its") and any `\x`/`\0`/`\a` sequence, including in JSON parsed through this tokenizer.
unique.fix: Add a `default:` branch that either throws a LiteException for an invalid escape or appends the backslash and the character verbatim; also restructure so the `if (_char == quote)` case does not fall through into the switch.
unique.rationale: ReadString's escape switch has no default, so an unrecognised escape and its marker both vanish: 'C:\dir\file' becomes a different string and the predicate silently matches nothing. Affects Windows paths in SQL literals and JSON through this tokenizer.

unique.title: MATCH returns CLR null instead of BsonValue.Null for non-string input
unique.mech: `MATCH` returns bare `null` on the type-check failure path while returning `BsonValue.Null` on the no-match path three lines later — an internal inconsistency. As with FIRST/LAST, the compiler nests calls directly (`Expression.Call(method, args)`, BsonExpressionParser.cs:983) with no null guard, so any enclosing method dereferences the null immediately.
unique.fail: Document `{_id:1, code:12345}` (a number, not a string). `SELECT LOWER(MATCH($.code, '[0-9]+', 0)) FROM col` → MATCH's `value.IsString == false` branch returns CLR null → `LOWER` evaluates `value.IsString` on null → NullReferenceException escapes the query. `SELECT MATCH($.code, '[0-9]+', 0) FROM col` on its own silently yields null only because BsonDocument's setter coalesces.
unique.fix: `return BsonValue.Null;` on line 273.
unique.rationale: MATCH returns CLR null on the type-check path while returning BsonValue.Null three lines later, so any enclosing method NREs on a non-string input. Same class as [119], single function.

unique.title: ABS and ROUND throw unhandled exceptions on edge-value arguments instead of returning Null
unique.mech: `Math.Round(double, int)` throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException when digits < 0 or > 15 (decimal: > 28), and `Math.Abs` throws OverflowException for Int32.MinValue and Int64.MinValue (their absolute value is not representable). Neither argument is validated, and both functions otherwise follow the file's convention of returning BsonValue.Null for anything they cannot handle, so the exception is unexpected and aborts the whole query (QueryExecutor rethrows non-IO exceptions).
unique.fail: (a) `SELECT ROUND($.price, -2) FROM products` — negative digits is valid in T-SQL and a natural thing to write — throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Rounding digits must be between 0 and 15`. (b) Collection with `{_id:1, delta:-2147483648}` (Int32.MinValue, a legitimately stored value): `SELECT ABS($.delta) FROM col` throws `OverflowException: Negating the minimum value of a twos complement number is invalid`, killing the query for every row.
unique.fix: Validate/clamp `digits` to the legal range (or return BsonValue.Null when out of range), and widen ABS for the MinValue cases (e.g. `Math.Abs((long)value.AsInt32)`, and `value.AsInt64 == long.MinValue ? (BsonValue)Math.Abs((decimal)value.AsInt64) : ...`).
unique.rationale: ABS throws OverflowException for Int32/Int64.MinValue and ROUND throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for digits outside 0..15, against the file's convention of returning Null - ROUND(x,-2) is natural to write. Canonical of the three reports.

unique.title: DATEDIFF('s'|'h'|'d') and DATEADD overflow/throw on wide but realistic date ranges
unique.mech: DATEDIFF narrows the interval with `Convert.ToInt32(Math.Truncate(...TotalSeconds))`, which throws OverflowException once the span exceeds Int32.MaxValue seconds (~68 years). DATEADD converts the operand with `number.AsInt32` (`Convert.ToInt32`, throws for out-of-Int32 doubles) and then calls `DateTime.AddYears/AddMonths/AddDays`, which throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException when the result leaves DateTime's range. Both functions otherwise return BsonValue.Null for unusable input, so callers have no reason to expect a throw.
unique.fail: `SELECT DATEDIFF('s', $.birthdate, NOW()) FROM people` where `birthdate` is 1950-01-01: the span is ~2.4e9 seconds > Int32.MaxValue (2147483647) → `System.OverflowException: Value was either too large or too small for an Int32`, aborting the query. Separately, `SELECT DATEADD('y', 10000, NOW())` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException: The added or subtracted value results in an un-representable DateTime`.
unique.fix: Return Int64 for DATEDIFF's second/minute/hour/day parts (BsonValue supports Int64), and range-check DATEADD's operand/result, returning BsonValue.Null rather than throwing.
unique.rationale: DATEDIFF narrows through Convert.ToInt32, overflowing past ~68 years in seconds, and DATEADD throws for out-of-range results - both against the file's Null-on-bad-input convention. Ordinary birthdate-vs-now queries hit it.

unique.title: Empty JSON object key throws IndexOutOfRangeException out of the parser and breaks LiteDB's own JSON export/import round trip
unique.mech: ReadObject indexes key[0] to test for the '$' extended-type prefix without first checking key.Length. An empty string is a legal JSON member name, and Tokenizer.ReadString returns "" for the input "" (LiteDB/Utils/Tokenizer.cs:624-663: the opening quote is consumed, the loop sees the closing quote immediately and exits), so token.Value is "" and Expect(String, Word) passes. key[0] then throws IndexOutOfRangeException -- a raw framework exception escaping a parser whose documented failure mode is LiteException.UnexpectedToken.
unique.fail: JsonSerializer.Deserialize("{\"\":1}") throws IndexOutOfRangeException. This is not merely adversarial input: BsonDocument accepts empty keys (BsonDocument.cs:47-59 has no key validation) and BufferWriter.WriteCString only rejects '\0', so doc[""] = 1 persists to disk. JsonWriter then emits {"":1}, so the sequence Insert(doc with empty key) -> SELECT $ INTO $file_json('dump.json') -> SELECT * FROM $file_json('dump.json') fails with IndexOutOfRangeException on import: LiteDB cannot read back JSON it wrote. In query context, SELECT JSON($.payload) with payload = '{"":1}' also lets IndexOutOfRangeException escape, because Misc.cs:29 catches only LiteException/UNEXPECTED_TOKEN.
unique.fix: Guard the length: if (key.Length > 0 && key[0] == '$' && obj.Count == 0).
unique.rationale: key[0] is indexed before any length check and an empty member name is legal JSON that BsonDocument and BufferWriter both accept, so LiteDB cannot re-import its own $file_json export of such a document - IndexOutOfRangeException escapes the LiteException-based guards. Canonical of the pair.

unique.title: JsonWriter does not escape document keys, producing invalid JSON and allowing structural injection into exported JSON
unique.mech: WriteKeyValue writes the key verbatim between two quote characters, while values go through WriteString, which escapes quotes, backslashes and control characters. BsonDocument applies no key validation (BsonDocument.cs:47-59, Add at :118), and the on-disk encoder only rejects '\0' (BufferWriter.NetCore.cs:15). Any key containing '"', '\\', a newline or another control character therefore terminates or corrupts the emitted key token, so the whole serialized document is not parseable JSON. Because the key text lands unescaped in the structural position, a key can also inject arbitrary JSON syntax.
unique.fail: col.Insert(new BsonDocument { ["say \"hi\""] = 1 }) then db.Execute("SELECT $ INTO $file_json('dump.json') FROM col") writes {"_id":{"$oid":"..."},"say "hi"":1}. Re-importing with SELECT * FROM $file_json('dump.json') fails (LiteException.UnexpectedToken) for the entire file, not just that document, so the export is an unusable backup. The same document's BsonValue.ToString() (BsonValue.cs:542) returns invalid JSON. A crafted key such as a\":0,\"b serializes as {"a":0,"b":<value>}, i.e. the attacker-chosen key fabricates an extra field in the consumer's view of the export.
unique.fix: Call this.WriteString(key) instead of writing the raw key between manual quotes (WriteString already emits the surrounding quotes and full escaping).
unique.rationale: Document keys are written verbatim between quotes while values go through WriteString, so a key containing a quote, backslash or control char makes the whole export unparseable, and a crafted key can fabricate fields in the consumer's view. Requires an unusual key, but breaks the entire file.

unique.title: Double values are serialized with a fixed 9-decimal format, silently zeroing small magnitudes and truncating precision
unique.mech: The custom format string "0.0########" permits at most nine fractional digits and no exponent. .NET rounds the value to nine decimal places, so every double whose information lives beyond the ninth decimal place is truncated, and every non-zero double with |x| < 5e-10 is rendered as exactly "0.0". The reader (JsonReader.cs:93) parses whatever digits it is given, so the loss is silent and unrecoverable -- there is no round-trip ("R"/"G17"/shortest-roundtrip) formatting anywhere on this path.
unique.fail: doc["x"] = 1e-15 serializes to {"x":0.0}; importing that back via $file_json yields 0.0, so a column of scientific measurements becomes all zeros after an export/import cycle with no error or warning. doc["pi"] = Math.PI (3.141592653589793) serializes as 3.141592654, losing 6 significant digits; doc["v"] = 1.2345678901234567e-5 becomes 0.000012346. The same formatting drives BsonValue.ToString(), so tools built on it (LiteDB.Studio, logs, SELECT output) display 0.0 for 1e-15 as if it were the stored value. BsonType.Vector goes through the same WriteValue (line 120-124), so exported embedding components below 5e-10 are also zeroed.
unique.fix: Format with the round-trip specifier (value.AsDouble.ToString("R", _numberFormat) on netstandard2.0, or the default shortest-round-trippable ToString on net8.0+), appending ".0" only when the produced text has no '.', 'e' or 'E', so the token still lexes as TokenType.Double.
unique.rationale: The fixed "0.0########" format caps doubles at nine decimals with no exponent, so 1e-15 serializes as 0.0 and Math.PI loses six significant digits - silent, unrecoverable precision loss through export/import and through every ToString-based tool.

unique.title: Integer literals larger than Int64.MaxValue raise an unhandled OverflowException from the JSON parser
unique.mech: Tokenizer.ReadNumber classifies a run of digits with no '.', 'e' or 'E' as TokenType.Int regardless of magnitude (Tokenizer.cs:581-619). ReadValue then tries Int32.TryParse and, on failure, calls Int64.Parse with no overflow fallback. JSON imposes no bound on integer magnitude, so a perfectly well-formed document produces an OverflowException instead of a value or a LiteException.
unique.fail: JsonSerializer.Deserialize("{\"a\":99999999999999999999}") throws OverflowException("Value was either too large or too small for an Int64"). Via SQL, SELECT JSON($.payload) over a stored field containing that text lets OverflowException escape the expression evaluator, because Misc.cs:29 only catches LiteException/UNEXPECTED_TOKEN; the whole query aborts with a non-LiteDB exception type. Importing a third-party JSON file containing a large id (Twitter/Discord-style snowflakes are near the Int64 boundary; anything past it overflows) fails the same way mid-stream in SysFileJson.Input, after earlier documents have already been yielded into the destination collection.
unique.fix: Use Int64.TryParse and fall back to Decimal.TryParse and then Convert.ToDouble, or throw LiteException.UnexpectedToken(token), so no raw OverflowException escapes.
unique.rationale: Int64.Parse with no overflow fallback turns a well-formed JSON integer above Int64.MaxValue into an OverflowException that escapes the UNEXPECTED_TOKEN-based guards, aborting an import mid-stream after earlier documents were already inserted.

unique.title: Extended data types pass unvalidated token text to framework constructors, leaking FormatException/ArgumentException/ArgumentNullException from the parser
unique.mech: ReadObject calls ReadExtendedDataType(key, token.Value) for any first key starting with '$' without checking that the value token is even a string, and ReadExtendedDataType hands that raw text straight to Convert.FromBase64String, ObjectId, Guid, DateTime.Parse and Convert.ToInt64/ToDecimal.
