For a non-string token, token.Value is the token's lexeme ('{', '[', 'null', '123'), and for a truncated document it is the EOF token's null Value. None of the resulting framework exceptions are wrapped in a LiteException, so they bypass every UNEXPECTED_TOKEN-based guard in the engine.
unique.fail: JsonSerializer.Deserialize("{\"$binary\":\"zz\"}") throws FormatException; {"$oid":"zzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz"} throws FormatException from Convert.ToByte inside ObjectId.FromHex (ObjectId.cs:135); {"$oid":"abc"} throws ArgumentException (ObjectId.cs:129); {"$binary":null} passes the literal text "null" to FromBase64String and throws FormatException; {"$oid": truncates to EOF, so value is null and ObjectId.FromHex throws ArgumentNullException (ObjectId.cs:128); {"$guid":{"a":1}} passes "{" to new Guid and throws FormatException while also leaving the nested object unconsumed. In every case SELECT JSON($.payload) over such a stored string aborts the query with a non-LiteException, because Misc.cs:29 filters on LiteException/UNEXPECTED_TOKEN only -- the intended behaviour there is clearly to return BsonValue.Null for unparseable JSON.
unique.fix: Require token.Type == TokenType.String before treating a $-key as an extended type, and wrap the conversions so failures surface as LiteException.UnexpectedToken (or fall through to treating the object as a plain document).
unique.rationale: $-prefixed extended types hand unvalidated (and possibly non-string or null) token text to FromBase64String/ObjectId/Guid/DateTime.Parse, so FormatException/ArgumentException/ArgumentNullException bypass every LiteException-based guard - notably JSON($.payload), which is meant to return Null for unparseable input.

unique.title: $date is parsed with the ambient CurrentCulture although it is always written with the invariant ISO-8601 round-trip format
unique.mech: JsonWriter.cs:101 emits value.AsDateTime.ToUniversalTime().ToString("o"), which is culture-independent. The reader parses it with DateTime.Parse(value), the single-argument overload, which resolves the text through CultureInfo.CurrentCulture.DateTimeFormat -- including that culture's Calendar and era. The class already holds an invariant _numberFormat (line 14) and uses it for every numeric extended type, and every other DateTime parse in the library passes an explicit format provider (Document/Expression/Methods/DataTypes.cs:335, 357, 377, 399), so this one site is the outlier. DateTimeStyles.RoundtripKind is also not requested.
unique.fail: With Thread.CurrentThread.CurrentCulture = new CultureInfo("th-TH"), whose calendar is ThaiBuddhistCalendar, JsonSerializer.Deserialize(JsonSerializer.Serialize(new BsonValue(new DateTime(2015,1,1)))) resolves the year field 2015 in the Buddhist era rather than the Gregorian one, so the round-tripped DateTime is off by ~543 years and is stored as such -- a silently wrong date, not an exception. Under a culture whose calendar cannot represent the written year (for example ar-SA with UmmAlQuraCalendar) the same call throws instead. An application whose UI thread culture differs from the one that wrote the export therefore reads back different instants from the same JSON file.
unique.fix: Parse with the invariant culture and round-trip styles: DateTime.Parse(value, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.RoundtripKind | DateTimeStyles.AdjustToUniversal), matching the writer's "o" format.
unique.rationale: $date is written with the invariant "o" format but parsed with CurrentCulture and no RoundtripKind, so a non-Gregorian-calendar culture reads back a date shifted by centuries (silently) or throws - while every other extended type here uses the invariant provider.

unique.title: Reflection.CreateInstance reads the shared ctor cache Dictionary outside the lock that guards its writes
unique.mech: `_cacheCtor` is a plain `Dictionary<Type, CreateObject>` (line 30). Writes happen under `lock (_cacheCtor)` (lines 62 and 94), but the fast path at line 39 does `TryGetValue` with no lock at all. `Dictionary<K,V>` is explicitly documented as unsafe for a read concurrent with a write: an `Add` that grows the table reallocates `_buckets`/`_entries` and rewrites the collision chains, and a reader that observes a torn combination of those fields can index out of range or walk a corrupted `next` chain. There is no memory barrier or volatile read here, and no double-checked-locking discipline (the unlocked read is not repeated under the lock before use).
unique.fail: A shared LiteDatabase (BsonMapper.Global) is used from two threads — a very common ASP.NET/worker setup. Thread A deserializes the first document of type X: it takes the lock and `_cacheCtor.Add(typeof(X), ...)` triggers a resize. Thread B is simultaneously in the unlocked `TryGetValue(typeof(Y))` at line 39. Outcomes: (a) IndexOutOfRangeException inside Dictionary.FindEntry, which the surrounding catch at line 44 rewrites into `LiteException.InvalidCtor(type)` — a completely misleading "invalid ctor" error for a perfectly valid type; (b) on netstandard2.0 consumers (.NET Framework, whose Dictionary.FindEntry has no concurrent-operation guard) an endless walk of a corrupted bucket chain, i.e. a query thread spinning at 100% CPU forever with no exception and no lock held; (c) on net8/net10, InvalidOperationException("Operations that change non-concurrent collections must have exclusive access") surfacing as InvalidCtor.
unique.fix: Make `_cacheCtor` a `ConcurrentDictionary<Type, CreateObject>` (same as `_entities` in BsonMapper.GetEntityMapper.cs), or perform the fast-path read inside the same lock. `_cacheName` (line 283) already does all access under its lock and shows the intended pattern.
unique.rationale: The ctor cache Dictionary is read outside the lock that guards its writes, with no volatile read or double-checked locking, so a resize concurrent with a read yields IndexOutOfRangeException rewritten as a misleading InvalidCtor - or, on netstandard2.0, a spin on a corrupted bucket chain. Common shared-mapper setup.

unique.title: Dictionary key/value types are taken from the type's own generic arguments, so a single-type-parameter Dictionary subclass throws IndexOutOfRangeException on both serialize and deserialize
unique.mech: Both the serialize and deserialize dictionary paths assume that if the type is generic, its own generic argument list is `[TKey, TValue]`. For a type that *derives* from `Dictionary<K,V>` with a different arity the assumption is wrong: `type.GetGenericArguments()` returns the subclass's own parameters. With one type parameter, `generics[1]` throws IndexOutOfRangeException. The deserialize side (BsonMapper.Deserialize.cs:241-245) is worse: it tests `instance.GetType().IsGenericType` but then reads the arguments from `type`, so the guard and the indexed access are on different types.
unique.fail: Entity property `public NamedList<int> Buckets { get; set; }` where `class NamedList<T> : Dictionary<string, T> { }` (or the same value held in an `object`-declared property, since line 134 replaces `object` with the runtime type). Insert -> Serialize: `obj is IDictionary` is true, `type.GetTypeInfo().IsGenericType` is true, `type.GetGenericArguments()` == `[typeof(int)]`, and `generics[1]` throws `IndexOutOfRangeException: Index was outside the bounds of the array` out of Insert. Read hits the identical crash at BsonMapper.Deserialize.cs:243.
unique.fix: Resolve the key/value types from the closed `IDictionary<,>` interface actually implemented by the type (walk `type.GetInterfaces()` for `IsGenericType && GetGenericTypeDefinition() == typeof(IDictionary<,>)` and take its two arguments), falling back to `typeof(object)` when none is found. Apply the same fix on the deserialize side and base the decision on one type, not on `instance.GetType()` for the test and `type` for the arguments.
unique.rationale: Both dictionary paths assume the type's own generic arguments are [TKey,TValue], so a single-type-parameter Dictionary subclass throws IndexOutOfRangeException on serialize and deserialize; the deserialize side even guards on instance.GetType() while indexing type.

unique.title: Deserializing into a non-generic subclass of Dictionary<K,V> keeps keyType=object, producing string keys that the target dictionary rejects
unique.mech: The key/value types are resolved only when `instance.GetType().IsGenericType` is true. A class that closes the generic in its declaration (`class X : Dictionary<int,string>`) is not itself generic, so keyType and valueType stay `typeof(object)`. DeserializeDictionary then takes `TypeDescriptor.GetConverter(typeof(object))`, whose CanConvertFrom(string) is false, falls into `Convert.ChangeType(element.Key, typeof(object))` which returns the BSON field name unchanged as a String, and assigns `dict["5"] = ...` through the non-generic IDictionary indexer of a `Dictionary<int,string>`. Serialization of the same type works (SerializeDictionary falls back to `key.GetType()` for the converter), so writes succeed and only reads fail.
unique.fail: Entity property `public ErrorCodeMap Codes { get; set; }` where `class ErrorCodeMap : Dictionary<int, string> { }`. Insert stores `{ "5": "not found" }` correctly. FindAll -> Deserialize -> DeserializeDictionary(keyType=object) produces the String key "5" and `dict["5"] = "not found"` throws `ArgumentException: The value \"5\" is not of type \"System.Int32\" and cannot be used in this generic collection.` The stored documents are unreadable through the typed API.
unique.fix: Resolve TKey/TValue from the closed `IDictionary<,>` interface implemented by `instance.GetType()` (or `type`), which works for both direct generic dictionaries and subclasses that close the generic; only fall back to `typeof(object)` for non-generic dictionaries such as Hashtable.
unique.rationale: A non-generic subclass of Dictionary<K,V> leaves keyType=object, so keys come back as strings and the typed indexer throws ArgumentException - writes succeed and only reads fail, making the stored documents unreadable through the typed API.

unique.title: Constructor parameter matching uses culture-sensitive ToLower(), so immutable entities fail to deserialize under Turkish/Azeri cultures
unique.mech: GetTypeCtor pairs constructor parameters with mapped members using `member.MemberName.ToLower() == par.Name.ToLower()`. `String.ToLower()` uses CurrentCulture; under tr-TR/az-Latn the uppercase 'I' maps to 'ı' (U+0131) while a lowercase 'i' stays 'i', so a PascalCase member and its conventional camelCase constructor parameter stop comparing equal whenever the name contains an 'I'/'i' pair. No parameter match means the ctor is skipped; with no parameterless ctor either, `GetTypeCtor` returns null and Deserialize (BsonMapper.Deserialize.cs:230-234) falls back to `Reflection.CreateInstance`, whose `Expression.New(type)` fails for a type without a default ctor.
unique.fail: Immutable entity `class Customer { public int Id {get;} public string Name {get;} public Customer(int id, string name) { ... } }` (idiomatic camelCase ctor parameters). On a machine whose CurrentCulture is tr-TR, "Id".ToLower() == "ıd" but "id".ToLower() == "id", so the parameter never matches, the ctor is rejected, and `col.FindAll()` throws LiteException.InvalidCtor("Failed to create instance for type 'Customer'..."). The same code path works correctly on en-US. "ItemId"/"itemId" fails identically.
unique.fix: Compare with `string.Equals(member.MemberName, par.Name, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` (or ToLowerInvariant) instead of culture-sensitive ToLower().
unique.rationale: Constructor parameter matching uses culture-sensitive ToLower, so under tr-TR/az any name containing i/I stops matching and immutable entities fail with InvalidCtor; the expression parser deliberately uses ToUpperInvariant, so this is an oversight.

unique.title: DateTimeOffset dictionary keys are written with CurrentCulture but always parsed invariantly, making the documents unreadable
unique.mech: SerializeDictionary formats DateTimeOffset keys with `ToString(CultureInfo.CurrentCulture)` while every other key type is deliberately made culture-invariant (see the comment immediately above at lines 211-213). DeserializeDictionary (BsonMapper.Deserialize.cs:349) always reads keys back with `keyConverter.ConvertFromInvariantString(element.Key)`, i.e. DateTimeOffsetConverter parsing under InvariantCulture. Any CurrentCulture whose date/time spelling is not invariant-parseable produces a field name that can never be converted back.
unique.fail: Entity property `public Dictionary<DateTimeOffset, decimal> Prices { get; set; }`. On a de-DE machine the key is stored as the field name "01.01.2024 10:00:00 +01:00". Any subsequent read (on any machine, since the read side is fixed to InvariantCulture) calls DateTimeOffsetConverter.ConvertFromInvariantString("01.01.2024 10:00:00 +01:00") -> `FormatException: \"01.01.2024 10:00:00 +01:00\" is not a valid value for DateTimeOffset` escaping FindAll. Cultures with a non-Gregorian default calendar (e.g. ar-SA, th-TH) corrupt the key value outright.
unique.fix: Write DateTimeOffset keys with a round-trippable invariant format (`ToString("o", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`), matching the DateTime branch directly above, and if legacy files must keep loading, accept both invariant and CurrentCulture parses on the read side rather than keeping the write side culture-dependent.
unique.rationale: DateTimeOffset dictionary keys are written with CurrentCulture but always read with ConvertFromInvariantString, so documents written on a de-DE machine are permanently unreadable on any machine - and the adjacent comment shows invariance was the intent.

unique.title: Bitwise & and | are translated to logical AND/OR, producing an InvalidCastException at query execution
unique.mech: `ExpressionType.And`/`Or` is the node type C# produces for the *bitwise* operators on integral (and enum) operands, as well as for non-short-circuiting boolean `&`/`|`. GetOperator maps both to ` AND ` / ` OR ` unconditionally. The parser compiles AND/OR as `left.AsBoolean && right.AsBoolean` (BsonExpressionParser.CreateLogicExpression, line 1362-1370), and `BsonValue.AsBoolean` is a hard unbox: `(bool)this.RawValue` (Document/BsonValue.cs:230). A numeric or string BsonValue therefore throws. On top of that, the emitted text `($.Flags AND @p0 = @p1)` is re-associated by the parser as `$.Flags AND (@p0 = @p1)` because `=` has higher precedence than AND.
unique.fail: The standard flags test `col.Find(x => (x.Permissions & 4) == 4)` (or the enum form `(x.Perm & Perm.Write) == Perm.Write`) generates `($.Permissions AND @p0 = @p1)`. At execution `$.Permissions` is an Int32 BsonValue, so `AsBoolean` runs `(bool)(object)4` and throws System.InvalidCastException ("Unable to cast object of type 'System.Int32' to type 'System.Boolean'") from inside the query pipeline, with no hint that the LINQ translation was wrong.
unique.fix: Map `ExpressionType.And`/`Or` to AND/OR only when `node.Type == typeof(bool)` (or `bool?`); for integral operands throw NotSupportedException (there is no bitwise operator in BsonExpression) rather than silently emitting a logical operator.
unique.rationale: ExpressionType.And/Or covers bitwise operators on integrals, so the standard flags test `(x.Flags & 4) == 4` becomes ` AND ` and AsBoolean's hard unbox throws InvalidCastException from inside the pipeline, with the emitted text also mis-associated.

unique.title: _dbRefType leaks past a terminal DbRef member access and rewrites the root document's _id to $id
unique.mech: ResolveMember stores the DbRef type in the instance field `_dbRefType` so that a *child* `_id` access can be renamed to `$id`. The field is only reset by the next ResolveMember call, so if a DbRef member is the last member in its chain the flag stays set for the remainder of the expression. The guard `member.DeclaringType.IsAssignableFrom(_dbRefType)` is satisfied by any later Id member whose declaring type is the DbRef type itself (self-referencing entity) or a base class shared with it, so an unrelated sibling access is rewritten.
unique.fail: `class Node { [BsonId] public int Id; [BsonRef("nodes")] public Node Parent; }` and `col.Find(x => x.Parent == null && x.Id == 5)`. Visiting `x.Parent` sets `_dbRefType = typeof(Node)`; visiting `x.Id` then sees `Node.IsAssignableFrom(Node)` and FieldName "_id", so it emits `$.$id`. The final expression `(($.Parent = @p0) AND ($.$id = @p1))` resolves `$.$id` to null at the root document and returns 0 documents instead of the node with Id 5. The same leak makes `x => new Node { Parent = p, Id = 5 }` emit `{Parent:..., $id:@p0}`, which fails to parse.
unique.fix: Track the DbRef type positionally instead of in a sticky field — e.g. clear it when the member-access chain ends (in VisitMember after the pop) or derive "parent is DbRef" from the parent MemberExpression on `_memberAccessNodes` rather than from mutable visitor state.
unique.rationale: _dbRefType persists past a terminal DbRef member access, so a sibling Id access on a self-referencing entity is rewritten to $.$id and the query returns zero rows. Silently wrong but needs the specific self-referencing DbRef shape.

unique.title: Commit()/Rollback() dispose the engine in their finally when the engine throws, silently discarding a still-active transaction and making retry impossible
unique.mech: `LiteEngine.Commit` throws `LiteException("Current transaction contains open cursors. Close cursors before run Commit()")` (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Transaction.cs:42) *before* committing, leaving the transaction in `TransactionState.Active` so the caller can close its cursors and retry. `SharedEngine.Commit`'s `finally` runs regardless: it clears `_transactionRunning` and calls `CloseDatabase()`, which disposes the engine. `LiteEngine.Close` -> `TransactionMonitor.Dispose` -> `TransactionService.Dispose` releases the transaction's dirty pages without committing them (LiteDB/Engine/Services/TransactionService.cs:412-445), so the pending writes are discarded.
unique.fail: Shared mode, single thread: `db.BeginTrans(); col.Insert(a); col.Insert(b); var r = db.Execute("SELECT $ FROM c"); r.Read(); db.Commit();`. `Commit` throws the open-cursor `LiteException`; the application follows the message, disposes `r`, and calls `db.Commit()` again — which now returns `false` because `_engine` was nulled by the finally. Documents a and b were dropped by the engine teardown, yet the second `Commit()` reports "nothing to commit", so the caller has no signal that the write was lost.
unique.fix: Only clear `_transactionRunning`/close the database when the commit (or rollback) actually terminated the transaction — e.g. move the teardown into the success path and leave the transaction intact when `_engine.Commit()` throws a recoverable LiteException.
unique.rationale: Commit's finally disposes the engine even when LiteEngine.Commit threw a recoverable open-cursor error, discarding the still-active transaction's dirty pages; the retry the message invites then returns false, so the loss is reported as 'nothing to commit'.

unique.title: SharedDataReader.Dispose leaks the cross-process mutex if the inner reader's Dispose throws
unique.mech: `_dispose()` — the callback that runs `SharedEngine.CloseDatabase()` and releases the named mutex — is invoked after `_reader.Dispose()` with no `try/finally`. `_reader` is a `BsonDataReader` whose `Dispose` disposes the query enumerator, which runs the `QueryExecutor` pipeline's `finally`/`OnDispose` blocks (snapshot exit, `_monitor.ReleaseTransaction`, `transaction.Dispose`, which can throw `AggregateException` per LiteDB/Engine/Services/TransactionService.cs:444). `_disposed` is already set to true, so a second Dispose attempt is a no-op and the mutex acquisition is lost permanently.
unique.fail: A shared-mode query whose snapshot/page release fails during teardown (e.g. an I/O error while releasing the transaction's pages) throws out of `_reader.Dispose()`. `_dispose()` never runs, so `Global\...Mutex` stays owned by the current thread and `_engine` stays non-null: every other process blocks forever on `OpenDatabase`, and the exception the caller sees is the teardown error rather than a released-and-reported failure.
unique.fix: `try { _reader.Dispose(); } finally { _dispose(); }`.
unique.rationale: _dispose() (mutex release + CloseDatabase) runs after _reader.Dispose() with no try/finally and _disposed is already set, so a teardown error permanently leaks the cross-process mutex acquisition. Same family as the other SharedEngine leaks.

unique.title: Long database paths on Linux/macOS bypass the SHA-1 mutex-name fallback and fail mutex creation
unique.mech: Both `CreateUsingUriEncodingWithFallback` (Default strategy) and `CreateUsingUriEncoding` apply the length guard and SHA-1 fallback only `if (IsWindows())`. On Unix, .NET's named mutexes are backed by files under `/tmp/.dotnet/shm/global/<name>`, so the name is bounded by the filesystem's `NAME_MAX` (255); the runtime maps an over-long name to `ERROR_FILENAME_EXCED_RANGE` and `Mutex`'s constructor turns that into `ArgumentException`. `SharedEngine`'s constructor (lines 28-36) only translates `NotSupportedException`, so this escapes raw. URI escaping inflates the name aggressively: every `/` becomes `%2F`, every space `%20`, and each non-ASCII character 9 characters (3 UTF-8 bytes x %XX).
unique.fail: On Linux, a user whose data directory contains non-ASCII names — e.g. `/home/пользователь/документы/приложение/данные/база.db` (~30 non-ASCII characters) — escapes to well over 250 characters. `new LiteDatabase("Filename=...;Connection=shared")` then throws `ArgumentException` (name too long) from `SharedMutexFactory.Create` -> `new Mutex(false, fullName)` instead of taking the SHA-1 fallback the Default strategy promises; shared mode is unusable for that path and the error names none of the real cause.
unique.fix: Apply the length guard on all platforms (using a byte-length bound appropriate for the Unix shared-memory name limit), not just on Windows.
unique.rationale: The length guard and SHA-1 fallback are gated on IsWindows(), so long or non-ASCII Unix paths bypass the fallback the Default strategy promises. Plausible, but the exact runtime failure for an over-long Unix named mutex (ArgumentException vs other) should be confirmed on the target platform.

unique.title: Everything after the first statement's `;` is silently discarded — multi-statement SQL executes only the first command with no error
unique.mech: `SqlParser.Execute()` dispatches exactly one command and returns its reader. Every command parser terminates with `Expect(TokenType.EOF, TokenType.SemiColon)`, i.e. a `;` is accepted as a valid terminator, but neither `Execute()` nor any caller ever checks that the tokenizer is actually at EOF afterwards, and nothing loops over remaining statements. The only callers create the parser and call `Execute()` once (LiteDatabase.cs:250 and :264, SysQuery.cs:26). So text following the semicolon is neither executed nor reported — it is silently dropped. The parser accepting `;` at all is what makes this a trap: without `;` support the trailing text would be rejected by the final `Expect`.
unique.fail: `db.Execute("CREATE INDEX idx_name ON customers ($.Name); UPDATE customers SET Active = false WHERE $.LastLogin < @0;", cutoff)` returns a successful reader for the CREATE INDEX and reports no error, while the UPDATE never runs. A migration/seed script executed with one Execute call therefore applies only its first statement, and the user has no signal that the rest was ignored.
unique.fix: Either loop in `Execute()` until the tokenizer reaches EOF (executing each statement in turn), or, after the command returns, assert `_tokenizer.LookAhead().Type == TokenType.EOF` and throw `LiteException.UnexpectedToken` on leftover input.
unique.rationale: Command parsers accept ';' as a terminator but nothing checks for EOF afterwards and nothing loops, so everything after the first statement is silently discarded - a migration script applies only its first statement with no error.

unique.title: Statement and auto-id keyword dispatch uses culture-sensitive ToUpper(), breaking lowercase `insert`/`begin`/`commit`/`rebuild`/`checkpoint`/`explain` under Turkish-family cultures
unique.mech: `ahead.Value.ToUpper()` uses `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`. In tr-TR/az-* cultures lowercase 'i' uppercases to 'İ' (U+0130), so `"insert".ToUpper()` yields "İNSERT", which never matches the ordinal switch label "INSERT" and falls through to `default: throw LiteException.UnexpectedToken(ahead)`. Every other keyword comparison in the parser goes through `Token.Is`/`Token.Expect`, which correctly use `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` (Tokenizer.cs:165-170), and the expression parser deliberately uses `ToUpperInvariant()` (BsonExpressionParser.cs:127, 1300) — so this is an inconsistency, not a deliberate choice. The identical bug exists at LiteDB/Client/SqlParser/Commands/Insert.cs:47 (`switch(type.Value.ToUpper())`) for the auto-id names GUID/INT/OBJECTID.
unique.fail: On a machine whose current culture is tr-TR (or with `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = new CultureInfo("tr-TR")`), `db.Execute("insert into orders values {_id:1}")` throws `LiteException` "Unexpected token `insert`", while `db.Execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES {_id:1}")` works. Affected statements are exactly those whose keyword contains a lowercase 'i': insert, begin, commit, rebuild, checkpoint, explain. Likewise `INSERT INTO orders:guid VALUES {...}` throws "Expected `DATE, GUID, INT, LONG, OBJECTID`" even though `guid` is spelled correctly.
unique.fix: Use `ToUpperInvariant()` in both places (or compare with `string.Equals(..., StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`).
unique.rationale: Statement and auto-id dispatch use culture-sensitive ToUpper against ordinal switch labels, so under tr-TR every lowercase keyword containing 'i' (insert/begin/commit/rebuild/checkpoint/explain) throws UnexpectedToken; every other keyword comparison in the parser is OrdinalIgnoreCase.

unique.title: BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK silently swallow an unrecognized trailing clause and execute anyway
unique.mech: The token after the verb is validated only as "some Word, EOF or ;". If it is a Word other than TRANS/TRANSACTION, the `if` body is skipped, the terminator is never validated, and the transaction command is executed regardless — the rest of the statement is never read. The same three lines appear in Rollback.cs:18-23, Commit.cs:18-23 and Begin.cs:18-23. A malformed transaction-control statement therefore performs a full, unqualified operation instead of raising `UnexpectedToken`.
unique.fail: A user porting SQL writes `db.Execute("ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1")`. LiteDB has no savepoints, so the expected outcome is a parse error; instead `token` is the Word "TO", the TRANS check fails, `SAVEPOINT sp1` is never read, and `_engine.Rollback()` discards the *entire* transaction — all work since BEGIN is lost with no error returned. Similarly `COMMIT TRANSACTIONS` (typo) commits, and `BEGIN WORK` opens a transaction while silently ignoring `WORK`.
unique.fix: After the optional TRANS/TRANSACTION word, require EOF/`;` in all branches: if the token is a Word that is not TRANS/TRANSACTION, throw `LiteException.UnexpectedToken(token, "TRANS|TRANSACTION")`.
unique.rationale: An unrecognised word after BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK skips the terminator check and the command executes anyway, so `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1` silently discards the entire transaction instead of raising a syntax error.

unique.title: Collation implements IEqualityComparer<BsonValue> with a hash code that contradicts its Equals
unique.mech: Collation.Equals(x,y) delegates to Compare -> BsonValue.CompareTo(other, collation), which is culture- and CompareOptions-aware (case-insensitive by default) and also numerically cross-type (Int32 5 compares equal to Double 5.0). GetHashCode(obj) instead returns obj.GetHashCode(), which is `17*37 + Type.GetHashCode()` then `*37 + RawValue.GetHashCode()` (LiteDB/Document/BsonValue.cs:678-683) - i.e. ordinal, case-sensitive, and type-discriminating. Equal-per-comparer values therefore produce different hash codes, violating the IEqualityComparer<T> contract. Collation is public API and is declared as IEqualityComparer<BsonValue>, so callers can legitimately hand it to HashSet<BsonValue>, Dictionary, Distinct, GroupBy or Except. (Inside the engine only the direct Equals call in GroupByPipe.cs:110 is used, so the library itself does not currently hit this.)
unique.fail: new[] { new BsonValue("ABC"), new BsonValue("abc") }.Distinct(Collation.Default) returns 2 items even though Collation.Default.Equals("ABC","abc") is true (CurrentCulture/IgnoreCase), because the two values land in different hash buckets and Equals is never consulted. Same for new BsonValue(5) vs new BsonValue(5.0) under any collation: Equals is true, hash codes differ (Type is part of the hash), so a HashSet<BsonValue>(collation) happily stores both.
unique.fix: Compute a hash consistent with Compare: for strings use `_compareInfo.GetHashCode(value, SortOptions)` (or GetSortKey), and normalize numeric types to a single representation so Int32/Int64/Double/Decimal that compare equal hash equally.
unique.rationale: Collation implements IEqualityComparer<BsonValue> with Equals via collation-aware CompareTo but GetHashCode via BsonValue's type-and-ordinal hash, so Distinct/HashSet/GroupBy over a public Collation silently fail to unify equal values. Public API contract violation; the engine itself only calls Equals directly.

unique.title: DictionaryExtensions.GetValue swallows every exception and discards the original as inner, hiding the real connection-string error
unique.mech: The whole conversion body is wrapped in `catch (Exception)` and replaced by `new LiteException(0, $"Invalid connection string value type for `{key}`")` - the caught exception is not passed as the inner exception, and ErrorCode 0 is used (so LiteException.IsCritical and any ErrorCode-based handling see an unclassified error). The catch is also unfiltered, so it converts genuinely unrelated failures (OutOfMemoryException, a TypeInitializationException raised while resolving the target enum, InvalidCastException from the (T)(object) casts) into the same misleading 'invalid value type' message. Note also that the fall-through path uses Convert.ChangeType(value, typeof(T)) with the ambient CurrentCulture, so numeric parsing of connection-string values is culture-dependent.
unique.fail: new LiteDatabase("Filename=db.db; Transaction Pages=abc") -> ConnectionString.cs:122 calls _values.GetValue<int>("transaction pages") -> Convert.ChangeType throws FormatException('Input string was not in a correct format'), which is discarded; the user gets LiteException(ErrorCode 0, "Invalid connection string value type for `transaction pages`") with InnerException == null, so neither the offending value nor the underlying parse failure is recoverable from the exception. The same wrapper is used for `collation`, so a bad collation string (e.g. 'Collation=en-US/ignorecase', where Enum.Parse is case-sensitive) also loses the real ArgumentException.
unique.fix: Catch only the expected conversion exceptions (FormatException, OverflowException, ArgumentException, InvalidCastException), include the offending value, and pass the original exception through the `LiteException(int, Exception, string, params object[])` ctor that already exists at LiteException.cs:88. Use an invariant culture for Convert.ChangeType.
unique.rationale: An unfiltered catch replaces every failure with LiteException(0, 'Invalid connection string value type') and discards the original as inner, so the real parse error (and unrelated failures like OOM/TypeInitialization) is unrecoverable; Convert.ChangeType also uses CurrentCulture.

unique.title: On a mapping failure the half-built EntityMapper is removed from the cache but a concurrent thread keeps using it, silently serializing documents with missing fields
unique.mech: GetEntityMapper publishes an empty EntityMapper shell into _entities before BuildEntityMapper fills mapper.Members (needed for recursion). A concurrent caller reads that shell through TryGetValue and holds the reference. If BuildEntityMapper throws, `_entities.TryRemove(type, out _)` removes it from the dictionary but cannot revoke the reference the other thread already holds; the finally then cancels the initialization token, so that thread's WaitForInitialization returns successfully and it proceeds with a partially populated Members list.
unique.fail: Thread A and thread B first-map the same entity type; A's BuildEntityMapper throws halfway (e.g. Reflection.CreateGenericSetter fails on a member, or a user ResolveMember callback throws) after adding 3 of 10 members. A surfaces a LiteException MAPPING_ERROR, but B's WaitForInitialization returns normally and B calls SerializeObject with the 3-member mapper, inserting documents that silently lack the other 7 fields.
unique.fix: Record the build outcome on the EntityMapper itself (success/failed + the exception) and have WaitForInitialization rethrow the stored failure instead of returning a mapper that was abandoned.
unique.rationale: On a build failure the half-built mapper is removed from the cache but a concurrent thread already holds the reference, and the finally cancels the token so its WaitForInitialization succeeds - documents are then serialized with fields silently missing. Same publish-before-build root cause as [183], different symptom.

unique.title: ARRAY_INDEX passes an unclamped negative index straight to the array indexer (`arr.Count > idx` accepts negative idx)
unique.mech: Negative array indexing is a supported syntax: the parser explicitly accepts `[-N]` (LiteDB/Document/Expression/Parser/BsonExpressionParser.cs:1117-1121, `index = -Convert.ToInt32(...)`). ARRAY_INDEX converts it with `idx = arr.Count + index` but then only validates the **upper** bound (`if (arr.Count > idx)`). When `|index| > arr.Count`, `idx` is negative and the guard is trivially satisfied, so `arr[idx]` is evaluated. `BsonArray.this[int]` (LiteDB/Document/BsonArray.cs:49-53) forwards to `List<BsonValue>`'s indexer, which throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Nothing between the compiled expression and QueryExecutor catches it. The same hole is reachable through the `expr.Type == Parameter` branch (line 291) with a negative parameter value.
unique.fail: Document `{_id:1, items:[10,20,30]}`. Query `db.Execute("SELECT $.items[-5] FROM col")` (or `col.Find("$.items[-5] = 10")`, or `SELECT $.items[@0]` with `@0 = -5`): `idx = 3 + (-5) = -2`, the guard `3 > -2` passes, and `arr[-2]` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Index was out of range` out of the query instead of returning `BsonValue.Null` (which is what every other out-of-range index returns).
unique.fix: Validate both bounds: `if (idx >= 0 && idx < arr.Count) return arr[idx]; return BsonValue.Null;`
unique.rationale: ARRAY_INDEX validates only the upper bound after `idx = arr.Count + index`, so a supported negative index whose magnitude exceeds Count reaches List's indexer and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException instead of returning Null like every other out-of-range index.

unique.title: SortContainer.Insert validates key length after writing it, so oversized sort keys surface as ArgumentOutOfRangeException instead of the intended LiteException
unique.mech: The length guard runs one statement too late. `WriteIndexKey` for a String/Binary value computes `strLength = (ushort)Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount(str)` and calls `ExtendedLengthHelper.WriteLength`, whose first line is `if (length > 1023) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(length));` (LiteDB/Utils/ExtendedLengthHelper.cs:33). So for every string sort key of 1024..65535 UTF-8 bytes the write throws first and the carefully worded `LiteException.InvalidIndexKey("Sort key must be less than 1023 bytes.")` on the next line is unreachable. The `(ushort)` cast also silently wraps for keys above 65535 bytes, so the value handed to the length guard is not the real key length; for a 65636-byte key the wrapped length (100) passes WriteLength and a length byte of 100 is persisted while `offset` advances by the true 65638 bytes, leaving the on-container framing inconsistent — that particular corruption is currently masked only because line 74's post-write check then aborts the whole sort.
unique.fail: `col.Insert(new BsonDocument { ["_id"]=1, ["body"]=new string('x',2000) }); db.Execute("SELECT $._id FROM col ORDER BY $.body")` fails with `ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Specified argument was out of the range of valid values. (Parameter 'length')` thrown from deep inside ExtendedLengthHelper, with no mention of sort keys or of the 1023-byte limit, instead of the intended LiteException. Callers cannot distinguish this from an internal bug.
unique.fix: Move the `keyLength`/`MAX_INDEX_KEY_LENGTH` check above `buffer.WriteIndexKey(...)`, and compute it from the un-truncated byte count (`IndexNode.GetKeyLength(item.Key, false)`) rather than relying on the ushort cast inside WriteIndexKey.
unique.rationale: The key-length guard runs one statement after the write, so ExtendedLengthHelper throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException('length') first and the intended LiteException about the 1023-byte sort-key limit is unreachable. Misleading error, no data impact. Canonical of the pair.

unique.title: Sorting a grouped projection buffers every group and its sort key in memory with no spill path
unique.mech: Document-level ORDER BY spills to the temp sort file through SortService/SortDisk, which is why `BasePipe.OrderBy` can sort arbitrarily large result sets in bounded memory. `OrderGroupedResult` cannot use that machinery (grouped projections are synthesized documents with no datafile RawId to re-load), so it materialises the full grouped result set — one `BsonDocument` plus one `SortKey` array per group — into a `List<>` before sorting. `query.Limit`/`query.Offset` are applied only after the buffer is fully built (lines 266-285), so a small LIMIT does not bound the footprint. The number of groups is O(number of documents) for a high-cardinality group key.
unique.fail: `SELECT $._id, COUNT($._id) FROM big GROUP BY $._id ORDER BY $._id LIMIT 10` over a collection with several million documents produces one GroupedResult per document; the List grows to millions of BsonDocument + SortKey pairs and the process OOMs, even though only 10 rows are ever returned and the equivalent non-grouped `SELECT $._id FROM big ORDER BY $._id LIMIT 10` completes in bounded memory via the disk sorter.
unique.fix: For the limit/offset case keep only a bounded top-(offset+limit) heap instead of the whole buffer, and/or spill grouped projections to the sort disk by serializing the projected document alongside the key.
unique.rationale: OrderGroupedResult materialises every group plus its sort key before applying LIMIT/OFFSET, with no spill path, so a high-cardinality GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10 OOMs where the equivalent ungrouped query streams in bounded memory. Design limit rather than a leak.

unique.title: FileReaderV7.ReadPage() ignores the short-read count and reuses an uncleared buffer, parsing a mix of two pages
unique.mech: `_buffer` is a single 4096-byte field reused for every page and never cleared, and the return value of `_stream.Read(_buffer, 0, V7_PAGE_SIZE)` is discarded. FileReaderV7 never calls IStreamFactory.GetLength() (which is what crops a file to a PAGE_SIZE multiple), so a v4 file whose length is not a multiple of 4096 is read as-is. When the requested page only partially exists (or any Stream returns a short read - EngineSettings.DataStream lets callers supply an arbitrary Stream), the tail of `_buffer` still holds the previously read page, and the resulting BsonDocument is a Frankenstein of two pages: header/itemCount from the new bytes, block data from the old page. FileReaderV8.ReadPage does validate this (`ENSURE(read == PAGE_SIZE, ...)` at line 536); V7 does not.
unique.fail: A v4 datafile of 10*4096+500 bytes (truncated mid-page, e.g. copy interrupted). During `Upgrade=true`, ReadPage(10) reads 500 fresh bytes; bytes 500..4095 are page 9's content. If the partial page is pageType 4, its block list is built from stale page-9 bytes, so `block["data"]` holds another document's bytes; BsonSerializer.Deserialize either throws (aborting the whole upgrade, since FileReaderV7 has no try/catch) or succeeds and a corrupted/duplicated document is inserted into the new v5 database and presented as genuine upgraded data.
unique.fix: Read in a loop until PAGE_SIZE bytes are obtained, treat a short read as end-of-page (return null / raise a recorded error), clear `_buffer` before each read, and change the bounds guard to `(pageID + 1) * V7_PAGE_SIZE > _stream.Length`.
unique.rationale: The short-read count is discarded and the single 4096-byte _buffer is never cleared, so a v4 file whose length is not a page multiple is parsed as a mix of two pages and a corrupted or duplicated document can be inserted into the upgraded database as genuine. FileReaderV8 validates this; V7 does not.

unique.title: FileReaderV7 dereferences ReadPage()'s null result in three places - NullReferenceException aborts the v4 upgrade
unique.mech: ReadPage() returns null for any pageID beyond the stream length (line 189), but only VisitIndexPages (line 422) checks for null. GetDocuments dereferences the result at line 148 (`dataPage["pageType"]`), GetIndexes at line 105 (`page["indexes"]` after ReadPage at 103) and ReadExtendData at line 391 (`page["pageType"]`). Page IDs come straight from the file (`(uint)dataBlock["pageID"].AsInt32` - any negative value other than -1 becomes a huge uint, any stale/corrupt id points past EOF). FileReaderV7 has no try/catch anywhere, so the NullReferenceException propagates through RebuildContent (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Rebuild.cs:105-110), which calls this.Close(ex) and rethrows out of the LiteEngine constructor.
unique.fail: A v4 datafile truncated from 12 to 10 pages (or with one corrupted dataBlock pageID). Opening it with `Upgrade=true`: GetDocuments reads an index node whose dataBlock.pageID is 11; ReadPage(11) returns null because 11*4096 > file length; line 148 throws NullReferenceException. The user gets an opaque NRE instead of a LiteDB 'invalid datafile' error, the upgrade aborts, the v4 file can never be opened by v5, and a stray '-temp' database file is left behind.
unique.fix: Return a typed failure (or throw LiteException.InvalidDatafileState) from ReadPage for out-of-range pages and null-check every call site; better, mirror the V8 reader and record recoverable read failures instead of throwing.
unique.rationale: ReadPage's null return is checked in only one of four call sites, so a truncated or corrupt v4 file aborts the upgrade with an opaque NullReferenceException (V7 has no try/catch anywhere) and leaves a stray -temp file.

unique.title: FileReaderV7.ReadPage() uses unvalidated length/level fields from the file: negative array size and out-of-range copies
unique.mech: Every length/count in the page body is taken verbatim from the (untrusted) file and handed to ByteReader, which performs no bounds checks: ByteReader.ReadBytes does `new byte[count]` + Buffer.BlockCopy (LiteDB/Engine/FileReader/Legacy/ByteReader.cs:106-115) and ReadString does `Encoding.UTF8.GetString(_buffer, _pos, length)` with an Int32 length read from the file (line 121-128). Concretely: (1) line 335 `reader.ReadBytes((levels - 1) * (6 + 6))` where `levels` is a raw byte - levels == 0 yields ReadBytes(-12) -> `new byte[-12]` -> OverflowException; (2) line 359 `block["data"] = reader.ReadBytes(length)` with a ushort length up to 65535 against a 4096-byte buffer -> ArgumentException from BlockCopy; (3) line 371 `reader.ReadBytes(page["itemCount"].AsInt32)` for extend pages, same overflow; (4) collection-page `reader.ReadString()` with a garbage Int32 length -> ArgumentOutOfRangeException. None of these is caught in FileReaderV7, so the non-LiteDB exception escapes RebuildContent (which first calls this.Close(ex)) and aborts the whole upgrade, masking the real cause ('invalid datafile') behind OverflowException/ArgumentException.
unique.fail: A v4 file with one corrupted index page (itemCount > 0 and a node whose `levels` byte was zeroed by a torn write) is opened with `Upgrade=true`. ReadPage(pageType 3) reaches line 335 with levels == 0 and throws OverflowException ('Arithmetic operation resulted in overflow') from inside `new byte[-12]`. The database cannot be upgraded or opened at all, and the reported exception points at nothing the user can act on - while the V8 reader would have logged the page in _rebuild_errors and continued.
unique.fix: Validate against the page buffer before every read (add bounds checks in ByteReader / clamp counts to the remaining 4096 bytes), reject levels == 0, and wrap per-page parsing in a try/catch that records a FileReaderError (as FileReaderV8 does) instead of aborting the upgrade.
unique.rationale: Length/level/count fields are taken verbatim from the file into ByteReader, which does no bounds checking, so levels==0 yields new byte[-12] (OverflowException) and oversized lengths throw from BlockCopy - aborting the whole upgrade with an unactionable exception where V8 would log and continue.

unique.title: FileReaderV7.Open() throws NullReferenceException when page 0 is not parsed as a header page
unique.mech: IsVersion() (line 81-87) only checks the HEADER_INFO string at offset 25 and the version byte at offset 52; it does not check the pageType byte at offset 4. ReadPage() only fills `userVersion`/`password`/`salt`/`collections` when `page["pageType"] == 1` (line 219). If a file passes IsVersion but its pageType byte is not 1, `_header["salt"]` returns BsonValue.Null (BsonDocument indexer returns Null for a missing key, LiteDB/Document/BsonDocument.cs:55), `.AsBinary` returns null (`RawValue as byte[]`, BsonValue.cs:227) and `IsFullZero()` dereferences it (`int len = data.Length;` in LiteDB/Utils/Extensions/BufferExtensions.cs:35) -> NullReferenceException. The same holds for `_header["password"]` and for GetPragmas()'s `_header["userVersion"].AsInt32`. GetCollections()/GetIndexes() would likewise NRE on `_header["collections"].AsDocument` being null.
unique.fail: A v4 file whose first byte block was partially overwritten so that the pageType byte at offset 4 is 0 while bytes 25..52 still contain '** This is a LiteDB file **' and version 7 (or a deliberately crafted 4 KB file with those bytes at offset 25/52). RebuildService's ctor accepts it as _fileVersion = 7, FileReaderV7.Open() then throws NullReferenceException at the `_header["salt"].AsBinary.IsFullZero()` check instead of LiteException.InvalidDatabase, so the caller cannot distinguish 'not a LiteDB file' from a real bug.
unique.fix: Have ReadPage(0) require pageType == 1 (throw LiteException.InvalidDatabase otherwise), or check `_header.ContainsKey("salt")` in Open() before dereferencing; also include the pageType byte in IsVersion().
unique.rationale: IsVersion checks only the header string and version byte, not pageType, so a file that passes it but is not a header page NREs on _header['salt'].AsBinary.IsFullZero() instead of raising InvalidDatabase - the caller cannot tell 'not a LiteDB file' from an engine bug.

unique.title: FileReaderV8 extend-block loop skips the footer position/length validation applied to the first block
unique.mech: For the first data block the reader validates the footer slot (line 159-160: `ENSURE(position > 0 && length > 0)` and `ENSURE(position + length < PAGE_SIZE)`). Inside the extend chain only `ENSURE(length > 0)` is checked (line 199) - `position` may be 0 (empty slot) or position+length may run past the 8192-byte page, and BufferSlice.Slice performs no bounds validation at all (LiteDB/Utils/BufferSlice.cs:129-141, and the underlying PageBuffer array is exactly PAGE_SIZE bytes, allocated at line 514). The slice therefore either reads bytes belonging to a different segment of the same page (silently splicing unrelated bytes into the middle of the document byte stream) or, when Offset+Count exceeds the array, throws IndexOutOfRangeException/ArgumentException that is only classified as a generic page error.
unique.fail: A v8 page whose footer slot for an extend block holds position=100,length=8000 (corrupted footer). db.Rebuild() slices 8000 bytes starting at offset 100 - well past the real 200-byte segment - and appends them after the first block's bytes. The merged buffer is then parsed by BufferReader.ReadDocument, which reads field values out of unrelated page content: the document is either rejected with a misleading BSON error or reconstructed with wrong field values and inserted into the rebuilt database as if it were valid.
unique.fix: Apply the same two ENSUREs (position > 0, position + length < PAGE_SIZE, and length > DataBlock.P_BUFFER) to every block read inside the extend loop before slicing.
unique.rationale: The extend-chain loop validates only length>0, dropping the position>0 and position+length<PAGE_SIZE checks applied to the first block, so a corrupt footer splices unrelated page bytes into the middle of the reconstructed document and the rebuild may accept it as valid.

unique.title: Recovery ignores EngineSettings.ReadOnly and destructively renames/replaces a read-only database
unique.mech: `Recovery` is invoked from `LiteEngine.Open()` when `buffer[HeaderPage.P_INVALID_DATAFILE_STATE] != 0 && _settings.AutoRebuild` (LiteDB/Engine/LiteEngine.cs:113). Neither `Recovery` nor `RebuildService.Rebuild` consults `_settings.ReadOnly` at any point. `RebuildService` builds the destination engine with `new EngineSettings { Filename = tempFilename, Collation, Password }` - `ReadOnly` is not propagated, so the temp engine is fully writable - and then unconditionally performs `File.Move(logFile, backupLogFilename)`, `File.Move(_settings.Filename, backupFilename)` and `File.Move(tempFilename, _settings.Filename)` (LiteDB/Engine/Services/RebuildService.cs:88-104). By that point all read handles on the source have been closed by the enclosing `using` blocks, so the moves succeed. `EngineSettings.ReadOnly` is documented as "engine will open files in readonly mode (and will not support any database change)".
unique.fail: A process crashed earlier and left `P_INVALID_DATAFILE_STATE = 1` in `data.db`'s header. An auditing/reporting tool opens it with `new LiteDatabase("Filename=data.db;readonly=true;auto-rebuild=true")` expecting a guaranteed-nondestructive read. Instead, `Open()` runs a full rebuild: `data-log.db` becomes `data-log-backup.db`, the original `data.db` becomes `data-backup.db`, and a newly written file takes its place (with a `_rebuild_errors` collection added, since `IncludeErrorReport = true`). A reader mutated the filesystem and replaced the file another process may still be reading.
unique.fix: Refuse recovery when `_settings.ReadOnly` is set - either skip the auto-rebuild branch in `LiteEngine.Open()` (surfacing the invalid-state error to the caller) or throw a clear `LiteException` from `Recovery` explaining that a read-only database cannot be auto-rebuilt.
unique.rationale: Neither Recovery nor RebuildService consults EngineSettings.ReadOnly, so opening a flagged file read-only with auto-rebuild renames the data and log files and installs a new one - a reader mutating the filesystem, directly contradicting the documented ReadOnly contract.

unique.title: Auto-rebuild on a stream-backed database fails with ArgumentNullException from Path.Combine
unique.mech: `Recovery` does not check that `_settings` describes an OS file, unlike `LiteEngine.Rebuild` which at least tests `string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings.Filename)`. When the engine is constructed with `DataStream` set, `Filename` is null; `RebuildService.Rebuild` immediately calls `FileHelper.GetSuffixFile(_settings.Filename, "-backup", true)` (LiteDB/Engine/Services/RebuildService.cs:40), which does `Path.Combine(Path.GetDirectoryName(filename), ...)` (LiteDB/Utils/FileHelper.cs:20-23). `Path.GetDirectoryName(null)` returns null on .NET Core/5+ and `Path.Combine(null, ...)` throws `ArgumentNullException`. `Open()`'s catch calls `Close(ex)` and rethrows the raw `ArgumentNullException`.
unique.fail: `new LiteEngine(new EngineSettings { DataStream = appOwnedStream, AutoRebuild = true })` where a previous error-close wrote the recovery marker via `DiskService.MarkAsInvalidState()` into that stream's header byte 191. Every subsequent open takes the auto-rebuild branch and throws `System.ArgumentNullException: Value cannot be null. (Parameter 'path1')`, which gives the operator no hint that the real problem is an invalid-state marker plus a non-file data source. Because the marker is persisted in the stream, the database stays unopenable until `AutoRebuild` is turned off in code.
unique.fix: Guard the auto-rebuild branch in `LiteEngine.Open()` (or the top of `Recovery`) with the same file-source test used by `Rebuild`, and throw a descriptive `LiteException` ("database needs rebuild but auto-rebuild requires a file-based database") when the source is a stream, `:memory:` or `:temp:`.
unique.rationale: Recovery does not check that the settings describe an OS file, so a stream-backed engine with AutoRebuild throws ArgumentNullException from Path.Combine; because the marker persists in the stream the database stays unopenable until the code changes.

unique.title: ReadFull turns a legal short read into a bogus 'invalid datafile state' instead of completing the page read
unique.mech: Stream.Read is only contractually required to return at least one byte; ReadFull treats anything but a full PAGE_SIZE as datafile corruption. ENSURE is not compiled out (Constants.cs:151-164) and throws LiteException.InvalidDatafileState. The rented stream can legitimately return a short read for any caller-supplied Stream, because ConcurrentStream.Read (ConcurrentStream.cs:73-83) forwards exactly one underlying Read with no completion loop. ReadFull is on the startup/recovery/checkpoint path (LiteEngine.cs:103 and :126, WalIndexService.cs:202 RestoreIndex and :324 CheckpointInternal), so the misclassification hits opening the database and checkpointing. Worse, InvalidDatafileState is exactly the exception class LiteEngine.Close(ex) keys on (LiteEngine.cs:225-231): the engine responds by writing the recovery marker via MarkAsInvalidState, so a healthy file is flagged for rebuild. The same file loops correctly in MarkAsInvalidState (lines 279-284) and PromoteVectorFormat, showing the intended pattern.
unique.fail: An application uses the public Stream constructor with a Stream whose Read returns fewer bytes than requested (any stream layered over a chunked/queued source — legal Stream behaviour). On open, `_disk.ReadFull(FileOrigin.Data).First()` gets 4096 of 8192 bytes for the header page and throws LiteException 'ReadFull must read PAGE_SIZE bytes [4096]'; Open's catch calls Close(ex), which sees InvalidDatafileState and writes the invalid-state flag into the header — so a correct database is reported as corrupt and, with AutoRebuild, rebuilt on the next open.
unique.fix: Read the page in a loop until PAGE_SIZE bytes are accumulated, and only fail (with EndOfStreamException, not InvalidDatafileState) when the stream actually returns 0 before the page is complete.
unique.rationale: ReadFull treats a legal short read as corruption via a non-conditional ENSURE, and InvalidDatafileState is exactly what Close(ex) keys on - so a healthy database behind a caller-supplied stream is reported corrupt and gets the recovery marker written. The same file loops correctly elsewhere, showing the intended pattern. Shares the short-read root cause with [18]/[23].

unique.title: Checkpoint() called from inside an explicit transaction throws LockRecursionException instead of a LiteDB error
unique.mech: `_transaction` is a ReaderWriterLockSlim created with LockRecursionPolicy.NoRecursion (LockService.cs:20). A thread inside a transaction holds its read lock. EnterExclusive only short-circuits when the *write* lock is already held (line 98) and otherwise calls TryEnterWriteLock; ReaderWriterLockSlim with NoRecursion throws LockRecursionException ("Write lock may not be acquired with read lock held") rather than returning false when the calling thread holds a read lock, so the `throw LiteException.LockTimeout("exclusive", ...)` branch is never reached. WalIndexService.Checkpoint (line 272) calls EnterExclusive unguarded and is reachable from the public LiteDatabase.Checkpoint()/LiteEngine.Checkpoint(). The automatic path (TryCheckpoint) is guarded by `_transaction.IsReadLockHeld || CurrentReadCount > 0` (LockService.cs:120); the explicit path has no such guard.
unique.fail: `db.Insert(...); db.BeginTrans(); db.Checkpoint();` - the first insert leaves at least one entry in WalIndexService._confirmTransactions so the early-out at WalIndexService.cs:270 does not fire; EnterExclusive then calls TryEnterWriteLock on a thread that holds the transaction read lock and a raw System.Threading.LockRecursionException escapes the engine to the caller, bypassing LiteException/EngineState.Handle entirely.
unique.fix: In EnterExclusive, check `_transaction.IsReadLockHeld` first and throw a clear LiteException ("cannot checkpoint inside a transaction") - or have LiteEngine.Checkpoint reject the call when TransactionMonitor.GetThreadTransaction() is non-null - rather than letting ReaderWriterLockSlim raise LockRecursionException.
unique.rationale: EnterExclusive short-circuits only on IsWriteLockHeld, so Checkpoint() from a thread inside a transaction raises a raw LockRecursionException that bypasses LiteException/EngineState.Handle entirely - the TryCheckpoint path has the guard this one lacks. Canonical of the pair (fix in LockService).

unique.title: CollectionIndex slot allocation overflows a byte after index churn, giving two live indexes the same slot and corrupting the per-document index node chain
unique.mech: `InsertCollectionIndex` picks `slot = (byte)(_indexes.Max(x => x.Value.Slot) + 1)`. The guard above it only rejects `_indexes.Count == 255` and the serialized-size limit; nothing bounds the maximum *slot* value, and the `(byte)` cast wraps 256 to 0. Slots are the identity used to map an IndexNode back to its CollectionIndex: `GetCollectionIndexesSlots()` (line 151-161) builds a dense array keyed by Slot and blindly overwrites `indexes[index.Slot]`, so two indexes sharing a slot silently collapse to whichever the dictionary enumerates last. `IndexService.DeleteAll`/`DeleteList` then do `this.DeleteSingleNode(node, indexes[node.Slot])` (IndexService.cs:233, 256).
unique.fail: On one collection (PK `_id` occupies slot 0): create 254 extra indexes with 1-char names/exprs, so Count = 255 and slots are 0..254 (255 * ~24 serialized bytes = ~6.1 KB, well inside the 8096-byte limit). Drop any index other than the slot-254 one (Count = 254, Max still 254), then create a new index — it gets slot 255 and Max becomes 255. Drop any index other than the slot-255 one (Count = 254, Max still 255), then create one more index: `(byte)(255 + 1)` = 0, the same slot as `_id`. Now `GetCollectionIndexesSlots()[0]` returns whichever of `_id` and the new index the Dictionary yields last. Deleting any document walks its node chain and unlinks the `_id` node using the *other* index's Head/Tail/FreeIndexPageList, so the PK skip-list keeps a dangling node (or the wrong list is spliced). Subsequent `_id` lookups return stale or missing documents — a silent index corruption, with no error raised.
unique.fix: Allocate the lowest unused slot instead of max+1 (`for (int s = 0; s < 256; s++) if (!_indexes.Values.Any(i => i.Slot == s)) ...`), and throw when no slot is free. Same change is needed in `InsertVectorIndex` (line 229).
unique.rationale: Slot allocation is (byte)(Max+1) with only Count bounded, so index churn past slot 255 wraps to 0 and two live indexes share a slot - GetCollectionIndexesSlots then silently collapses them and deletes unlink the wrong list, corrupting the PK skip-list with no error. Sound arithmetic, but needs 255 indexes plus a specific drop/create sequence.

unique.title: AesStream.Seek adds the page offset for every origin and returns the underlying stream position instead of the logical one
unique.mech: AesStream presents a logical stream shifted PAGE_SIZE bytes into the physical file (`Position => _stream.Position - PAGE_SIZE`, `Length => _stream.Length - PAGE_SIZE`). Seek adds PAGE_SIZE to the offset unconditionally, which is only correct for SeekOrigin.Begin; for Current and End the +PAGE_SIZE is a spurious displacement. It also returns the raw underlying position, so Seek's return value disagrees with the Position property by exactly PAGE_SIZE, violating Stream's contract that Seek returns the new position within the current stream. AesStream is public API; engine code is unaffected because it only assigns Position (which routes to SeekOrigin.Begin and discards the return value).
unique.fail: `var aes = new AesStream(pwd, fileStream);` then `var p = aes.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin);` returns 8192 while `aes.Position` is 0, so any caller tracking position from the return value is off by one page. `aes.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Current)` silently advances the logical position by 8192 bytes instead of staying put, so the next Read returns the wrong page. `aes.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.End)` lands one page past the logical end: a following Read returns 0 bytes and a following Write appends a page of garbage past EOF.
unique.fix: Only offset Begin-relative seeks, translate Current/End against the logical view, and return `_stream.Seek(...) - PAGE_SIZE`.
unique.rationale: Seek adds PAGE_SIZE for every origin and returns the underlying position, so on public AesStream a Current seek silently advances a page and an End seek lands past the logical end. Contract violation on public API; engine code only assigns Position so it is unaffected.

unique.title: GetFreeIndex's byte loop wraps around forever when HighestIndex == byte.MaxValue, hanging the writer thread while it holds the collection write lock
unique.mech: `for (byte index = _startIndex; index <= this.HighestIndex; index++)` — when `HighestIndex == byte.MaxValue` the condition `index <= 255` is always true, and `index++` at 255 wraps to 0 in C#'s default unchecked context, so the loop never terminates unless some slot's 2-byte position field reads 0. Unlike `GetUsedIndexs` (line 672-677), which guards with `if (this.ItemsCount == 0) yield break;` and documents "safe for byte loop - because this.HighestIndex can't be 255", `GetFreeIndex` has no guard even though `InternalInsert` calls it precisely when `HighestIndex == byte.MaxValue` (every insert into an empty page). For a legitimately empty page the footer is all zeros (`MarkAsEmtpy` clears bytes 32..8191, `MemoryCache.NewPage` clears the whole frame) so slot 0 returns immediately; the loop only diverges on a page whose HighestIndex byte is 0xFF while the 1024-byte footer region contains no zero-valued position, i.e. a corrupt or hostile file.
unique.fail: Craft an IndexPage in a .db file with: P_HIGHEST_INDEX = 0xFF, P_ITEMS_COUNT = 1, P_USED_BYTES = U, P_FRAGMENTED_BYTES = 0, P_NEXT_FREE_POSITION = 32+U, P_INITIAL_SLOT = 0, and all 1024 footer bytes = 0xFF; point the collection index's FreeIndexPageList at it. On the next AddNode: GetFreeIndexPage passes `ENSURE(FreeBytes > bytesLength)` (FooterSize is 0 because HighestIndex == 255, so FreeBytes = 8160-U) and `ENSURE(PageListSlot == 0)`; InternalInsert's consistency gate `ENSURE(continuousBlocks == PAGE_SIZE - NextFreePosition - FooterSize - SLOT_SIZE)` also passes exactly (both sides equal 8156-U by construction); control reaches GetFreeIndex, which scans indexes 0..255, finds every position non-zero, wraps to 0 and spins at 100% CPU forever. The thread is inside the collection write lock, so every other writer on that collection blocks until its lock timeout and the file is effectively wedged for writes until the process is killed. A secondary path to the same state: `MarkAsEmtpy` resets HighestIndex to 255 but does not reset `_startIndex`, so the loop can also begin above 0 on a recycled page object.
unique.fix: Use an int loop bounded by the real slot count and bail out early: `if (this.HighestIndex == byte.MaxValue) return 0;` then `for (int index = _startIndex; index <= this.HighestIndex; index++)`. Also reset `_startIndex = 0` in `MarkAsEmtpy()` alongside the other block-information fields.
unique.rationale: GetFreeIndex's byte loop wraps forever when HighestIndex==255 and no footer position reads 0, spinning at 100% CPU inside the collection write lock. Real wedge, but it needs a crafted or corrupt page - the sibling GetUsedIndexs documents the guard this one is missing.

unique.title: ReadBytes/ReadString allocate directly from an unvalidated 32-bit on-disk length, allowing OutOfMemoryException on a corrupt file
unique.mech: `ReadBytes(int count)` allocates `new byte[count]` before any read, and `ReadString(int count)` calls `_bufferPool.Rent(count)` (BufferReader.NetCore.cs:41 / BufferReader.NetStd.cs:192) before any read. Both are driven straight from a 4-byte length read off disk by BsonElementReader: line 60-62 does `var length = reader.ReadInt32(); ... reader.ReadBytes(length);` and line 45-46 does `var length = reader.ReadInt32(); reader.ReadString(length - 1);`. There is no check that `length` is non-negative or that it is within the remaining readable bytes. The `ENSURE(count == bufferPosition, ...)` in Read() would catch the short read, but only *after* the allocation has already been attempted, and ArrayPool.Rent for a huge size allocates a fresh array rather than pooling.
unique.fail: A data block whose binary-element length field decodes to 0x7FFFFFF0 (a single flipped byte in a 4-byte length prefix is enough) makes `reader.ReadBytes(0x7FFFFFF0)` attempt `new byte[2147483632]` -> OutOfMemoryException on a 64-bit process with a normal working set, and on 32-bit it fails immediately. A negative length (0x80000000) makes `new byte[count]` throw OverflowException. Either way the caller of col.FindAll() gets OutOfMemoryException/OverflowException instead of LiteException.InvalidDatafileState, and OOM in particular can destabilise the whole host process rather than just failing the query.
unique.fix: Bound the requested size before allocating: reject negative counts and counts larger than the reader's remaining source length (or than MAX_DOCUMENT_SIZE), throwing LiteException.InvalidDatafileState.
unique.rationale: ReadBytes/ReadString allocate from an unvalidated on-disk 32-bit length before any read, so one flipped byte yields OutOfMemoryException/OverflowException instead of InvalidDatafileState - OOM in particular can destabilise the host. Corrupt-input hardening.

unique.title: BufferSliceExtensions.ReadVector trusts the on-disk element count with no bound against the slice, and page slices share one multi-page array so an overread silently returns other pages' bytes
unique.mech: `count` is a UInt16 read straight from the slice (0..65535) and the loop then reads `count * 4` bytes at `buffer.Array[buffer.Offset + offset + i*4]` with no check against `buffer.Count`. `BufferSlice`'s accessors perform no bounds validation of their own (BufferSlice.cs:39-51 just does `Array[Offset + index]`), and the cache allocates one array per *segment* of up to 128 pages -- `PageFramePool.cs:198: var buffer = new byte[PAGE_SIZE * segmentSize]` with MEMORY_SEGMENT_SIZES = {8,128}. So an inflated count does not reliably throw; it walks forward inside the same 1 MB array and quietly harvests bytes belonging to other cached pages (which may belong to other collections) into the returned float[]. Only once it passes the array end does BitConverter.ToSingle raise ArgumentException. The count is written consistently on the write path (`WriteIndexKey` -> `Write(float[])` at line 290), so this needs a corrupted/mismatched key byte to trigger -- hence low.
unique.fail: An index node holding a 2-element vector key whose stored count word is corrupted from 0x0002 to 0x07D0 (2000): `IndexNode`'s constructor -> `segment.ReadIndexKey(P_KEY)` -> `ReadVector` reads 8000 bytes starting inside page N of a 128-page cache segment, crossing into pages N+1..N+2. No exception is raised; `node.Key` becomes a 2000-element float[] built from unrelated pages' contents, which is then fed to `BsonValue.CompareTo` during the skip-list walk, producing wrong index ordering/results rather than a corruption error. (A count near 65535 instead reaches past the array and throws ArgumentException from BitConverter.ToSingle.)
unique.fix: Validate `2 + count * 4 <= buffer.Count - offset` before allocating/reading (ENSURE, which throws in Release too), and add bounds checks to BufferSlice's indexer/extensions so an off-by-one fails loudly instead of reading a neighbouring cached page.
unique.rationale: ReadVector trusts the on-disk UInt16 count with no bound against the slice, and page slices share one array per 128-page segment, so a corrupted count silently harvests other pages' bytes into the float[] and produces wrong index ordering rather than an error. Needs a corrupt key byte.

unique.title: VectorIndexNode trusts on-disk neighbour-count and inline-dimension counts, reading past the node segment
unique.mech: GetNeighbors reads a raw byte (0..255) and then reads that many 5-byte PageAddresses, although only MaxNeighborsPerLevel = 8 slots (41-byte LEVEL_STRIDE) exist per level; ReadVector (line 290) likewise trusts the ushort dimension prefix and reads 4*count bytes. BufferSlice's accessors perform no bounds checking at all (LiteDB/Utils/Extensions/BufferSliceExtensions.cs:20-45 use buffer.Array[buffer.Offset + offset] and BitConverter directly with no length assertion), so an out-of-range count reads other nodes' bytes inside the page, the page footer, or beyond the page frame in the shared pooled byte[].
unique.fail: A single flipped byte in a VectorIndexPage (torn write, bad sector) turns a level's neighbour count from 3 into 250. GetNeighbors then reads 1250 bytes starting mid-level: for a 2-dimension node the whole segment is only 180 bytes, so it returns ~250 garbage PageAddresses harvested from adjacent node data and the page footer. GreedySearch/TryFindNode feed those to GetNode -> Snapshot.GetPage, which either fails ENSURE(pageID <= _header.LastPageID) with an InvalidDatafileState exception or loads an unrelated page and throws LiteException.InvalidPageType — an unbounded read and a confusing error instead of a clean "corrupt index node" diagnosis. A corrupt ushort dimension prefix makes ReadVector read up to 256 KB past a 180-byte segment.
unique.fix: Clamp/validate on read: reject count > MaxNeighborsPerLevel and an inline length that disagrees with the segment size (and with VectorIndexMetadata.Dimensions), throwing LiteException.InvalidDatafileState. Adding ENSUREs on offset+size <= Count in the BufferSlice read helpers would catch the whole class.
unique.rationale: GetNeighbors and ReadVector trust on-disk counts (a raw byte, a ushort) against fixed 8-slot/segment sizes with no bounds-checked accessors, so one flipped byte yields garbage PageAddresses and a confusing InvalidPageType instead of a clean corrupt-node diagnosis.

unique.title: PageBuffer finalizer throws LiteException, terminating the process when a cache with pinned frames is collected without disposal
unique.mech: In DEBUG/TESTING builds `PageBuffer` declares a finalizer whose body is `ENSURE(this.ShareCounter == 0, ...)`. `Constants.ENSURE` is not `[Conditional]` -- it unconditionally `throw LiteException.InvalidDatafileState(message)`. An exception that escapes a finalizer is unhandled on the finalizer thread and terminates the .NET process; it cannot be caught by the code that dropped the object. The precondition is reachable because `MemoryCache.Dispose()` deliberately refuses to run while any frame is pinned/loading/writable: `_pool.EnsureIdleForDisposalLocked()` (MemoryCache.cs:485, PageFramePool.cs:313-318) throws BEFORE `_disposed = true`, so on that path every pinned frame keeps its non-zero ShareCounter, and `DiskService.Dispose()` has already set its own `_disposed` flag (DiskService.cs:398) so the cache can never be disposed again. The engine's shutdown paths swallow that failure into a TryCatch/AggregateException (LiteEngine.cs:198/234) and continue, after which the whole segment graph becomes unreachable with ShareCounter > 0. As a secondary cost, giving every frame a finalizer puts thousands of PageBuffer objects on the finalization queue, requiring two GC cycles to reclaim each 8 KB-backed frame.
unique.fail: In a TESTING/DEBUG build, a transaction rollback fails (e.g. `TransactionPageCleanup.ReleasePage` collects an exception) so one readable frame stays pinned with ShareCounter == 1. `LiteEngine.Close()` runs: `_monitor.Dispose()` records the error, `_disk.Dispose()` -> `_cache.Dispose()` -> `EnsureIdleForDisposalLocked()` throws InvalidOperationException, which TryCatch records; the caller sees an AggregateException and drops the engine. The MemoryCache, its PageFramePool, and all PageBuffer frames become garbage with ShareCounter == 1. On the next GC the finalizer thread runs `~PageBuffer()`, `ENSURE(1 == 0)` throws LiteException, and the test/host process dies with an unhandled exception on the finalizer thread instead of surfacing the original rollback failure.
unique.fix: Never throw from a finalizer. Wrap the check in try/catch and report via Debug.Fail / Debugger.Break / a diagnostic counter, or drop the finalizer entirely and assert leaked share counters from MemoryCache.Dispose() instead.
unique.rationale: The finalizer's ENSURE throws on the finalizer thread and terminates the process, and the precondition is reachable because MemoryCache.Dispose refuses to run with pinned frames. Confined to DEBUG/TESTING builds, so it costs test-host crashes plus a finalization-queue tax rather than production impact.

unique.title: Close()'s disposed guard is a non-atomic check-then-set, so two concurrent closes can interleave and skip the invalid-datafile marker
unique.mech: Both Close() (LiteEngine.cs:182-184) and Close(Exception) (LiteEngine.cs:219-221) guard with `if (_state.Disposed) return ...; _state.Disposed = true;` on a plain, non-volatile public bool field (EngineState.cs:16) with no interlocked operation or lock. Close(Exception) is invoked from EngineState.Handle, which runs on whatever worker thread hit the IOException / INVALID_DATAFILE_STATE inside AutoTransaction (Transaction.cs:95-105), while Close() runs on the thread calling Dispose(). Only Close(Exception) writes the recovery marker (`tc.Catch(() => _disk?.MarkAsInvalidState())`, LiteEngine.cs:227-231); Close() does not. If the plain Dispose path wins the race, the error path returns immediately and the marker is never written. The underlying services are individually idempotent (DiskService.Dispose and TransactionMonitor.Dispose both use Interlocked.Exchange), so the double-teardown itself is benign - the lost marker is the real consequence.
unique.fail: A worker thread's write transaction fails with LiteException(INVALID_DATAFILE_STATE) and enters EngineState.Handle; at the same moment the owning thread runs db.Dispose() -> Close(), which sets _state.Disposed = true. Handle's subsequent Close(ex) sees Disposed == true and returns without calling _disk.MarkAsInvalidState(), so HeaderPage.P_INVALID_DATAFILE_STATE stays 0. On the next Open() the AutoRebuild branch (LiteEngine.cs:113-130) is not taken and the known-bad file is opened as if healthy, with no recovery and no diagnostic.
unique.fix: Make the guard atomic - e.g. an int field flipped with Interlocked.Exchange(ref _disposedFlag, 1) - and hoist the invalid-state decision so it is honoured regardless of which Close overload wins.
unique.rationale: Close()'s disposed guard is a non-atomic check-then-set on a plain bool, and only Close(Exception) writes the recovery marker, so a Dispose racing an error-close silently loses the invalid-state flag. Services are individually idempotent, so the lost marker is the only real consequence.

unique.title: LiteEngine.Checkpoint() skips the engine-state check and operates on disposed services
unique.mech: Every other public engine entry point calls _state.Validate() first (Insert.cs:32, Update.cs:33, Transaction.cs:17/34/59/80, etc.), which throws LiteException.EngineDisposed or the stored close-exception. Checkpoint() forwards directly to _walIndex.Checkpoint(). After Close()/Dispose(), _walIndex is still non-null while _disk, _sortDisk and _locker are disposed, so WalIndexService.Checkpoint (Services/WalIndexService.cs:267-285) either short-circuits to 0 on the stale cached log length or reaches _locker.EnterExclusive() on a disposed ReaderWriterLockSlim.
unique.fail: db.Dispose(); db.Checkpoint(); - since Close() already performed a soft checkpoint the log length is 0, so Checkpoint() returns 0 and reports success on a disposed engine instead of throwing EngineDisposed. If the soft checkpoint was skipped or failed (log length > 0), the same call instead surfaces an ObjectDisposedException from ReaderWriterLockSlim, masking the real 'engine is disposed' condition.
unique.fix: Add _state.Validate() before delegating: `public int Checkpoint() { _state.Validate(); return _walIndex.Checkpoint(); }`.
unique.rationale: Checkpoint() is the one public entry point that skips _state.Validate(), so on a disposed engine it either reports success on stale state or surfaces ObjectDisposedException from a disposed ReaderWriterLockSlim instead of EngineDisposed.

unique.title: MarkAsInvalidState can stall error-close for 60 seconds and then silently fail to persist the recovery marker
unique.mech: FileHelper.TryExec (FileHelper.cs:75-94) retries the action for up to `timeout` seconds while the failure is a lock-type IOException (IOExceptionExtensions.WaitIfLocked rethrows anything else) and, on giving up, returns false rather than throwing. MarkAsInvalidState ignores that bool, so the caller (LiteEngine.Close(ex) at LiteEngine.cs:230, inside tc.Catch) cannot distinguish 'marker written' from 'marker never written'. The marker is the sole mechanism by which AutoRebuild learns the file needs recovery on the next open (LiteEngine.cs:112-127), so losing it silently means the engine reopens a file it already knows is in an invalid state and proceeds as if it were sound. Secondarily, the retry loop sleeps 25 ms per attempt for the full 60 s budget, so disposing/closing an engine after a fatal error can block for a minute with no diagnostic.
unique.fail: The engine hits an InvalidDatafileState error and Close(ex) calls MarkAsInvalidState while another process holds a byte-range lock on the data file (backup/AV). Every write attempt fails with a lock IOException, TryExec spins for 60 s (blocking LiteDatabase.Dispose for that whole time) and returns false, which is discarded. No error surfaces. The next open with AutoRebuild=true sees a header whose P_INVALID_DATAFILE_STATE is still 0, skips Recovery, and runs against the known-bad file.
unique.fix: Check the TryExec result and, when it is false, add an explicit exception (or at minimum a distinct error) to the close-time exception list so the failure to persist the recovery marker is reported rather than dropped.
