unique.rationale: TryExec's bool result is discarded, so error-close can block ~60s and then silently fail to persist the very marker AutoRebuild depends on, reopening a known-bad file as healthy. Narrow (needs a competing byte-range lock) but it defeats the recovery mechanism.

unique.title: Dispose materialises the log writer only to read Length, deleting the log file even for a ReadOnly engine
unique.mech: The emptiness test forces StreamPool.Writer for the log, which opens a brand new stream during disposal, and the result is used to delete a file. EngineSettings.ReadOnly is documented as 'will not support any database change', and FileStreamFactory honours it only for the FileAccess of the handle (FileStreamFactory.cs:237-241) — it does not gate Delete(). So with ReadOnly=true and a leftover zero-length db-log.db (left by a crash, or by a previous close whose delete failed), Exists() is true, the read-only handle reports Length==0, and _logFactory.Delete() unlinks the file from a read-only engine. On a read-only medium or a directory without delete rights this instead surfaces as an UnauthorizedAccessException/IOException collected into the AggregateException thrown by Dispose. For an encrypted read-only engine the same line is worse: the AesStream constructor sees Length < PAGE_SIZE, takes the isNew branch and calls _stream.WriteByte(1) on a read-only stream (AesStream.cs:62-73), so Dispose records a NotSupportedException instead of simply skipping the check.
unique.fail: A crash leaves a zero-byte db-log.db next to db.db. The file is then opened with EngineSettings { ReadOnly = true } (e.g. a monitoring/reporting process). On Dispose, DiskService opens a read-only handle to the log, observes Length==0, and deletes db-log.db — a filesystem mutation from an engine the caller explicitly opened read-only. With Password set as well, the same line instead throws NotSupportedException from inside the AesStream constructor, which becomes part of the AggregateException Dispose raises.
unique.fix: Skip the emptiness probe entirely when the writer Lazy was never created (IsValueCreated == false) or when the engine is read-only, and determine emptiness from _logFactory.GetLength()/_logLength instead of opening a new writer stream during disposal.
unique.rationale: Dispose materialises the log writer just to read Length and then deletes the file even for a ReadOnly engine - a filesystem mutation from a read-only open, or (encrypted) a NotSupportedException from the AesStream isNew branch folded into Dispose's AggregateException.

unique.title: MAX_ITEMS_COUNT is computed in wrapping uint arithmetic, producing a near-zero loop limit on very large databases
unique.mech: The cast binds to the parenthesised page count, so the multiplication is `uint * (int constant 255)`. Per C#'s constant-operand promotion rule the 255 converts to uint and the product is evaluated as unchecked uint — this is provable from the code itself, since the property type is uint and the expression compiles (a long-typed expression would not). The product therefore wraps modulo 2^32 once ((dataLength+logLength)/8192 + 10) * 255 >= 2^32, i.e. once data+log reaches roughly 16,843,010 pages ~ 138 GB. The value is consumed as an anti-infinite-loop guard by ENSURE(counter++ < _maxItemsCount) in IndexService (lines 114, 212, 231, 252, 353, 383) and DataService (line 170), where ENSURE is NOT conditional (Constants.cs:137-164) and throws LiteException.InvalidDatafileState. So the wrap does not merely weaken a debug check — it converts healthy traversals into hard 'corrupt datafile' failures, and because LiteEngine.Close(ex) treats InvalidDatafileState as a rebuild trigger (LiteEngine.cs:225-231 -> MarkAsInvalidState), a healthy large file gets flagged for AutoRebuild.
unique.fail: A database whose data file plus log reaches ~138 GB: MAX_ITEMS_COUNT wraps from 4,294,967,... to a tiny value (at the boundary it is ~0, then grows again slowly). The very first index Find/FindAll or document read that walks more nodes than the wrapped limit throws LiteException 'Detected loop in FindAll(...)' / 'Detected loop in data Read(...)' on a perfectly consistent file, so ordinary queries start failing; with AutoRebuild enabled the resulting InvalidDatafileState drives MarkAsInvalidState, and the next open performs a full unnecessary rebuild of a 138 GB file.
unique.fix: Compute in long/ulong and saturate: e.g. `var pages = ((_dataLength + _logLength) / PAGE_SIZE) + 10; var items = pages * byte.MaxValue; return items > uint.MaxValue ? uint.MaxValue : (uint)items;`
unique.rationale: MAX_ITEMS_COUNT wraps in unchecked uint arithmetic past ~138GB of data+log, and because it feeds non-conditional ENSUREs a healthy large file starts throwing 'detected loop' and gets flagged for rebuild. Real but only at extreme sizes.

unique.title: WalIndexService.Clear() resets transaction-ID and read-version bookkeeping before the log truncation that justifies it
unique.mech: Resetting `_lastTransactionID` to 0 is only safe because the log is about to be emptied - `RestoreIndex` (line 252-257) documents precisely why IDs must not be reused: "Reusing one would make its old pages appear committed." But the reset happens two statements before the truncation, and the two intervening calls can throw: `_disk.Cache.Clear()` -> `MemoryCache.Invalidate()` throws `ObjectDisposedException` via `ThrowIfDisposedLocked()` or `LiteException.InvalidDatafileState` via its `ENSURE` guards (note `ENSURE` is *not* `[Conditional("DEBUG")]` - see LiteDB/Utils/Constants.cs:137 - so those checks are live in release builds), and `_disk.SetLength(0, FileOrigin.Log)` can throw `IOException`. If either throws, the exception propagates out of `CheckpointInternal` while the engine keeps running with `_index`/`_confirmTransactions` cleared, `_lastTransactionID == 0`, and a log file that still physically contains confirmed pages from transaction IDs 1..N at positions 0..N*8192 (`_logLength` is unchanged, so new pages append after them). New transactions are then handed IDs 1, 2, 3... that collide with those still-present confirmed pages.
unique.fail: A checkpoint's `WriteDataDisk` succeeds and is fsynced, then `SetLength(0, Log)` fails with an I/O error. The engine stays open; the application keeps writing. A new transaction gets ID 1 and its commit appends a confirm page at the end of the log. The process later crashes. On reopen, `RestoreIndex` walks the log in position order: it first sees the stale, already-checkpointed pages of old transaction 1 and confirms them at read-version 1, then accumulates them again in `positions[1]` and, on hitting the *new* transaction 1's confirm page, calls `ConfirmTransaction(1, positions[1])` - republishing the stale pre-checkpoint page images at the newest read version. Reads then see page contents that were superseded before the checkpoint, i.e. committed data appears rolled back. Confidence is low because I could not prove a concrete, non-exceptional trigger for the intervening throws under the checkpoint's exclusive lock (`_pinnedPages` should be 0 there); the ordering defect itself is certain.
unique.fix: Truncate the log first and only then reset the in-memory bookkeeping, or wrap `Clear()` so that any failure after the ID reset forces the engine closed (`_state.Handle` / `Close(ex)`) instead of continuing with reusable transaction IDs over a non-empty log.
unique.rationale: The ordering defect is certain (counters reset two statements before the truncation that justifies them) but the author could not identify any non-exceptional trigger under the checkpoint's exclusive lock. Reorder the statements; do not treat the described corruption as observed.

unique.title: Snapshot constructor cleanup releases the collection write lock outside a finally, so a failure while discarding pages wedges the collection permanently
unique.mech: EnterLock(_collectionName) is taken at SnapShot.cs:76 before the try, and the only release on the failure path is this bare statement after the cleanup loop. Both loop bodies can throw: MemoryCache.DiscardPage asserts via ENSURE (always-on, Constants.cs:137) that the frame is Writable and owned (MemoryCache.cs:425-431) and dereferences page.Segment (MemoryCache.cs:328), and page.Buffer itself runs EnsurePageOwnership (BasePage.cs:755) which throws in DEBUG/TESTING builds. If any page in the batch fails, the loop aborts, the remaining PageBuffer frames are never returned to the pool, and ExitLock is skipped. CollectionLock is never re-released elsewhere for this snapshot (the snapshot never reaches TransactionService._snapshots, so TransactionPageCleanup/Dispose never see it), so the semaphore stays taken for the lifetime of the process.
unique.fail: A write snapshot is being created for collection "orders" with addIfNotExists=true; CollectionService.Add has already allocated the collection page and several index pages into _localPages when IndexService.CreateIndex fails (e.g. LiteException from InsertCollectionIndex space exhaustion, or a disk read error). If the first _disk.Cache.DiscardPage call then also fails (disposed/reclaimed frame during concurrent engine shutdown, or the DEBUG ownership assert), the remaining frames leak and ExitLock("orders") never runs. Every subsequent write to "orders" from any thread then fails with LiteException.LockTimeout("write", "orders") until the process restarts.
unique.fix: Wrap the cleanup in try/finally: aggregate per-page release failures (as TransactionPageCleanup.Release already does) and release the collection lock in the finally so lock release can never be skipped.
unique.rationale: The constructor's failure-path ExitLock sits after a cleanup loop that can throw, so a failure while discarding pages wedges the collection permanently. Needs a compound failure during snapshot creation; the fix is a one-line try/finally.

unique.title: DropCollection overwrites the transaction's existing deleted-page chain instead of appending to it
unique.mech: TransactionPages.FirstDeletedPageID/LastDeletedPageID/DeletedPages are per-transaction, shared by every snapshot in that transaction (TransactionService.cs:24 hands the same instance to each Snapshot). DropCollection assigns them absolutely rather than splicing, so any chain already built by DeletePage in the same transaction (from a prior delete on another collection, an index drop, or an earlier DropCollection) is discarded: its head pointer is lost and its old tail no longer matches LastDeletedPageID, so TransactionService.cs:175-185 never links it into _header.FreeEmptyPageList. Those pages are written to the log as Empty but become unreachable file space. Today this is unreachable because LiteEngine.DropCollection refuses to run inside an existing transaction (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Collection.cs:27, `if (_locker.IsInTransaction) throw LiteException.AlreadyExistsTransaction()`) and its AutoTransaction does nothing else, so the reset always runs on a virgin chain — it is a latent invariant break that activates the moment that guard is relaxed or Snapshot.DropCollection gains a second caller.
unique.fail: If DropCollection were permitted inside an explicit transaction (or called twice in one AutoTransaction): BEGIN; DELETE FROM a WHERE _id > 0;  /* DeletePage builds a chain of N freed pages */  DROP COLLECTION b;  COMMIT; — at commit _header.FreeEmptyPageList is set to b's chain only, and all N pages freed from collection a are permanently orphaned (Empty on disk, absent from the free list, invisible in $page_list, never reused by NewPage).
unique.fix: Splice instead of reset: keep the existing LastDeletedPageID if one is set (link the collection page's NextPageID to the current FirstDeletedPageID and only overwrite FirstDeletedPageID), and use `_transPages.DeletedPages++` rather than `= 1`.
unique.rationale: DropCollection assigns the shared transaction deleted-page chain absolutely instead of splicing, orphaning any chain already built. Unreachable today because DropCollection refuses to run inside a transaction - a latent invariant break that activates if that guard is relaxed.

unique.title: The "content area must be zero" DEBUG assertions skip the last page byte, which is the high byte of slot 0's segment position
unique.mech: `_buffer.Slice(PAGE_HEADER_SIZE, PAGE_SIZE - PAGE_HEADER_SIZE - 1)` spans bytes 32..8190 — 8159 bytes, one short of the 8160-byte content+footer area. The excluded byte 8191 is exactly the MSB of segment-0's position field, since `CalcPositionAddr(0)` = PAGE_SIZE - 4 + 2 = 8190 and the value is a little-endian UInt16 at 8190..8191. The same off-by-one is repeated in `Delete` at line 460 ("all content area must be 0"). By contrast `MarkAsEmtpy` correctly clears `PAGE_SIZE - PAGE_HEADER_SIZE` (line 285) and `Defrag`'s fill is computed from FooterSize, so the code that zeroes uses the right extent — only the assertions that verify it are short.
unique.fail: A page buffer that is clean everywhere except byte 8191 = 0x01 passes both assertions even in a DEBUG/TESTING build. `new BasePage(buffer, pageID, type)` then accepts it as a fresh page with HighestIndex = byte.MaxValue, while slot 0 reads position = 0x0100 = 256 (non-zero, i.e. "in use"). The first `Insert` on that page reaches `GetFreeIndex`, which skips index 0 as occupied and returns 1; `InternalInsert`'s `ENSURE(index == (byte)(this.HighestIndex + 1))` then computes (byte)(255+1) = 0 != 1 and aborts the insert with InvalidDatafileState. The assertion that exists specifically to catch a dirty recycled frame is blind to the one byte that causes this, so the failure surfaces later and far from its cause.
unique.fix: Drop the `- 1`: `buffer.Slice(PAGE_HEADER_SIZE, PAGE_SIZE - PAGE_HEADER_SIZE)` in both line 165 and line 460, matching the extent that `MarkAsEmtpy` actually clears.
unique.rationale: The content-area DEBUG assertions span one byte too few, excluding exactly the MSB of slot 0's position, so the assertion written to catch a dirty recycled frame is blind to the byte that causes the later InternalInsert failure. Diagnostics quality only.

unique.title: BufferReader.ReadDateTime applies the utcDate flag inverted relative to BsonElementReader
unique.mech: Both readers receive the same `_utcDate` value (it comes from `EnginePragmas.UtcDate`, threaded through SortService.cs:111/120 and DatafileLookup.cs:31), but they interpret it oppositely. `BsonElementReader.cs:88` does `return utcDate ? date : date.ToLocalTime();` -- i.e. utcDate=true means "hand back UTC". `BufferReader.ReadDateTime` does the reverse, `return _utcDate ? date.ToLocalTime() : date;`, so with the pragma ON it converts to local time and with it OFF it leaves the value in UTC. One of the two is wrong by inspection. The impact is currently masked: `ReadDateTime` is reachable only from `ReadIndexKey` (line 379), whose result is used by SortContainer for ordering, and `BsonValue.CompareTo` normalizes both operands with `if (d.Kind != DateTimeKind.Utc) d = d.ToUniversalTime()` (BsonValue.cs:616-620), so the comparison still comes out right. That normalization is what keeps this from being a wrong-results bug today.
unique.fail: Set `PRAGMA UTC_DATE = true` and ORDER BY a non-indexed DateTime field: BsonElementReader hands the document's value back as Kind=Utc (honouring the pragma) while BufferReader.ReadIndexKey hands the sort key back as Kind=Local for the same stored ticks -- the two decoders disagree about the same on-disk bytes. Any future consumer of ReadIndexKey that reads `.Kind`, formats the value, or compares it with something other than BsonValue.CompareTo (e.g. surfacing sort keys in a projection or diagnostic) gets a value shifted by the machine's UTC offset.
unique.fix: Make it match BsonElementReader: `return _utcDate ? date : date.ToLocalTime();`
unique.rationale: BufferReader.ReadDateTime applies utcDate inverted relative to BsonElementReader - one of the two is wrong by inspection - but BsonValue.CompareTo normalises both operands to UTC, so nothing observable is wrong today.

unique.title: Unvalidated VectorDistanceMetric is persisted and later throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException out of the engine, wedging the index
unique.mech: Nothing validates the metric byte on the way in or out of storage: VectorIndexOptions (LiteDB/Client/Vector/VectorIndexOptions.cs:20) only checks dimensions, CollectionPage.InsertVectorIndex passes it through, VectorIndexMetadata.UpdateBuffer writes (byte)Metric and VectorIndexMetadata(BufferReader) casts an arbitrary byte back with `(VectorDistanceMetric)reader.ReadByte()` (LiteDB/Engine/Structures/VectorIndexMetadata.cs:54). C# enums accept any underlying value, so an out-of-range metric survives a round trip to the collection page and then reaches ComputeDistance's `default:` arm, which throws a raw ArgumentOutOfRangeException rather than a LiteException.
unique.fail: collection.EnsureIndex(x => x.Embedding, new VectorIndexOptions(4, (VectorDistanceMetric)9)) succeeds and persists metric 9 in the collection page. The first insert returns early (metadata.Root is empty); the second insert reaches GreedySearch -> ComputeDistance and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException("metric") out of LiteEngine.Insert. From then on every insert, update and query against that collection throws the same low-level exception, and the only recovery is dropping the index — the bad value is already on disk. The same arm is reachable from a corrupted or forward-version metric byte.
unique.fix: Validate the metric in the VectorIndexOptions constructor (Enum.IsDefined) and again in VectorIndexMetadata(BufferReader), throwing LiteException.InvalidDatafileState for an unknown persisted value.
unique.rationale: An out-of-range VectorDistanceMetric is neither validated on input nor on read-back, so it persists in the collection page and every later insert/query throws a raw ArgumentOutOfRangeException from ComputeDistance. Requires the caller to cast a bad enum value.

unique.title: LiteStorage.Delete removes the file document before its chunks, orphaning unreachable chunk documents
unique.mech: `_files.Delete(fileId)` and `_chunks.DeleteMany(...)` are two independent implicit transactions, with the metadata removed first. Once the files document is gone there is no API path left to enumerate or delete the remaining chunks (FindById returns null, Delete's second statement is gated on `deleted`, which is now false), so the space is unreclaimable through the public API.
unique.fail: A 1 GB file (≈4000 chunks) is deleted with `storage.Delete(id)`. The files-collection delete commits; the process is killed (or DeleteMany throws, e.g. an engine/IO error) before the chunk deletion commits. On restart the file no longer appears in FindAll, but up to 4000 chunk documents holding ~1 GB remain in the chunks collection forever; calling Delete(id) again returns false without touching them, so the space is never reclaimed.
unique.fix: Delete chunks first and the files document last, and/or wrap both statements in one explicit transaction.
unique.rationale: Delete removes the files document before its chunks in a separate transaction, so an interruption leaves chunks that no API path can enumerate or reclaim - bounded space leak, no incorrect data. Same non-atomic-two-statement shape as [55].

unique.title: RenameCollection leaves the auto-id sequence cache keyed to the old collection name
unique.mech: _sequences (LiteEngine.cs:48) caches the last numeric _id per collection name. DropCollection explicitly evicts the entry (Collection.cs:42: _sequences.TryRemove(name, ...)), but RenameCollection only registers the header rename callback and never moves or removes the cached sequence. Afterwards the stale entry is still keyed by the old name, and GetSequence's AddOrUpdate (Sequence.cs:17-37) prefers the cached value over GetLastId whenever the key is present - so a freshly created, empty collection reusing the old name inherits the renamed collection's high-water mark instead of starting at 1. Entries also accumulate for names that no longer exist.
unique.fail: Collection 'a' with BsonAutoId.Int32 and 100 documents (_sequences["a"] == 100). engine.RenameCollection("a", "b") succeeds. engine.Insert("a", new[]{ new BsonDocument() }, BsonAutoId.Int32) creates a brand-new empty collection 'a', but GetSequence finds the stale cache entry and assigns _id = 101 instead of the documented 1. Any code that relies on auto-ids starting at 1 in a new collection (or on the id reflecting the row count) reads wrong values.
unique.fix: In the same AutoTransaction body, do `if (_sequences.TryRemove(collection, out var seq)) _sequences[newName] = seq;` (or simply TryRemove(collection), forcing a recompute from GetLastId).
unique.rationale: RenameCollection never moves or evicts the cached sequence (DropCollection does), so a new collection reusing the old name inherits the renamed one's high-water mark instead of starting at 1, and stale entries accumulate.

unique.title: Find/FindAll add the collection's includes twice, doubling include work per document
unique.mech: `Query()` already applies the collection's includes (`new LiteQueryable<T>(...).Include(_includes)`, line 17), and `Include(List<BsonExpression>)` does `_query.Includes.AddRange(paths)` with no de-duplication (LiteQueryable.cs:56-60). `Find(BsonExpression, ...)` (line 30) and `FindAll()` (line 98) call `.Include(_includes)` on top of that, so every path ends up twice in `Query.Includes`; `QueryOptimization.DefineIncludes` copies them verbatim into `IncludeBefore`/`IncludeAfter` with no distinct filter, and `BasePipe.Include` is therefore run twice over the result set. The second pass is a no-op for resolved refs (`$ref` was removed), but it still re-evaluates the path expression and materialises `.ToList()` for every document, and for refs that were *not* found `$ref` is kept, so the whole PK index lookup is repeated per document.
unique.fail: `var col = db.GetCollection<Order>().Include(x => x.Customer); col.FindAll().ToList();` over 100 000 orders evaluates the `$.Customer` path expression and allocates its `ToList()` 200 000 times instead of 100 000; if the referenced customers were deleted, it also performs 200 000 PK index lookups instead of 100 000 to set `$missing` twice.
unique.fix: Drop the redundant `.Include(_includes)` from `Find` and `FindAll` (Query() already applies them), or make `LiteQueryable.Include(List<BsonExpression>)` skip paths already present.
unique.rationale: Query() already applies the collection includes and Find/FindAll add them again with no de-duplication, so the include pass runs twice per document - doubled path evaluation and, for missing refs, doubled PK lookups. Cost only.

unique.title: SortService allocates an 800 KB LOH buffer per sort operation while its ArrayPool field is never used
unique.mech: `disk.ContainerSize` is `CONTAINER_SORT_SIZE = 100 * PAGE_SIZE = 819200` bytes (LiteDB/Utils/Constants.cs:100, wired in LiteEngine.cs:151). A fresh `SortService` — and therefore a fresh 819200-byte array — is constructed by `BasePipe.OrderBy` for every ORDER BY (and every GROUP BY pre-sort) that cannot be served by an index, no matter how few rows are sorted. 819200 > 85000 so each allocation goes on the Large Object Heap, which is only compacted on demand and collected with gen-2. The class already declares `_bufferPool = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` at line 36 but never reads it (SortContainer.GetSourceFromStream uses its own pool instead), so the intended pooling was left unwired. `Dispose()` simply drops the reference (`_buffer = null`, line 87).
unique.fail: A service issuing 1000 `ORDER BY <unindexed field> LIMIT 20` queries per second churns ~800 MB/s of LOH allocations for sorts that touch a handful of keys, driving repeated gen-2 collections and LOH fragmentation. Nothing is functionally wrong, but the cost is entirely avoidable.
unique.fix: Rent the container buffer from `_bufferPool` in the constructor and return it (clearArray: true) in `Dispose()`, mirroring what SortContainer.GetSourceFromStream already does for its page buffer.
unique.rationale: Every non-indexed ORDER BY/GROUP BY allocates a fresh 819200-byte LOH buffer regardless of row count, while the class's ArrayPool field is declared and never read. Pure avoidable cost with a clear intended fix.

unique.title: SortDisk.Dispose skips temp-file deletion if closing the stream pool throws
unique.mech: `StreamPool.Dispose()` collects every failure from disposing its reader streams, its writer and the factory into a list and ends with `if (errors.Count > 0) throw new AggregateException(errors);` (LiteDB/Engine/Disk/StreamPool.cs:114). Because `_factory.Delete()` is sequenced after that call with no try/finally, a single failing `Stream.Dispose()` (e.g. an IOException flushing the temp file on a full or disconnected volume) aborts `SortDisk.Dispose` before the `-tmp` sort file is unlinked. Nothing else deletes it: `SortDisk.Dispose` is the only caller of `IStreamFactory.Delete()` for the temp factory, and `LiteEngine.Dispose` does not retry.
unique.fail: Open an engine on a volume that fills up while a large ORDER BY is spilling, then dispose the engine: flushing the temp writer throws, StreamPool.Dispose rethrows it as AggregateException, and the multi-hundred-megabyte `<db>-tmp` file is left behind on disk for the lifetime of the machine. Repeated over process restarts this accumulates orphaned temp files.
unique.fix: Wrap the pool disposal so deletion always runs: `try { _pool.Dispose(); } finally { _factory.Delete(); }` (aggregating any delete failure with the pool failure rather than replacing it).
unique.rationale: _factory.Delete() is sequenced after _pool.Dispose() with no try/finally and StreamPool deliberately throws AggregateException, so one failing stream close orphans a multi-hundred-megabyte -tmp file with no diagnostic. Canonical of the pair.

unique.title: Deserialize and DeserializeArray silently ignore trailing content after the first JSON value
unique.mech: Deserialize reads one value and returns it without asserting that the next token is TokenType.EOF; DeserializeArray likewise stops at the matching CloseBracket and never checks what follows. The Tokenizer holds the rest of the reader, but nothing consults it. Malformed or truncated-and-concatenated documents are therefore accepted as valid, and the discarded remainder is invisible to the caller.
unique.fail: JsonSerializer.Deserialize("{\"a\":1} {\"b\":2}") returns {a:1} with no error, so a file that was appended to twice, or a corrupted export whose closing brace landed early, imports as a single truncated document while reporting success. JsonSerializer.Deserialize("[1,2,3]]]]") returns [1,2,3]; JsonSerializer.Deserialize("true false") returns true. SELECT JSON($.payload) reports a value rather than BsonValue.Null for such inputs, so the engine cannot distinguish well-formed from malformed JSON -- the documented purpose of that method's isJson flag.
unique.fix: After ReadValue in Deserialize (and after the CloseBracket in DeserializeArray), call _tokenizer.ReadToken().Expect(TokenType.EOF) so trailing content raises LiteException.UnexpectedToken.
unique.rationale: Deserialize/DeserializeArray never assert EOF, so concatenated or truncated-and-appended JSON is accepted as a single value and JSON($.payload) cannot distinguish well-formed from malformed input - defeating that method's isJson purpose.

unique.title: LIMIT/OFFSET use Convert.ToInt32 on the raw token, so a large integer literal escapes as System.OverflowException instead of a parse error
unique.mech: The tokenizer classifies any run of digits as `TokenType.Int` without range validation (Tokenizer.cs:581-619 — "it's accepts all number char, but not validate"), so `Expect(TokenType.Int)` passes for values far beyond Int32. `Convert.ToInt32(string)` then throws `System.OverflowException` ("Value was either too large or too small for an Int32"), which is not a `LiteException`, carries no token position, and bypasses the parser's uniform error contract. The expression parser handles the same situation gracefully by falling back to Int64 when `Int32.TryParse` fails. Identical code at Select.cs:174 for OFFSET.
unique.fail: `db.Execute("SELECT $ FROM orders LIMIT 3000000000")` (a common idiom for "no limit") throws System.OverflowException from inside LiteDatabase.Execute. Callers that catch `LiteException` to report SQL syntax errors (e.g. LiteDB.Shell's Display.WriteError, which reads `err.Position`) do not recognize it, and the user gets no indication of which token is at fault.
unique.fix: Use `int.TryParse(limit, NumberStyles.None, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out var n)` and throw `LiteException.UnexpectedToken(token, "32-bit integer")` on failure (or clamp to int.MaxValue for LIMIT).
unique.rationale: LIMIT/OFFSET use Convert.ToInt32 on a token the tokenizer never range-validates, so `LIMIT 3000000000` throws a positionless OverflowException instead of a LiteException; the expression parser already falls back to Int64 in the same situation.

unique.title: REBUILD with an options document never validates the statement terminator, so trailing input is silently ignored
unique.mech: The EOF/`;` check exists only in the no-options branch (line 27). After `new JsonReader(_tokenizer).Deserialize()` returns, ParseRebuild falls straight through to `_engine.Rebuild(options)` without consuming or checking the terminator, unlike every other command parser (Create.cs:46, Rename.cs:25, Drop.cs:27/37, Pragma.cs:42, Checkpoint.cs:19). Anything after the JSON document is therefore discarded without an error, and the destructive full-file rebuild runs.
unique.fail: `db.Execute("REBUILD {\"collation\":\"en-US/None\"} WITH PASSWORD 'x'")` performs the rebuild and reports success; the `WITH PASSWORD 'x'` fragment is silently dropped, so the user believes a password was applied when it was not. Any typo after the closing brace is likewise accepted.
unique.fix: Add `_tokenizer.ReadToken().Expect(TokenType.EOF, TokenType.SemiColon);` after the JSON branch (or once before calling Rebuild).
unique.rationale: The options branch of REBUILD never validates the statement terminator (every other command parser does), so trailing text like `WITH PASSWORD 'x'` is silently dropped while the destructive rebuild runs - the user believes a setting was applied.

unique.title: REBUILD result truncates the long byte-difference to int, reporting a wrong or negative saving for large files
unique.mech: `_engine.Rebuild` returns a `long` byte difference (`backup.Length - rebuilt.Length`, RebuildService.cs:109-111). The unchecked `(int)diff` cast wraps for magnitudes above Int32.MaxValue; LiteDB supports multi-gigabyte data files, so the reclaimed-space figure can exceed 2 GB.
unique.fail: A 10 GB data file with 3 GB of free pages is rebuilt via `db.Execute("REBUILD {...}")`. The true diff (~3.22e9) wraps to about -1.07e9, so the reader returns a negative number, telling the operator the database grew by ~1 GB when it actually shrank by 3 GB.
unique.fix: Return the value as Int64: `new BsonDataReader(diff)` (BsonValue has a long conversion).
unique.rationale: Unchecked (int) cast of the long byte difference makes REBUILD report a negative saving for multi-gigabyte reclamations. Cosmetic/reporting only; same narrowing class as [100].

unique.title: ToSQL formats the vector target and threshold with the current culture and re-appends a predicate already present in Where
unique.mech: Two defects in the same block. (1) string.Join(",", float[]) and the interpolation of VectorMaxDistance both use float/double.ToString() with CurrentCulture. In a comma-decimal culture (de-DE, fr-FR, pt-BR ...) the element separator and the decimal separator collide, so the emitted vector literal has a different length and value than the real target, and the threshold breaks the expression grammar. (2) The WhereNear predicate produced by LiteQueryable.Vector.cs:26 is already an element of Query.Where, so the vector comparison is printed twice - once from Where and once appended by this block. For TopKNear, VectorMaxDistance is double.MaxValue (LiteQueryable.Vector.cs:91), so the rendered statement claims a `<= 1.7976931348623157E+308` bound that the query never had. ToSQL output is public API and feeds the sql column of $open_cursors and the QUERY log.
unique.fail: Thread culture de-DE, col.Query().WhereNear(x => x.Embedding, new[]{1f, 0.5f}, 0.25): ToSQL renders `VECTOR_SIM($.Embedding, [1,0,5]) <= 0,25` - a three-element vector instead of two, and a threshold token that stops the expression parser at '0'. Reading $open_cursors while that query runs shows this text, and feeding it to db.Execute throws instead of reproducing the query.
unique.fix: Format with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture (e.g. v.ToString("R", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)) for both the vector elements and VectorMaxDistance, skip the appended comparison when VectorFilter is already in Where, and omit the bound when VectorMaxDistance is double.MaxValue.
unique.rationale: ToSQL formats the vector target and threshold with CurrentCulture (comma-decimal cultures collide with the element separator) and re-appends a predicate already present in Where. Diagnostics/round-trip only; overlaps [50].

unique.title: BufferSliceExtensions.ReadCString mixes slice-relative and array-absolute indices and computes a nonsensical length
unique.mech: Three index-space errors in six lines. (1) `length = buffer.Count - buffer.Offset - offset` subtracts an absolute array offset from a slice-relative count, which is meaningless and goes negative whenever `Offset + offset > Count`. (2) The scan starts at `i = offset + buffer.Offset` but dereferences `buffer[i]`, and `BufferSlice`'s indexer already adds `Offset` (BufferSlice.cs:44), so the probe lands at `Array[2*Offset + offset]` -- off by a whole `Offset`. (3) The loop bound `i < buffer.Count` compares that absolute-ish index against the slice's relative length, so for any slice with `Offset >= Count` the loop never executes at all. The final `Encoding.UTF8.GetString(buffer.Array, buffer.Offset + offset, length - 1)` then uses the bogus length. Note this is dead code today: a repo-wide grep for `ReadCString(this BufferSlice` / `.ReadCString(` on a BufferSlice finds only this definition -- the live CString readers are `BufferReader.ReadCString()` and `BufferExtensions.ReadCString(byte[])` -- which is why it is rated low rather than high.
unique.fail: Any future caller passing a page-derived slice hits it immediately: a typical index-node segment is BufferSlice{Offset=2048, Count=64}. `ReadCString(segment, 12, out var len)` computes len = 64 - 2048 - 12 = -1996, the loop `for (i = 2060; i < 64; ...)` never runs so len is never corrected, and `Encoding.UTF8.GetString(Array, 2060, -1997)` throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. With a slice at Offset=0 the scan reads the wrong bytes and can return a string that runs past the terminator.
unique.fix: Work entirely in slice-relative space: `for (var i = offset; i < buffer.Count; i++) if (buffer[i] == 0) { length = i - offset + 1; break; }` with `length` defaulting to `buffer.Count - offset`; or delete the unused method.
unique.rationale: Three index-space errors (slice-relative vs array-absolute, double-applied Offset, nonsensical length) make this overload wrong for any slice with Offset>0 - but grep shows no caller, so it is latent until someone uses it. Canonical of the pair.

unique.title: Legacy v7 ByteReader.ReadCString indexes the buffer before its bounds check, so the intended fallback is dead code
unique.mech: The loop reads `_buffer[pos]` first and only afterwards tests `pos > _length`. Since `_length == _buffer.Length`, the first out-of-range position is `pos == _length`, which throws IndexOutOfRangeException on the read at line 157 before the `pos > _length` branch on line 163 can ever be evaluated. The `return "_"` guard is therefore unreachable, and an unterminated CString produces an IndexOutOfRangeException instead of the intended graceful fallback. This path runs during the v7->v8 upgrade: LiteDB/Engine/FileReader/Legacy/BsonReader.cs:73 calls `reader.ReadCString()` for every element name of every legacy document.
unique.fail: Upgrading a truncated or partially corrupt LiteDB v7 datafile whose last data page contains an element name with no `\0` before the end of the page buffer: `FileReaderV7`/`BsonReader` reaches the end of `_buffer`, `_buffer[pos]` with `pos == _buffer.Length` throws `IndexOutOfRangeException` from deep inside the upgrade instead of the `"_"` placeholder the code intends, aborting the migration with an opaque error.
unique.fix: Check the bound first: `while (pos < _length) { if (_buffer[pos] == 0) {...} pos++; length++; } return "_";`
unique.rationale: The buffer is indexed before the bounds test, so the intended 'return "_"' fallback is unreachable and an unterminated legacy CString aborts the v7 upgrade with IndexOutOfRangeException instead. Legacy path, opaque error.

unique.title: LiteDB.Shell hangs forever and grows a string without bound when a non-terminated statement reaches EOF or --exit
unique.mech: ReadCommand() guards only the FIRST ReadLine() against null (lines 28-33). Once a line is not recognized as a shell command, it enters `while (!cmd.EndsWith(";"))` and calls the private ReadLine() again, whose null/exhaustion cases are never handled by the loop. Two exhaustion modes exist: (a) queue empty and AutoExit==false -> Console.ReadLine() returns null at EOF, so `cmd += Environment.NewLine + null` appends only a newline and the terminator can never appear; (b) queue empty and AutoExit==true -> ReadLine() returns the literal "exit" on every call, which also never ends with ';'. Either way the loop never exits, Console.Write("| ") is emitted forever, and `cmd` is re-allocated at ever-growing length (O(n^2) allocation) until the process is OOM-killed.
unique.fail:
Run the documented CLI form `LiteDB.Shell mydb.db --exec "db.mycol.find()" --exit` (no trailing semicolon, exactly as Program.cs's own usage doc describes --exec/--exit). Program.cs enqueues "open mydb.db" then "db.mycol.find()". The second command is not a shell command, so the loop starts; the queue is now empty and AutoExit is true, so ReadLine() returns "exit" every iteration and cmd becomes "db.mycol.find()
exit
exit
exit...". The shell never runs the query, never exits, spins at 100% CPU writing "| " and dies with OutOfMemoryException. The same happens for `echo 'db.mycol.find()' | LiteDB.Shell mydb.db` (EOF -> null).
unique.fix: Break out of the continuation loop when ReadLine() returns null (set Running=false/AutoExit=true and return what was read), and treat the AutoExit sentinel as end-of-input rather than as a continuation line. Use a StringBuilder for the accumulation.
unique.rationale: The continuation loop never handles ReadLine exhaustion (null at EOF, or the literal 'exit' under AutoExit), so the documented `--exec ... --exit` form without a trailing semicolon spins and grows a string until OOM. Real but confined to the Shell tool, not the library.

unique.title: CI helper script hardcodes a local-account password and creates interactive Windows accounts that survive an interrupted run
unique.mech: The script embeds a fixed plaintext credential (`Test@Password123!`) in source control and uses it with New-LocalUser to create the accounts LiteDBTest1/LiteDBTest2, adding both to the local Users group so they are real interactive logon accounts. Deletion happens only in the `finally` block's Cleanup, and Remove-TestUser swallows every failure via `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`/catch. A PowerShell process killed by Ctrl-C, a CI step timeout, an agent reboot, or a failure inside Remove-LocalUser therefore leaves permanent accounts whose password is published in a public repository. The script also Set-Acl grants those accounts FullControl over the test database under $env:TEMP.
unique.fail: A maintainer runs this script elevated on a Windows workstation or a self-hosted CI runner (it requires Administrator, per the check on line 140) and the job is cancelled after the users are created but before Cleanup completes - e.g. the CI step hits its timeout and the runner kills the process tree. LiteDBTest1 and LiteDBTest2 remain on the machine forever with the password Test@Password123! that anyone can read from GitHub; any attacker who can reach that host (RDP, SMB, WinRM, or local console) authenticates as a member of Users and obtains a local foothold for further escalation.
unique.fix: Generate a random password at runtime (e.g. from RandomNumberGenerator) instead of hardcoding one, randomise the account names per run, and register a reliable teardown (trap/Register-EngineEvent plus an idempotent pre-run sweep that deletes any leftover LiteDBTest* accounts) rather than relying solely on `finally`.
unique.rationale: A hardcoded plaintext credential in a public repo plus interactive local accounts whose deletion happens only in a finally with SilentlyContinue - an interrupted elevated run leaves permanent accounts with a published password. CI-tooling hygiene, not a product defect.

unique.title: Shell 'ed' command writes the last command - which may contain the database password - to a predictable path in the shared temp directory
unique.mech: The temp path is a constant: `Path.GetTempPath() + "LiteDB.Shell.txt"`. On Unix (the project targets net10.0, so Linux/macOS are supported) GetTempPath() returns the world-writable, world-readable shared /tmp, not a per-user directory as on Windows. File.WriteAllText then (a) creates the file with default permissions (0666 & ~umask, typically 0644, i.e. readable by every local account) and (b) follows an existing symlink at that path instead of failing. The content written is the previous history entry, and InputCommand.History records every command verbatim - including `open filename=mydb.db; password=...`, whose exact form is the documented example in Open.cs. Note the write happens before Process.Start("notepad.exe"), so it also occurs on platforms where the editor launch immediately fails.
unique.fail: Disclosure: a developer on a shared Linux host runs `open filename=/srv/app.db; password=Sup3rSecret` and then `ed`; /tmp/LiteDB.Shell.txt is created mode 0644 containing the connection string, and any other local user reads the database password. Tampering: a local attacker pre-creates the symlink /tmp/LiteDB.Shell.txt -> /home/victim/.bashrc; the next time the victim types `ed`, File.WriteAllText follows the link and overwrites .bashrc with the victim's last shell command, and the subsequent File.ReadAllText feeds that file's content back into the command queue.
unique.fix: Create the scratch file with a random name inside a per-user directory created with restrictive permissions (or use Path.GetRandomFileName plus FileMode.CreateNew so an existing symlink causes a failure rather than a follow), delete it afterwards, and avoid persisting history lines that contain a `password=` value.
unique.rationale: The shell 'ed' command writes the last command (possibly containing the connection-string password) to a fixed path in the world-readable shared /tmp and follows symlinks there. Developer-tool exposure, narrow audience.

duplicates.title: SQL `REBUILD {json}` drops the database password, rewriting an encrypted data file as plaintext
duplicates.mech: ParseRebuild builds a brand-new `RebuildOptions()` and only fills `Password`/`Collation` when the user's JSON literally contains those keys; everything else is left at the type default (`Password = null`, `Collation = null`). It never seeds the options from the database's current state. `RebuildService.Rebuild` (LiteDB/Engine/Services/RebuildService.cs:47-60) reads the *old* file through `FileReaderV8(_settings, ...)` (so with the real password) but creates the destination engine with `Password = options.Password` / `Collation = options.Collation`; a null password means the temp file is written with no AesStream at all, and a null collation means `Collation.Default` (`LCID.Current` + IgnoreCase, see DiskService.Initialize line 99). The temp file then replaces the original (RebuildService.cs:99-105). Compare `LiteEngine.Rebuild()` (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Rebuild.cs:42-48), which explicitly preserves both: `new RebuildOptions { Password = _settings.Password, Collation = new Collation(this.Pragma(Pragmas.COLLATION)) }` — that overload documents the intended defaults which this parser path does not apply. Note COLLATION is also not among the pragmas copied from the old file (RebuildService.cs:79-83).
duplicates.fail: Database opened with `Filename=data.db;Password=secret`. User runs `db.Execute("REBUILD {\"collation\":\"en-US/None\"}")` to change collation. Result: the encrypted original is renamed to `data-backup.db` and `data.db` is rewritten completely unencrypted — every document is now readable without the password. The following `this.Open()` inside LiteEngine.Rebuild then throws `LiteException.FileNotEncrypted()` (AesStream.cs:77-83) because settings still carry the password, so the caller sees an unrelated error while the plaintext file stays in place. Symmetrically, `REBUILD {"password":"newpwd"}` on a database created with `Collation=en-GB/Ordinal` silently rewrites it with the machine's current culture + IgnoreCase, changing index key ordering and equality for every string index.
duplicates.fix: Seed the options from current engine state before applying the JSON overrides (password from the engine settings, collation from `_engine.Pragma(Pragmas.COLLATION)`), i.e. mirror what `LiteEngine.Rebuild()` does, and only replace the fields the user actually specified.
duplicates.rationale: Same root cause as [11]: RebuildOptions is trusted with no fallback to _settings.Password/COLLATION. Separate entry point (SQL REBUILD) so it needs its own fix, but one defense in RebuildService closes both.

duplicates.title: SharedEngine acquires the cross-process mutex on every call but only releases it when it also opened the engine, so an explicit transaction permanently leaks mutex ownership
duplicates.mech: OpenDatabase() unconditionally does _mutex.WaitOne() (line 48), incrementing the named mutex's per-thread recursion count, but returns true only when it also created the LiteEngine. QueryDatabase() (line 264) calls CloseDatabase() - the only place ReleaseMutex() runs - solely when `opened` is true. While an explicit transaction is open (_transactionRunning == true and _engine != null), OpenDatabase() takes the mutex again and returns false, so every operation issued inside the transaction adds one unmatched acquisition. Commit()/Rollback() call CloseDatabase() exactly once, releasing only one of them. The recursion count therefore never returns to zero and the Global\...Mutex stays owned by this process for its whole lifetime.
duplicates.fail: `using var db = new LiteDatabase("file.db;connection=shared"); db.BeginTrans(); db.GetCollection<Foo>("c").Insert(foo); db.Commit();` -> WaitOne count goes 1 (BeginTrans), 2 (Insert via QueryDatabase, opened==false so no release), then Commit releases once, leaving count 1. Any other process (or another SharedEngine instance on another thread) that opens the same file in shared mode blocks forever inside OpenDatabase()'s _mutex.WaitOne(); the database file is wedged for every other participant until the first process exits.
duplicates.fix: Make mutex acquisition and release symmetric: acquire in OpenDatabase and release in CloseDatabase on every call regardless of whether the engine was created (i.e. always call CloseDatabase in the finally, and let CloseDatabase decide whether to also dispose the engine), or track the acquisition count explicitly and release it the same number of times.
duplicates.rationale: Identical defect to [157], same line, same mechanism; severity raised to match the canonical (permanent cross-process wedge, not merely a resource leak).

duplicates.title: Find's walk can advance past the tail sentinel for key types that sort above BsonType.MaxValue, returning "not found" for keys that exist
duplicates.mech: Find relies on the tail sentinel comparing greater than every real key so the walk stops before it. That invariant was broken when BsonType.Vector was added with value 100 while MaxValue is 14 (LiteDB/Document/BsonType.cs:29-30): for a Vector search value, `tailNode.Key.CompareTo(value)` reduces to `BsonType.MaxValue.CompareTo(BsonType.Vector)` == -1, which is neither `order` (so no `break`) nor 0, so the loop executes `leftNode = rightNode` with rightNode == the tail. From then on `right = tail.Next[level]` is Empty at every remaining level, the inner loop never runs again, and Find returns null. AddNode is immune because its scan is explicitly bounded by `right != index.Tail` (line 112), so a Vector-keyed node is still inserted, correctly ordered, just before the tail — the writer and the reader disagree.
duplicates.fail: Store documents with a float[] field (BsonType.Vector) and create an ordinary index on it: `col.EnsureIndex("$.embedding")`; AddNode stores the vector as the index key (IndexNode.GetKeyLength/BufferSliceExtensions.WriteIndexKey both support Vector, so up to 255 dimensions is accepted). An equality lookup whose value is a genuine BsonVector — e.g. `col.Find("$.embedding = @0", new BsonValue(new float[]{1f,2f}))`, where the parameter expression has Fields.Count == 0 so QueryOptimization picks IndexEquals -> IndexService.Find — walks to the tail at the top populated level and returns null, so the query reports zero matches even though the document and its index node exist (the only case that accidentally works is when the sought node happens to hold the index's maximum level). Confidence is low only on the query-side reachability of a Vector-typed predicate value; the traversal defect itself is certain from the code.
duplicates.fix: Bound Find's traversal with the sentinels the way AddNode does (`while (right.IsEmpty == false && right != index.Tail)` for ascending, `!= index.Head` for descending) so leftNode can never land on a sentinel; independently, give BsonType.Vector a value below MaxValue (or special-case it in BsonValue.CompareTo) so MaxValue remains the largest type.
duplicates.rationale: Same missing tail-sentinel guard as [39] (verified: MaxValue.CompareTo(Vector) == -1 so the walk steps onto the tail and returns null). One added `right != index.Tail` bound fixes both. Author admits low confidence on reaching a Vector-typed predicate value.

duplicates.title: SUM()/AVG() accumulate Int32 documents with unchecked int arithmetic, silently returning a wrapped (negative) aggregate
duplicates.mech: `SUM` seeds the accumulator with `new BsonValue(0)`, which is `BsonType.Int32`. `BsonValue.operator +` (LiteDB/Document/BsonValue.cs:468) short-circuits `Int32 + Int32` to plain `left.AsInt32 + right.AsInt32`. The project sets no `CheckForOverflowUnderflow` (see LiteDB/LiteDB.csproj and Directory.Build.props), so that addition is unchecked and the accumulator stays Int32 forever when every input is Int32. The widening path at BsonValue.cs:473 (`left.AsDecimal + right.AsDecimal` with a `Math.Max` type promotion) is only taken for *mixed* types, so an all-Int32 column never widens. `AVG` (same file, line 83) has the identical accumulator and then divides the already-wrapped sum.
duplicates.fail: Collection `c` with two documents `{v: 1500000000}` and `{v: 1500000000}` (both valid Int32). `SELECT SUM($.v) FROM c` (or the LINQ form `q.Select(x => x.V).Sum()`, mapped to `SUM(@0)` by LiteDB/Client/Mapper/Linq/TypeResolver/EnumerableResolver.cs:50) returns **-1294967296** instead of 3000000000, with no error. `SELECT AVG($.v) FROM c` returns -647483648.0. Neither result is flagged, so the caller consumes a wrong number as if correct.
duplicates.fix: Accumulate in a wider type (long/decimal) or promote the accumulator on overflow: e.g. keep a `decimal`/`long` running total and only narrow at the end, or use `checked` and widen to Int64/Decimal when the add overflows (mirroring the mixed-type promotion already present in BsonValue.operator +).
duplicates.rationale: Identical to [117], same file and line.

duplicates.title: BufferSliceExtensions.ReadIndexKey destroys BsonType.Vector (100) through the 6-bit type mask, so any vector index key is unreadable
duplicates.mech: `WriteIndexKey` stores a vector key as a plain type byte `(byte)BsonType.Vector` = 100 = 0b0110_0100 followed by a UInt16 count and the floats (line 348 + line 382). `ReadIndexKey` decodes the type through `ExtendedLengthHelper.ReadLength`, which does `bsonType = (byte)(typeByte & 0b0011_1111)` (ExtendedLengthHelper.cs:21) because the top 2 bits are reserved as length-extension bits for string/binary. 100 & 63 = 36, which is not a member of BsonType, so the `case BsonType.Vector` at line 196 is dead code and the switch falls to `default: throw new NotImplementedException();` at line 198. The extended-length encoding is structurally incompatible with any BsonType value >= 64, and Vector = 100. Nothing upstream rejects a vector as an ordinary (non-vector) index key: `IndexService.AddNode` only rejects MinValue/MaxValue and a keyLength > 1023 (IndexService.cs:67 and :91); `Snapshot.CheckVectorVersion` merely promotes the file format. `IndexNode`'s read constructor eagerly decodes the key (`this.Key = segment.ReadIndexKey(P_KEY)`, IndexNode.cs:126) on every `IndexService.GetNode` -> `IndexPage.GetIndexNode`, so the node cannot be read back at all.
duplicates.fail: Create a regular (non-vector) index over a float[] field and insert more than one document: using var db = new LiteDatabase(":memory:"); var col = db.GetCollection<VectorDoc>("v"); col.Insert(new VectorDoc{Id=1,Embedding=new[]{1f,0f}}); col.Insert(new VectorDoc{Id=2,Embedding=new[]{0f,1f}}); col.EnsureIndex("Embedding", "Embedding"); -- LiteEngine.EnsureIndex (Engine/Index.cs:72) calls indexer.AddNode for each document. The first AddNode only walks head->tail, so it succeeds and writes a node with typeByte 100 and keyLength 1+2+8=11. The second AddNode does `leftNode = GetNode(index.Head)` and then, at level 0, `right = head.Next[0]` = node 1 (not empty, not tail), so `rightNode = this.GetNode(right)` constructs an IndexNode, which runs `segment.ReadIndexKey(P_KEY)` on the vector key -> type (BsonType)36 -> System.NotImplementedException escapes out of EnsureIndex mid-transaction. LiteDB.Tests/BsonValue/BsonVector_Tests.cs:67 exercises exactly this shape (EnsureIndex("Embedding","Embedding") after three inserts), so that test should currently be failing; I could not execute it (no dotnet toolchain in this environment), hence medium confidence on "no higher-layer guard" rather than on the decoding arithmetic, which is certain.
duplicates.fix: Either reject Vector (and any BsonType >= 64) as an ordinary index key at IndexService.AddNode with a clear LiteException, or stop routing non-string/non-binary types through the 6-bit mask: read the raw type byte first and only call ExtendedLengthHelper.ReadLength when the low 6 bits are String or Binary.
duplicates.rationale: Same 6-bit mask defect as [172], described from the ReadIndexKey side; one fix (widen the framing or reject Vector keys) closes both.

duplicates.title: GetFreeVectorPage trusts an index-page free-list threshold (1400 bytes) for vector nodes that can be up to 8156 bytes, so insert throws once a listed page has 1400..length free bytes
duplicates.mech: GetFreeVectorPage assumes "page is on the vector free list" implies "page has room for any vector node". That invariant is enforced by VectorIndexPage.FreeListSlot (LiteDB/Engine/Pages/VectorIndexPage.cs:50): slot 0 iff FreeBytes >= MAX_INDEX_LENGTH (1400, Constants.cs:60). AddOrRemoveFreeVectorList (SnapShot.cs:495) keeps a page in slot 0 while FreeBytes >= 1400. That threshold was chosen for *index* nodes, whose maximum size is INDEX_NODE_FIXED_SIZE(12) + 32*10 + 1023 = 1355 < 1400 — which is why the identical code in GetFreeIndexPage is safe. Vector nodes are not bounded by 1400: VectorIndexNode.GetLength returns 172 + 4*dimensions inline for any dimensions <= 1996 (VectorIndexNode.cs:113). There is no dimension cap anywhere except dimensions > 0 and the ushort type. So for dimensions > 307 the node length exceeds the slot-0 threshold and a page can sit on the free list with less free space than one node needs. ENSURE is not [Conditional] (Constants.cs:137), so it throws LiteException.InvalidDatafileState in Release builds; even if it were removed, BasePage.InternalInsert would throw LiteException.InvalidFreeSpacePage (BasePage.cs:346).
duplicates.fail: col.EnsureIndex(x => x.Embedding, new VectorIndexOptions(1536, VectorDistanceMetric.Cosine)) — a standard OpenAI text-embedding-3-small size. Node length = 172 + 4*1536 = 6316. Insert doc #1: metadata.Reserved == uint.MaxValue so NewPage<VectorIndexPage>() is used; after InsertNode, FreeBytes = 8192-32-6316-4 = 1840; AddOrRemoveFreeVectorList sees FreeListSlot(1840) == 0 and links the page into metadata.Reserved with PageListSlot = 0. Insert doc #2: VectorIndexService.Insert calls GetFreeVectorPage(6316, ref metadata.Reserved), which takes that page and evaluates ENSURE(1840 > 6316) -> false -> throws LiteException "this page shout be space enouth for this new vector node", aborting the insert and rolling back the transaction. The vector index is permanently unusable beyond one document. Other affected sizes (fail as soon as FreeBytes lands in [1400, length]): 512 dims fails on the 4th insert (FreeBytes 1488 vs length 2220), 768 dims fails on the 3rd (1664 vs 3244). Existing tests never catch this because they use 2, 3 or 32 dimensions (LiteDB.Tests/Engine/VectorMemoryManagement_Tests.cs:15), all below the 307-dimension threshold.
duplicates.fix: Give vector pages their own slot threshold based on the maximum vector node size for that index (or a per-length check), e.g. have AddOrRemoveFreeVectorList/FreeListSlot keep a page on the list only while FreeBytes >= the index's node length + SLOT_SIZE, and in GetFreeVectorPage fall back to NewPage<VectorIndexPage>() when the listed head cannot fit bytesLength instead of asserting.
duplicates.rationale: Same defect as [42] reported from the GetFreeVectorPage/ENSURE side.

duplicates.title: VectorIndexPage free-list threshold uses MAX_INDEX_LENGTH (1400) instead of the vector node size, so vector inserts throw LiteException for all common embedding dimensions
duplicates.mech: `VectorIndexPage.FreeListSlot` copies `IndexPage.FreeIndexSlot`'s rule verbatim: a page stays in the free list (slot 0) whenever `FreeBytes >= MAX_INDEX_LENGTH` (1400). That constant is the upper bound of a *b-tree* index node (INDEX_NODE_FIXED_SIZE 12 + 32*2*5 + key<=1023 = 1355 max), so the rule is sound for IndexPage. A vector node is `VectorIndexNode.GetLength` = 5 + 1 + (4 * (1 + 8*5)) + 2 + dimensions*4 = 172 + 4*dimensions bytes, which is inline (not spilled to a data page) for dimensions <= 1996 and can be up to 8156 bytes. So a vector index page whose free space has dropped to e.g. 1488 bytes is still reported as slot 0 and stays the head of `metadata.Reserved`. On the next insert `Snapshot.GetFreeVectorPage` (LiteDB/Engine/Services/SnapShot.cs:361) does `ENSURE(page.FreeBytes > bytesLength, "this page shout be space enouth for this new vector node")`. `ENSURE` is NOT `[Conditional]` (LiteDB/Utils/Constants.cs:137) — it is live in Release and throws `LiteException.InvalidDatafileState`. There is no fallback to `NewPage<VectorIndexPage>()`, so the exception propagates out of `VectorIndexService.Insert` (which only releases the external vector and rethrows) to the caller.
duplicates.fail:
Create a vector index with 512 dimensions (node length L = 172 + 2048 = 2220; each insert also consumes a 4-byte footer slot). Insert documents one at a time into a fresh VectorIndexPage (FreeBytes = 8192-32 = 8160):
  after doc1: FreeBytes = 8160 - 2224 = 5936 -> FreeListSlot = 0, page kept as free-list head
  after doc2: FreeBytes = 3712 -> slot 0, kept
  after doc3: FreeBytes = 1488 -> 1488 >= 1400, so still slot 0, kept
  doc4: GetFreeVectorPage(2220) fetches that page and evaluates ENSURE(1488 > 2220) -> false -> throws LiteException "this page shout be space enouth for this new vector node".
The 4th document insert fails with an InvalidDatafileState error on a perfectly healthy database. The same happens at doc3 for 768 dims (FreeBytes 1664 vs node 3244), at doc2 for 1024 dims (3888 vs 4268) and at doc2 for 1536 dims (1840 vs 6316). Every dimension count >= 307 can hit this; 512/768/1024/1536 — i.e. essentially every real embedding size — reliably do. The existing tests only use 6/8 dims (node < 1400, page leaves the list before it can be over-subscribed) and one 20376-dim case (spilled out of page, node = 177 bytes), which is why the window 307..1996 is uncovered.
duplicates.fix: The free-list predicate must be relative to the node size that will be stored, not a b-tree constant. Either (a) pass the required length in and keep the page listed only while `FreeBytes >= required + SLOT_SIZE`, (b) use per-dimension threshold `VectorIndexNode.GetLength(metadata.Dimensions, out _) + BasePage.SLOT_SIZE`, or (c) make `GetFreeVectorPage` fall back to `NewPage<VectorIndexPage>()` (and unlink the exhausted page) instead of asserting.
duplicates.rationale: Same defect as [42], same VectorIndexPage.cs:52 threshold.

duplicates.title: External-merge-sort key reader cannot decode extended-length keys: any ORDER BY whose key string is >= 256 bytes throws NotImplementedException
duplicates.mech: Sort keys are serialized with `BufferSlice.WriteIndexKey` (LiteDB/Utils/Extensions/BufferSliceExtensions.cs:321), which for String/Binary calls `ExtendedLengthHelper.WriteLength` and packs the two most-significant length bits into the *type* byte (`typeByte = lengthMSByte | bsonType`, LiteDB/Utils/ExtendedLengthHelper.cs:31-39). There are two readers for that format and only one of them understands it: `BufferSlice.ReadIndexKey(offset)` (BufferSliceExtensions.cs:155) calls `ExtendedLengthHelper.ReadLength`, but `BufferReader.ReadIndexKey()` (LiteDB/Engine/Disk/Serializer/BufferReader.cs:354-388) does `var type = (BsonType)this.ReadByte();` and then `this.ReadString(this.ReadByte())` — it never masks off the two borrowed length bits and only reads an 8-bit length. `SortContainer` is wired to the second (broken) reader in both of its modes: `InitializeReader` builds a `BufferReader` over the stream or over the in-memory BufferSlice (SortContainer.cs:91-103), and `MoveNext` reads keys with it. For a String key of N UTF-8 bytes with 256 <= N <= 1021, WriteLength sets lengthMSByte to 0x40/0x80/0xC0, so the byte read back is 70/134/198 (or 73/137/201 for Binary). None of those match any BsonType (0..14, 100), so the switch falls through to `default: throw new NotImplementedException();`. The guard in SortContainer.Insert only rejects keys above MAX_INDEX_KEY_LENGTH (1023), so the whole 256..1021 band is written and then cannot be read back. Regular index nodes are unaffected because IndexNode reads its key through `segment.ReadIndexKey(P_KEY)` (LiteDB/Engine/Structures/IndexNode.cs:126), the extended-length-aware reader.
duplicates.fail: Create a collection with a text field longer than 255 UTF-8 bytes and no index on it: `col.Insert(new BsonDocument { ["_id"]=1, ["body"]=new string('x',300) })` (3 documents is enough — the single-container in-memory path uses the same BufferReader). Run `db.Execute("SELECT $._id FROM col ORDER BY $.body")`. QueryOptimization sets QueryPlan.OrderBy, BasePipe.OrderBy (BasePipe.cs:160-185) feeds the 300-byte string keys into SortService/SortContainer, and the first `sorter.Sort()` -> `SortContainer.MoveNext()` -> `BufferReader.ReadIndexKey()` reads type byte 70 and throws `NotImplementedException`. The query fails with an unrelated, unactionable exception; the same ORDER BY over a <256-byte value works. The same crash hits GROUP BY (GroupByPipe.cs:42 sorts by the group expression) whenever the group key is a >=256-byte string.
duplicates.fix: Make `BufferReader.ReadIndexKey()` use `ExtendedLengthHelper.ReadLength(typeByte, lengthByte, out type, out len)` exactly as `BufferSlice.ReadIndexKey` does, so the two writers/readers of the index-key format stay symmetric.
duplicates.rationale: Same reader/writer framing mismatch as [25], reported from SortContainer.MoveNext.

duplicates.title: LiteFileStream write mode deletes all chunks but persists the reset metadata only on Flush, leaving Length>0/Chunks=0 on disk
duplicates.mech: The write-mode constructor deletes every chunk of an existing file through `_chunks.DeleteMany(...)`, which goes through `_engine.DeleteMany` -> `AutoTransaction` and is therefore committed immediately, while the matching `_file.Length = 0; _file.Chunks = 0;` are only in-memory field writes. The `_files` document is written back solely from `WriteChunks(flush: true)` (LiteFileStream.Write.cs:66-72), i.e. only from `Flush()`/`Dispose()`. If the stream is never flushed (the caller's upload loop throws, the process is torn down, or the stream is simply abandoned), the persisted `_files` row keeps the old `length`/`chunks` while no chunk exists. Reads then break silently: `Read` (LiteFileStream.Read.cs:12-42) starts with `_currentChunkData == null` (ctor GetChunkData(0) returned null), the `while (_currentChunkData != null ...)` body never executes and it returns `count - bytesLeft == 0` — indistinguishable from EOF. Seeking is worse: `SetReadStreamPosition` passes the `newPosition >= Length` guard, then dereferences the missing chunk at `seekStreamPosition += _currentChunkData.Length` (LiteFileStream.Read.cs:86).
duplicates.fail:
```
// existing 1 MB file "f1" with 4 chunks
var w = db.FileStorage.OpenWrite("f1", "f1.bin");   // chunks deleted + committed here
source.CopyTo(w);                                   // throws (network/IO error) -> w never disposed
```
Afterwards `db.FileStorage.FindById("f1").Length` still reports 1048576 and `chunks = 4`. `db.FileStorage.Download("f1", dest)` completes successfully and writes **zero bytes** to `dest`, returning a LiteFileInfo that claims 1 MB — silent data loss reported as success. And `using var r = db.FileStorage.OpenRead("f1"); r.Seek(1, SeekOrigin.Begin);` throws NullReferenceException from LiteFileStream.Read.cs:86.
duplicates.fix: Upsert the reset `_files` document in the same logical operation as the chunk delete (wrap both in an explicit transaction, or `_files.Upsert(_file)` right after resetting Length/Chunks), and make `GetChunkData`/`SetReadStreamPosition` fail loudly (or clamp to the real chunk total) when metadata and chunks disagree instead of NRE-ing / reporting EOF.
duplicates.rationale: Same defect and line as [55]; [55] additionally captures the ENSURE retry poisoning.

duplicates.title: JsonReader recurses once per nesting level with no depth limit, so untrusted JSON kills the process with StackOverflowException
duplicates.mech: ReadValue() dispatches OpenBrace -> ReadObject() and OpenBracket -> ReadArray(); both call ReadValue() again for each member (line 134 and line 155). Nesting depth in the input maps 1:1 to CLR stack depth and there is no depth counter or configurable limit anywhere in JsonReader or Tokenizer (grep for depth/MAX_ in Document/Json returns nothing). Since .NET Core, StackOverflowException cannot be caught: the runtime fails fast and terminates the process, so no try/catch in the hosting application can contain it. This is the parser behind the public LiteDB.JsonSerializer.Deserialize API and behind document literals in the SQL layer, both of which routinely receive caller-supplied text.
duplicates.fail: An application that imports user-supplied JSON via `LiteDB.JsonSerializer.Deserialize(text)` (or executes `INSERT INTO col VALUES <json>` built from user text) is handed a ~100 KB body consisting of 100000 '[' characters. ReadValue/ReadArray recurse 100000 frames deep, the 1 MB default stack is exhausted, and the whole host process is terminated immediately with 'Stack overflow' - a single small request takes the service down, and no exception handler or transaction rollback runs.
duplicates.fix: Thread a depth counter through ReadValue/ReadObject/ReadArray and throw a LiteException (e.g. UnexpectedToken/'depth limit exceeded') beyond a fixed maximum (System.Text.Json defaults to 64), or rewrite the reader with an explicit stack.
duplicates.rationale: Same unbounded JsonReader recursion as [125].

duplicates.title: SharedEngine.Query leaves the shared mutex held and the engine open when the underlying query throws
duplicates.mech: Every other SharedEngine operation routes through QueryDatabase(), which wraps the call in try/finally. Query() instead calls OpenDatabase() and then _engine.Query(...) with no try/catch: the CloseDatabase callback is only handed to the returned SharedDataReader. LiteEngine.Query throws synchronously on several realistic inputs (ArgumentNullException for a blank collection, GetSystemCollection for an unknown "$xxx" name, ObjectDisposedException/LiteException from TransactionMonitor.GetTransaction, LockTimeout from Snapshot creation). When it throws, the SharedDataReader is never constructed, so CloseDatabase() never runs: the named mutex acquisition made at line 144 is never released and the LiteEngine instance (with its open file handles) is never disposed.
duplicates.fail: With `connection=shared`, run `db.Execute("SELECT $ FROM $no_such_system_collection")` (or any query whose planning throws, e.g. a LockTimeout). SharedEngine.Query has already taken the mutex and created the engine; the exception propagates to the caller and the process keeps the Global mutex owned plus the data/log FileStreams open forever. A second process opening the same database in shared mode then blocks indefinitely in OpenDatabase().
duplicates.fix: Wrap `_engine.Query(...)` in try/catch and call CloseDatabase() (when opened) before rethrowing, mirroring QueryDatabase().
duplicates.rationale: Same missing try/finally in SharedEngine.Query as [158].

duplicates.title: Encrypted data files use AES in ECB mode, so identical page content yields identical ciphertext and blocks are freely splice-able
duplicates.mech: The engine's at-rest encryption sets `_aes.Mode = CipherMode.ECB` with `PaddingMode.None`, then reuses one _encryptor/_decryptor transform for every page at every file offset (the IV derived on line 99 is silently ignored by ECB). ECB is deterministic per 16-byte block under a fixed key: any two 16-byte plaintext blocks that are equal anywhere in the file encrypt to the same ciphertext, and every block decrypts independently of its position. There is also no MAC over the ciphertext. The result is (a) large-scale plaintext-structure leakage from a stolen .db file and (b) position-independent malleability: an attacker with write access to the file can copy, duplicate or reorder 16-byte ciphertext blocks and every one of them still decrypts to valid plaintext.
duplicates.fail: A user protects a LiteDB file with `password=...` and the file is exfiltrated from a backup. Because every page is ECB-encrypted with the same key, an analyst sees repeated ciphertext blocks wherever repeated plaintext exists - e.g. a `status` field that is either 'active' or 'revoked' in every document produces exactly two distinct ciphertext blocks at the same intra-document offset, so the analyst learns each record's status and the total counts without the password. Separately, an attacker with file write access can copy the 16-byte ciphertext block holding 'role=admin' from their own record over the corresponding block of another record; the engine decrypts it without error (there is no integrity check), silently granting the privilege.
duplicates.fix: Use a position-tweaked mode suited to random-access block storage - AES-CTR with a nonce derived from the page number, or AES-XTS with the page index as the tweak - and add a per-page authentication tag (or at minimum a keyed checksum) so tampering is detected. ECB should not be used even though pages are accessed at random offsets.
duplicates.rationale: Same ECB/no-integrity design as [57], same line.

duplicates.title: IndexCost coerces a LIKE operand with BsonValue.AsString without a type check, so an indexed LIKE against a non-string/null constant throws InvalidCastException/NullReferenceException from the planner
duplicates.mech: `BsonValue.AsString` is `(string)this.RawValue` (LiteDB/Document/BsonValue.cs:233) — an unchecked unbox-and-cast, not a conversion. `ChooseIndex` only requires `expr.Right.IsValue` (i.e. the operand has no document fields), never that it is a string, so `CreateIndex` is reached with any constant. For a numeric/boolean/date constant `(string)RawValue` throws `InvalidCastException`. For a null constant, `AsString` yields null, the implicit `string -> BsonValue` conversion produces `BsonType.Null` with `RawValue == null` (BsonValue.cs:80-84), and the `IndexLike` constructor then does `_pattern = value.AsString; _pattern.SqlLikeStartsWith(out _testSqlLike)` (LiteDB/Engine/Query/IndexQuery/IndexLike.cs:18-19) where `SqlLikeStartsWith` dereferences `str.Length` immediately (LiteDB/Utils/Extensions/StringExtensions.cs:175) -> NullReferenceException. The exception escapes during query *planning*, before any pipe runs, so it is not attributable to the user's expression in the message.
duplicates.fail: `col.EnsureIndex("name"); db.Execute("SELECT $ FROM col WHERE $.name LIKE 5")` -> ChooseIndex matches the `name` index because `5` satisfies `expr.Right.IsValue`, `IndexCost.CreateIndex` runs the Like branch and throws `InvalidCastException: Unable to cast object of type 'System.Int32' to type 'System.String'`. With a parameterised pattern bound to null (`... WHERE $.name LIKE @0`, @0 = null) the same path throws NullReferenceException from inside SqlLikeStartsWith. Dropping the index on `name` makes both queries stop crashing, which makes the failure look like index corruption.
duplicates.fix: Guard the Like branch: if the operand is not `IsString`, either fall back to a non-index plan (return null so the term stays a filter) or throw a descriptive LiteException naming the expression and the required operand type.
duplicates.rationale: Same unchecked AsString coercion as [67], reported at the IndexCost.CreateIndex call site.

duplicates.title: SUM/AVG throw OverflowException when the first numeric value exceeds Decimal range or is NaN/Infinity
duplicates.mech: The accumulator is seeded as Int32 0, so the first addition always has mismatched operand types (Int32 vs Double/Decimal/Int64) and therefore falls through every fast path of `BsonValue.operator+` into `var result = left.AsDecimal + right.AsDecimal;` (LiteDB/Document/BsonValue.cs:473). `AsDecimal` is `Convert.ToDecimal(RawValue)`, which throws OverflowException for any double whose magnitude exceeds ~7.9228e28, and for double.NaN / ±Infinity. A pure Double sequence would never need decimal conversion — it is only the Int32 seed that forces it.
duplicates.fail: Collection `readings` whose first document has the Double field `v = 1e30` (or `v` = double.PositiveInfinity / NaN produced by an earlier computed update). `SELECT SUM($.v) FROM readings` → `Convert.ToDecimal(1e30)` → `System.OverflowException: Value was either too large or too small for a Decimal`, thrown out of the query instead of returning 1e30. `AVG($.v)` fails identically. Rewriting the same data so a small double comes first makes the query succeed, which makes the failure look nondeterministic.
duplicates.fix: Seed the accumulator from the first element (or seed as Double when the sequence contains doubles) so that homogeneous Double sequences never route through the Decimal conversion path.
duplicates.rationale: Same Convert.ToDecimal routing as [190]; the Int32 seed in SUM/AVG is what forces the mixed-type path on the first addition.

duplicates.title: Int32 auto-id narrows a 64-bit sequence with an unchecked (int) cast, silently producing a negative _id
duplicates.mech: `_sequences` stores the sequence as `long` and increments it as `long` (`lastId.AsInt64 + 1`, `value + 1`). For `BsonAutoId.Int32` the result is narrowed with an unchecked `(int)` cast. `SetSequence` (same file, line 48) raises the cached sequence to any explicitly inserted numeric `_id`, so the sequence can be pushed to int.MaxValue without inserting 2^31 documents. The generated value is then not Null/MinValue/MaxValue, so `InsertDocument`'s validity check (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Insert.cs:65) passes and the wrapped id is persisted.
duplicates.fail: On a collection with `BsonAutoId.Int32` (the default for `int`-keyed entities): insert `{_id: 2147483647, name:'x'}` explicitly — `SetSequence` sets the cached sequence to 2147483647. Then insert a document with no `_id`: `GetSequence` computes `next = 2147483648L`, and `(int)next` wraps to **-2147483648**, which is stored as the document's `_id`. The caller believes it got the next id after int.MaxValue; instead every subsequent auto-id walks upward from int.MinValue, and after enough inserts collides with existing small ids and fails with IndexDuplicateKey.
duplicates.fix: Throw a LiteException when `autoId == BsonAutoId.Int32 && next > int.MaxValue` ("Int32 auto-id sequence exhausted") instead of wrapping, e.g. `checked((int)next)` wrapped in a clear error.
duplicates.rationale: Identical to [79], same file and line.

duplicates.title: DropIndex leaks every page owned by the dropped index - pages are emptied but never returned to the free page list
duplicates.mech: Index.cs:205 delegates to IndexService.DropIndex (LiteDB/Engine/Services/IndexService.cs:303-338). That method removes each node with `node.Page.DeleteIndexNode(node.Position.Index)` and finally deletes the head/tail nodes, but it never calls Snapshot.AddOrRemoveFreeIndexList or Snapshot.DeletePage. BasePage.Delete (Pages/BasePage.cs:406-466) only zeroes the segment and resets counters; it does not reclaim the page. Because index pages are effectively private to one index (each CollectionIndex has its own FreeIndexPageList, seeded by a fresh NewPage in IndexService.CreateIndex:38), every page that held only this index's nodes ends up with ItemsCount == 0, PageType still Index, and is linked into the dropped index's FreeIndexPageList - which is discarded together with the CollectionIndex entry by DeleteCollectionIndex. They are therefore never added to _header.FreeEmptyPageList and can never be allocated again by Snapshot.NewPage/TryAllocateFreePage. Contrast Snapshot.DropCollection (Services/SnapShot.cs:702-739), which explicitly marks each index/data page empty and chains it into _transPages.FirstDeletedPageID; a later DropCollection will not find these orphans either, since they are no longer reachable from any index head or from FreeDataPageList.
duplicates.fail: Collection with 200k documents; col.EnsureIndex("name", "$.name") allocates roughly 3-4k index pages (about 30 MB). col.DropIndex("name") leaves all of those pages allocated, empty and unreachable - the data file does not shrink and the space is never reused. A maintenance job that drops and recreates the index (e.g. nightly, or on each app start with a changed expression) grows the file by that amount on every cycle; the only recovery is LiteDatabase.Rebuild().
